README: Update to preferable coverage pattern for Rails

Preferred Rails configuration, as noted in the [Rails profile](https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/blob/main/lib/simplecov/profiles/rails.rb#L22)

Synthesize branch and method coverage for unloaded files

`SimulateCoverage` used to leave `branches` and `methods` as empty
hashes for files added via `cover` / `track_files` that were never
`require`'d during the run, on the rationale that "parsing source
ourselves" felt risky. That left those files invisible to the branch
and method denominators while their lines DID count — so a glob like
`cover "{app,lib}/**/*.rb"` over a project with files lacking specs
silently inflated branch% relative to line%. The OP's reproduction was
via SonarQube, which surfaces the asymmetry more visibly than the
SimpleCov HTML report.

A new `SimpleCov::StaticCoverageExtractor` walks the AST with Prism and
emits Coverage-shaped tuples without loading the file. Output matches
Ruby's own `Coverage.result` byte-for-byte for branches (every
`:if` / `:case` / `:while` / `:until` construct with its `:then` /
`:else` / `:when` / `:in` / `:body` arms, including the synthetic
`:else` that `ignore_branches :implicit_else` targets) and near-perfectly
for methods (the only difference is the class-name slot, which we
report as a string since we can't resolve the actual Class constant
without loading).

Prism is bundled with Ruby 3.3+. On older Rubies the require fails
gracefully — `StaticCoverageExtractor.available?` returns false and
SimulateCoverage falls back to the previous "empty hashes" behavior,
so the upgrade is a no-op for those Rubies (users who want the fix
can `gem install prism`).

The extractor is tested directly against Coverage's output shape for
each construct (`if`, `case/when`, `case/in`, `while`, postfix-if,
ternary) and the methods enumeration covers top-level, instance,
namespaced, and singleton-class shapes. SimulateCoverage's existing
behavior specs are updated to reflect the new hash-shape contract.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1059.

Pluggable parallel-test-runner adapter interface

Coordination with parallel test runners (picking the "final" worker,
waiting for siblings, knowing how many resultsets to expect) used to
hard-code the parallel_tests gem. Env-var-only runners like
parallel_rspec hit the wrong branch of `final_result_process?` and every
worker thought it was the final one. They clobbered each other's
resultsets.

Introduce `SimpleCov::ParallelAdapters`, a small registry and selection
layer with a four-method contract (`active?`, `first_worker?`,
`wait_for_siblings`, `expected_worker_count`). `ParallelTestsAdapter`
wraps the historical gem API. `GenericAdapter` handles the env-var
convention without needing any specific gem. Adapters are tried in
registration order, and the first whose `active?` returns true is
chosen. parallel_rspec works out of the box, and users with custom
runners can plug in their own adapter via:

    SimpleCov::ParallelAdapters.register MyAdapter

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1065.

Add :eval_generated filter for ignore_branches and ignore_methods

Rails delegate (and other module_eval / class_eval / instance_eval
macros that pass __FILE__ and __LINE__) inject method and branch entries
into a file's coverage data even when the static source has nothing at
that line. Ruby's Coverage library attributes the eval'd code to the
caller's position, so a single delegate call shows up as a missed def
and a missed if branch wherever the macro fires. The previous workaround
was to disable eval coverage entirely, which loses the legitimate
signal.

Adds the :eval_generated token to SimpleCov.ignore_branches and adds a
new SimpleCov.ignore_methods with the same token. Both filters walk the
static source through SimpleCov::StaticCoverageExtractor (Prism) and
drop any Coverage tuple whose start line lacks a real def keyword (for
methods) or branch construct (for branches). Line presence is the
matcher, so a real branch or def that shares a line with an
eval-generated entry survives. Prism ships with Ruby 3.3+, and on older
Rubies gem install prism enables the filter, otherwise the setting is a
no-op.

The filters are opt-in and stored regardless of which coverage criteria
are enabled at call time, matching the existing ignore_branches
lifecycle. Unknown tokens raise SimpleCov::ConfigurationError to catch
typos. README and CHANGELOG updated, with specs covering the DSL, the
new StaticCoverageExtractor.real_source_positions helper, and SourceFile
integration.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1046.

Include eval coverage in the strict profile

The strict profile pins line, branch, and method coverage at 100%, but
left eval coverage off. On Ruby 3.2+, code reached through Kernel#eval
(notably ERB templates whose ERB#filename= has been set) gets routed
through the standard line and branch counters, so leaving the toggle
off meant strict was quietly lenient on the exact code paths most
likely to grow untested.

The profile now flips `enable_coverage :eval` on when the runtime
supports it. The guard avoids the "Coverage for eval is not available"
warning that would otherwise fire every time the profile loaded on
Ruby 3.1 (the project's minimum), keeping graceful degradation
consistent with how the existing branch and method clauses no-op on
JRuby. A new spec asserts the toggle matches `coverage_for_eval_supported?`
on whichever runtime the suite is running on, and the README's
"equivalent" example mirrors the new conditional.
Remove unnecessary RuboCop rules
Reduce all classes and modules to 100 SLoC or less

Modernize HTML report frontend

Replace the `(window as any)._simplecov*` global stash with a typed
module-level `renderState` cache so the on-demand source-file
materializer reads from a single object rather than four loosely typed
properties.

Add `defer` to both `application.js` and `coverage_data.js` so the
parser does not block on the head script, and assign `content.innerHTML`
once via `join` instead of `+=` in a loop (the latter forced an
O(n^2) re-parse on reports with many groups). With `defer`, the
`init()` fallback for "SIMPLECOV_DATA isn't ready yet" is unreachable
and goes away.

Bump `tsconfig.json` `lib` to ES2023 so the SHA-1 hex conversion in
`hash.ts` can use `padStart` directly and `jumpToMissedLine` can use
the native `Array.prototype.findLast` instead of a hand-rolled helper.
Simplify `getVisibleChild`, `jumpToMissedLine`, and the dark-mode
preflight into more idiomatic shapes, and rebuild the compiled assets
under `public/`.

Harden HTML report rendering

Escape generated HTML without allocating DOM nodes, including attribute
quotes. The previous DOM-based `escapeHTML` only handled `&`, `<`, and
`>`, so a filename containing `"` or `'` could break out of a `title=`
attribute. Preserve real 0% branch and method coverage values in the
file-row renderer instead of treating them as falsy and substituting
the 100% fallback used for disabled criteria.

Add small `getThemePreference` / `setThemePreference` helpers around
`localStorage` so the toggle click and the prefers-color-scheme listener
match the head-script preflight's try/catch. localStorage can throw in
Safari private mode, sandboxed iframes, and browsers with storage
disabled, and the previous direct calls would crash dark-mode interaction
in those contexts.

Precompute sort keys before row reordering, avoid large spread appends,
simplify filter parsing and class updates, harden the dark-mode
preflight, and rebuild the public formatter assets. CHANGELOG entries
under Bugfixes document the attribute-escape and 0%-display fixes.

Tighten Ruby idioms across several files

Switch the project-root path check in UselessResultsRemover from `=~`
to `match?` (real boolean, skips `$~` capture) and rebuild the prefix
regex with `chomp + append` rather than a mutating `+= unless`. Rewrite
`ResultAdapter#adapt` as a `to_h` block over the input hash with an
`adapt_one` helper, separating the pre-0.18 array-shape path from the
modern hash-shape path.

Replace `!ENV.fetch("NAME", nil).nil?` with `ENV.key?("NAME")` across
the parallel-adapter detection paths, fold the double `key?` check in
`Profiles#fetch_proc` into one, read each env var once in
`CommandGuesser#parallel_data`, and replace the manual `each` plus
early `return` in `cli/coverage.rb`'s `lookup` with `Hash#find`. All
behavior-preserving.

Tighten remaining Ruby helpers

Use Hash#slice, ENV.values_at, Array#size, and compact glob assembly
where they express the same work directly. Build grouped-file membership
as a Set so ungrouped detection stays linear.

Rename the root regexp helper while keeping the legacy root_regx shim,
refresh it when SimpleCov.root changes, and update the focused specs
around the new helper shapes.

Reuse SimpleCov.grouped from Result#groups

`Result` carried a private `apply_groups` that was line-for-line
identical to `SimpleCov.grouped` except for the source of the file
set and group config. Add an optional `groups:` keyword to
`SimpleCov.grouped` (defaulted to `SimpleCov.groups`) so `Result#groups`
can delegate, and drop the duplicate.

Update copyright and credit all gem owners

Bump the copyright year in LICENSE and the README footer to 2026, and
list every RubyGems.org push-access owner of the gem (alphabetical by
last name): Erik Berlin, Benjamin Fleischer, Akira Matsuda, Christoph
Olszowka, Tobias Pfeiffer, David Rodríguez, and Xavier Shay.

Use Coverage.supported? to detect branch and method support

`branch_coverage_supported?` and `method_coverage_supported?` hardcoded
`RUBY_ENGINE != "jruby"`, which has been correct historically but is
brittle: any future runtime that lacks branch or method instrumentation
would silently appear to support it, and SimpleCov would then hand
unsupported keys to `Coverage.start`. The companion `coverage_for_eval_supported?`
already delegated to `Coverage.supported?(:eval)` (Ruby 3.2+), so this
just standardizes on the runtime check.

Extract a single `coverage_criterion_supported?` helper that calls
`Coverage.supported?` when the runtime exposes it and falls back to the
old engine check for older Rubies (line/branch/method on non-JRuby,
`:eval` never available). The fallback path runs on Ruby < 3.2 (below
the dogfood's runtime), so it carries a `simplecov:disable` directive
to keep coverage clean.

Document cover/skip precedence and the plugin profile convention

Two pieces of behavior that are clear from the code but not the README.
`cover` and `skip` operate on opposite sides of the filter chain: `skip`
drops matching files, `cover` restricts the report to files matching
at least one inclusion matcher, and `skip` runs first, so a file
matched by both is dropped not kept. The new section spells that out,
notes that the bundled default skips still apply unless
`no_default_skips` is used, and points out that string-glob matchers
trigger on-disk discovery while Regexp / Proc matchers don't.

The profile loader already tries `simplecov/profiles/<name>` (bundled)
and then `simplecov-profile-<name>` (third-party gem) when an unknown
profile name is passed to `SimpleCov.start`. The convention is now
documented under Profiles so plugin authors know what to name their
gem and how its entry point should register the profile.

Make SimpleCov.coverage_path side-effect-free on read

Reading `SimpleCov.coverage_path` materialized the directory on disk
the first time the memoization fired, even when nothing was about to
be written. That meant CLI subcommands that just interpolate the path
into a status line (`simplecov report`, `simplecov diff`,
`simplecov uncovered`) silently created an empty `coverage/` next to
the project on every invocation. Explicit assignment of a path
(`SimpleCov.coverage_path "/some/build/dir"`) still mkdirs, since the
user has signaled intent to write there.

The codepaths that actually write into the directory now ensure
existence themselves: `SimpleCov::LastRun.write` and
`SimpleCov::ResultMerger::ResultsetStore.write` / `.synchronize`
each `FileUtils.mkdir_p` before opening their file. The HTML and JSON
formatters already did. Tests continue to pass at 100% line / branch /
method coverage.

Add with_env spec helper and migrate ENV-stubbing specs

Stubbing `ENV[]` / `ENV.fetch` / `ENV.values_at` directly forced
spec rewrites every time the implementation changed which access
method it reached for. `with_env(KEY: value) { ... }` sets the
keys for the duration of the block and restores their prior values
(including absent) on exit, decoupling tests from the read shape.

Migrate `command_guesser_spec.rb`'s two parallel-data tests, which
had been the worst offender, off `allow(ENV).to receive(:values_at)`
and onto the helper. Other ENV-driven specs (the parallel-adapters
around-hooks) already use direct ENV assignment with their own
save/restore, which is robust to access-method changes for the same
reason and didn't need migration.

Fix LinesCombiner to preserve relevance and stop mutating its input

`LinesCombiner.combine` had two latent issues. It chose the longer of
the two input arrays as the accumulator and mutated it in place,
which could surprise a caller that held a reference to the same hash
across multiple merges (the parsed `coverage` key of a resultset
being passed into two ResultsCombiner runs in sequence). `combine`
now allocates a fresh array sized to the longer input and leaves both
inputs untouched.

`merge_line_coverage(nil, 0)` (and the symmetric case) returned `nil`,
silently dropping a relevant-but-uncovered line from the merged
result whenever the two runs disagreed about whether a position was
coverage-relevant. Resultset percentages calculated from such merges
overcounted as a result. The new rule: nil only when both sides are
nil, otherwise sum (treating nil as 0). The fixture `parallel_tests.rb`
that pinned the old behavior in `results_combiner_spec` and
`result_merger_spec` is updated to the corrected expectation.

Triple aruba's exit_timeout to soak up cold-cache flakiness

Three scenarios were retrying intermittently and pushing the suite's
wall time from ~2 minutes to 27+ minutes on cold runs:
`old_version_json:20`, `parallel_tests:59`, and
`test_unit_without_simplecov:9`. All three share the same shape:
`bundle exec <command>` in a freshly-copied test_project. With a
warm gem cache they finish in under a second; with a cold cache
they regularly exceed aruba's 20-second `exit_timeout` before the
process has even reported its result. `--retry 3 --no-strict-flaky`
masked the failures but burned the time anyway.

60 seconds (120 on JRuby, where the runtime takes longer to spin up)
covers first-bundle-activation latency on slow CI runners without
slowing the happy path: `exit_timeout` is a ceiling, not a sleep, so
fast invocations still finish in their natural sub-second time.

Skip threshold checks when parallel results are partial

The first worker in a parallel run is the only process that compares
the merged coverage total against `minimum_coverage` / `maximum_coverage`.
When `wait_for_parallel_results` timed out before every sibling
reported, the merged total was a strict subset of the real test
coverage, so the threshold check produced spurious "below minimum"
violations about the missing slice rather than a real shortfall. This
was the root of the `parallel_tests:59` cucumber flake.

`wait_for_parallel_results` now returns a boolean: true when every
expected worker reported before the deadline, false on timeout.
`wait_for_other_processes` captures the outcome in
`@parallel_results_complete`, which a new `parallel_results_complete?`
predicate exposes. `ready_to_process_results?` gates the threshold
check on it, so a timeout suppresses the check entirely rather than
firing against a partial total. On timeout the first worker prints a
yellow warning naming the missing-worker count, so the user can
distinguish "we waited and didn't hear from everyone" from "your
coverage really dropped". The wait deadline itself is bumped from 10
to 60 seconds (matching the aruba exit_timeout bump) so slow workers
have a comfortable budget.

Honor print_errors when reporting threshold violations

`SimpleCov.print_errors false` was already a documented kill switch
for SimpleCov's stderr output, but only the trailing "SimpleCov failed
with exit ..." summary and the deferred-report / previous-error
notices in `exit_handling.rb` actually checked it. The per-check
violation lines (the "Line coverage (X%) is below ..." messages, the
"Lowest-coverage files" listing, and the maximum-drop warnings)
reached `warn` directly from `lib/simplecov/exit_codes/*_check.rb`
and ignored the setting, so `print_errors false` still left the bulk
of the diagnostic noise on stderr. That gap was the reason issue
#1155 stayed open after the `silent:` option on `HTMLFormatter`
shipped, because the noise users wanted gone wasn't formatter output.

Gate the `report` call in `ExitCodes::ExitCodeHandling.call`, the
single point where a failing check fans out into stderr. Per-check
classes keep their existing `report` methods unchanged so they remain
unit-testable in isolation without stubbing global config. Widen the
`print_errors` docstring to describe its real scope.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1155.

Add SimpleCov.color config for explicit color control

`SimpleCov::Color.enabled?` defaults to `$stderr.tty?`, with `NO_COLOR`
and `FORCE_COLOR` env vars as the only escape hatches. That falls
flat in setups where stderr is piped through a wrapper that itself
renders ANSI in a terminal: each `parallel_tests --combine-stderr`
worker's stderr is a pipe to the parent, not a TTY, so TTY detection
returns false even though the parent terminal would render color
fine. Same shape under most CI runners that capture worker output,
log multiplexers, and so on. The existing FORCE_COLOR=1 workaround
covers the case but is undocumented in the README and easy to miss.

Add a `SimpleCov.color` config knob with three values: `true` (always
on), `false` (always off), `:auto` (default, current behavior). The
programmatic setting wins over NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR/TTY, mirroring
the precedence the CLI already uses for its `--no-color` flag.
`:auto` falls through to existing detection so the default behavior
is unchanged for everyone not setting the knob.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1157.

Restructure and condense README

The README had grown organically. Related topics were scattered (CLI
subcommands documented in seven separate places, coverage-type and
merging topics spread throughout), some content was redundant, some was
defunct (the Inch CI badge and the unused Gemnasium link), and the voice
drifted between crisp technical writing and chatty asides.

Reorganize into a logical top-to-bottom flow with one consistent voice:
getting started, configuration, coverage criteria, filters, groups,
profiles, merging and parallel tests, thresholds, formatters, output and
diagnostics, command-line interface, compatibility and troubleshooting,
then the project footer.

Consolidate the seven scattered CLI sections into one command-line
interface section with a summary table, and document the two subcommands
that shipped without docs (serve and clean). Group the coverage-type
sections (branch, oneshot, eval, primary, line-disabling) under one
heading, and make the merging and parallel-test topics contiguous. Fold
the redundant "Use it with any framework" content into getting started
and collapse the three repeated "start SimpleCov first" warnings into a
single callout. Move contact info into the footer alongside contributing.

Remove the dead Inch CI badge and the unused Gemnasium link, and add Lint
and Typecheck badges for the existing CI workflows.

Reflect that the HTML and JSON formatters are now built in rather than
separate gems, and replace the multiple-formatters example (which pulled
in the long unmaintained simplecov-csv gem) with simplecov-cobertura.

Drop the obsolete "supported in CRuby 2.5+" and "2.6+" caveats from
branch and oneshot-line coverage, since the gem now requires Ruby 3.1+
and those criteria are always available on supported CRuby versions. Eval
coverage keeps its caveat because it genuinely requires CRuby 3.2+. Add a
dedicated JRuby section noting that only line coverage is available there.

Every config method, option, env var, flag, deprecation note, code
example, and issue reference is preserved.

Collapse many-parameter render functions into option objects

QLTY flagged four functions in the frontend for having too many
positional parameters: renderTypeSummary (6), renderCoverageSummary (9),
lineStatus (6), and renderFileList (6). Replace each parameter list with
a single typed options object and update the call sites accordingly. This
also makes the call sites self-documenting, since every argument is now
named at the point of the call.

No behavior changes. The minified application.js bundle is regenerated in
a later commit once all frontend refactoring is done.

Reduce function complexity and early-return counts in app.ts

QLTY flagged several frontend functions for high cyclomatic complexity or
too many return statements: init (complexity 66, 8 returns), renderFileList
(26), renderSourceFile (24), and lineStatus (6 returns).

Decompose each into focused helpers:

- init now delegates to setupTableSorting, setupColumnFilters,
  setupSourceDialog, setupEventDelegation, setupTabs, and finishLoading,
  and its keyboard handler moves out to a top-level handleKeydown (itself
  split into focusActiveFilter / handleEscape / handleDialogKeys /
  handleFileListKeys). scheduleTimeago and thToTdIndex move to module scope.
- renderFileList splits into renderFileListHead and renderFileRow.
- renderSourceFile extracts per-line markup into renderSourceLine.
- lineStatus collapses its three trailing returns into one expression.

No behavior changes. tsc passes and the HTML formatter specs are green.
The minified application.js bundle is regenerated in the next commit.

Rebuild minified application.js bundle

Regenerate the shipped esbuild bundle from the refactored app.ts (the two
preceding commits). This is generated output, not hand-edited; produced by
the same command the assets:compile Rake task runs. No behavior changes.

Split app.ts into focused modules

QLTY's file-complexity smell flagged app.ts as a whole: a single 1250-line
file far over the per-file complexity threshold. Break it into cohesive
modules, each well under the threshold, bundled back together by esbuild
from the app.ts entry point (no build change, since esbuild follows
imports):

- types        — shared coverage-data interfaces
- dom          — query/escape/event helpers
- format       — percent/number formatting, timeago, file-id hashing
- render_cells — coverage cell and summary builders
- render_source, render_list, page — source view, file-list table, page assembly
- sort, filter, totals, bar_width — file-list table behaviors
- file_rows    — shared visible-row cache
- navigation, dialog, events, controls — source viewer, routing, keyboard, dark mode
- app          — entry point that wires it together on DOMContentLoaded

Each module owns its own mutable state; siblings read it through small
accessors (dialogIsOpen, getDialogBody, hasFocusedRow) rather than shared
globals, and the dependency graph stays acyclic. No behavior changes: tsc
passes, the HTML formatter specs are green, and application.js is rebuilt
from the new entry point.

Add qlty config excluding the generated HTML report bundle

simplecov-html's public/ directory is build output, not source:
application.js and application.css are minified esbuild bundles (the JS
bundle also inlines vendored highlight.js) and index.html is copied from
html_frontend/src. Analyzing a minified bundle is meaningless, so exclude
the directory from qlty. The analyzed source is the TypeScript under
html_frontend/src, which is now smell-free.

Also declare the standard test_patterns so the spec suites are recognized
as tests and held out of smell analysis, matching qlty's defaults.

Create the coverage directory before ResultMerger specs run

Several ResultMerger examples write the resultset cache file directly.
SimpleCov.coverage_path only creates the coverage directory when called
with an explicit path argument, so the no-arg form used by
ResultMerger.resultset_path can leave it absent. Whether the directory
already existed depended on RSpec example order, so under some seeds
(22150 on CI) the empty-file example raised Errno::ENOENT before it could
run. That failure also left a branch in resultset_file.rb uncovered and
tripped the 100% branch-coverage gate. A before hook now ensures the
directory exists, fixing both.

Group Result filter config into a value object

SimpleCov::Result#initialize took seven parameters: the coverage hash plus
command_name, created_at, not_loaded_files, filters, cover_filters, and
groups. The last three always travel together, always default to the
SimpleCov singleton's configuration, and are only overridden together in
tests. Bundle them into a small Result::FilterConfig value object so the
constructor takes five parameters instead of seven.

No behavior change. FilterConfig defaults each field to the matching
SimpleCov singleton, so ordinary callers are unaffected and the specs that
opt out of filters or groups pass a custom FilterConfig.

Add the criterion-first `coverage` configuration method

Configure each coverage criterion uniformly in one place. Because the
criterion is fixed by the enclosing call, every threshold value is a plain
percentage, so line, branch, and method coverage read identically and the
historical "a bare number means line coverage, every other criterion needs a
Hash" asymmetry goes away.

  SimpleCov.start do
    coverage :line do
      minimum           90
      minimum_per_file  80
      minimum_per_file  100, only: "app/mailers/request_mailer.rb"
      minimum_per_group 95, only: "Models"
      maximum_drop      5
    end
    coverage :branch, minimum: 80
    coverage :method, minimum: 100
  end

Naming a criterion enables it. The flat suite-wide setters (minimum_coverage,
maximum_coverage, expected_coverage, maximum_coverage_drop, refuse_coverage_drop)
stay as documented sugar. minimum_coverage_by_file and minimum_coverage_by_group
are deprecated in favor of minimum_per_file / minimum_per_group, with deprecation
warnings built from the caller's real arguments so the replacement can be pasted
straight into a config.

Also in the configuration layer: remove the vestigial SimpleCov.coverage_criterion
(a reader/writer for a value nothing consumed, fully duplicated by primary_coverage),
alphabetize the require_relative list, and drop two stray "DSL" comments.

Unify the coverage read API across criteria

Line metrics were unprefixed while branch and method had their own
differently-named methods. Parameterize the shared accessors by criterion so
the same call reaches any of them:

  result.covered_percent(:branch)          # was branches_coverage_percent
  result.covered_strength(:method)
  source_file.coverage_statistics(:branch) # was indexing the whole Hash

covered_percent and covered_strength now take a criterion argument (defaulting
to :line), and coverage_statistics takes an optional criterion that returns a
single CoverageStatistics rather than the whole Hash. SourceFile#branches_coverage_percent
and #methods_coverage_percent are deprecated in favor of covered_percent(:branch /
:method), and the bundled JSON formatter is migrated to the new calls.

The parallel-named count accessors (covered_branches and friends) are left as
is: they already read consistently and have divergent array-vs-count semantics
across SourceFile and FileList, so factoring them is a separate cleanup.

Add `uncovered --criterion` to rank by branch or method coverage

`simplecov uncovered` ranked only by line coverage. Add
`--criterion line|branch|method` (default line) so the lowest-coverage listing
can surface the worst branch or method coverage too, reading the matching
coverage.json fields for the chosen criterion.

Document the coverage configuration and reporting changes

Rewrite the README threshold section around the `coverage` method (with the
flat methods as suite-wide shortcuts and a deprecation note for the per-target
setters), extend the legacy-API migration table, document `uncovered
--criterion`, and add the matching CHANGELOG entries.

Collapse coverage threshold keywords into a single splat

The `coverage` method took five separate threshold keywords (minimum,
maximum, exact, maximum_drop, minimum_per_file) that each just forwarded
to the CoverageCriterion verb of the same name, putting it at ten
parameters. Gather them into a `**thresholds` splat and forward them
through a small private helper, dropping the signature to five.

The helper validates each option against an allow-list, so an unknown
keyword now raises a descriptive SimpleCov::ConfigurationError naming the
bad option and the supported ones rather than a generic ArgumentError.
The list excludes minimum_per_group, which needs an `only:` target and so
stays block-only.
Publish a JSON Schema for coverage.json

Pin schema canonical to a versioned path and reference it from the payload

Move the canonical schema to schemas/coverage-v1.0.schema.json with a
versioned $id, so each version is immutable. Keep
schemas/coverage.schema.json as a convenience alias for "the latest"
that mirrors the canonical except for $id, title, and description. A new
spec asserts the two stay structurally identical so the alias cannot
drift.

Add a top-level $schema field to every coverage.json holding the
versioned canonical URL, so each emitted document is self-describing and
consumers can resolve the exact contract without out-of-band knowledge.
meta.schema_version stays as the human-readable companion.

Upgrade coverage.json schema to JSON Schema 2020-12

Draft-07 is from 2018. 2020-12 is the current published draft, supported
by every modern validator (including json_schemer in the dev Gemfile)
and by every IDE that auto-resolves $schema URLs. There is no
compatibility reason to ship a 2018-era contract as the public schema.

Update the meta-schema URI in both schema files (the versioned canonical
and the unversioned alias) and switch the spec assertion from
JSONSchemer.draft7 to JSONSchemer.draft202012. Retitle the README
section to "JSON Schema for coverage.json" so it is searchable for
someone looking for "JSON schema simplecov" rather than for the internal
filename, and tighten the opening paragraph (the second bullet was
redundant with the prose that followed).

Make the source array in coverage.json opt-out

`coverage.json` always carried a full copy of every file's source
text alongside the per-line coverage data. Self-contained, but on
larger projects the source dominates the payload and downstream tools
that read source from disk (cov-loupe and similar) carry the cost
without benefit. Add `SimpleCov.source_in_json` (default true, so
existing consumers see no change), and have `JSONFormatter.build_hash`
take an `include_source:` kwarg that defaults to the config.

The HTML report's `coverage_data.js` always passes `include_source: true`
because the client-side viewer renders source from the embedded array
and would break without it. Only the side-file `coverage.json` written
alongside the HTML report honors the new setting, so users can keep
the rich HTML view while shrinking the JSON consumed by their own
tooling. When the setting is at its default, both files share a single
serialization.

Add maximum_coverage to errors schema

JSONFormatter's ErrorsFormatter emits a `maximum_coverage` key into the
errors object whenever `SimpleCov.maximum_coverage` is configured, but
the schema's errors block used `additionalProperties: false` with only
four permitted keys (minimum_coverage, minimum_coverage_by_file,
minimum_coverage_by_group, maximum_coverage_drop). Any project using
maximum_coverage was producing a coverage.json that failed its own
schema validation.

Add maximum_coverage as a fifth allowed key, reusing the expected_actual
shape the formatter already writes. Update the errors block description
and the README structural overview to list it.

Invert minimum_coverage_by_file errors nesting to filename then criterion

ErrorsFormatter wrote violations into minimum_coverage_by_file nested
as criterion -> filename, while minimum_coverage_by_group nested in the
opposite order (group -> criterion). Consumers looking up violations
for a specific file or group had to know which top-level bucket they
were in to know which key came first.

Flip minimum_coverage_by_file to filename -> criterion so it matches
the by_group convention. Pre-1.0 is the cheap window to fix this
asymmetry. The schema description and the affected spec assertions
are updated to match.

Add per-file omitted_lines and clarify total_lines semantics

Per-file payloads carried covered_lines, missed_lines, and total_lines,
where total_lines was covered + missed (executable lines only). The
project-wide total.lines block has had a separate omitted field for
non-executable (blank/comment) lines since the schema was introduced,
but the per-file shape did not, so consumers wanting per-file omitted
counts had to walk the `lines` array themselves and count nulls.

A natural reading of total_lines is also lines.length, which it is
not. Renaming total_lines to executable_lines was considered but
rejected: total_branches and total_methods follow the same
covered + missed convention, and renaming just one would create a
fresh asymmetry across the three criteria.

Emit per-file omitted_lines via SourceFile#never_lines, add descriptions
to the four line-count fields making the executable-only semantics
explicit, and require omitted_lines in source_file alongside the
others. Fixtures regenerated.

Mark branch and method stat fields as co-required in source_file

Each of the five branch stat fields (branches array,
branches_covered_percent, covered_branches, missed_branches,
total_branches) was an independently optional property in source_file,
likewise for the methods group. The formatter always emits all five
together (or none), but the schema did not encode that. A document
with branches_covered_percent and no branches array, or any other
partial combination, would pass validation even though it is
meaningless. Downstream consumers had to defensively probe each
field rather than rely on "all five present or none present" once
they saw any one of them.

Use JSON Schema 2020-12 `dependentRequired` so each of the five
branch fields makes the other four required, ditto for methods.
Also add descriptions to `branches` and `methods` noting the
co-required-group invariant and tying their presence to the
corresponding `meta.branch_coverage` / `meta.method_coverage` flag,
plus descriptions on total_branches / total_methods clarifying the
covered + missed semantics.

Describe report_line, strength, totals, and the line_coverage sentinel

A handful of fields in the schema had no description, even though
their meaning was not obvious from the name:

* `report_line` (inside a branch object) is the line of the
  conditional that owns the branch (the if, case, or && line), not
  the start of the branch body. Renderers want this for annotating
  the decision point.
* `strength` on line_statistic and coverage_statistic is the
  average number of executions across covered items (hits per
  covered line / branch / method).
* `total` on both statistic shapes is `covered + missed` and
  excludes `omitted`. Spell it out so it isn't conflated with
  "everything".
* `line_coverage` was described as a per-line sentinel, but the
  same three-way shape (integer / null / "ignored") is also reused
  for branch and method `coverage` fields. Note the reuse, and that
  `"ignored"` marks code inside a simplecov:disable / :nocov:
  region (which can happen for branches and methods too, not just
  lines).

Make line stats conditionally required in the coverage schema

When a project runs with `disable_coverage :line` (turning off the
line criterion entirely), the JSON formatter drops every line key
from `total`, per-file payloads, and group totals. The schema
previously required those fields unconditionally, so a valid
SimpleCov payload produced in that configuration failed validation
against its own published schema. Caught by Copilot in PR #1184
review.

* Add a `line_coverage` boolean to the meta block (mirroring
  `branch_coverage` and `method_coverage`) so the line-enabled
  status is discoverable at the document level instead of
  inferred from the absence of fields.
* Drop `lines` from the hard-required list in `totals`,
  `source_file`, and `group`. Add `anyOf` clauses requiring at
  least one of (lines, branches, methods) to be present, since
  SimpleCov refuses to start with all criteria disabled.
* Extend `source_file`'s `dependentRequired` to cover the line
  group (lines + the five line stat fields), matching the same
  "all or nothing" guarantee already in place for branches and
  methods.
* Update the `lines` array description to note the
  `meta.line_coverage` invariant and the co-required group,
  mirroring the wording added for `branches` and `methods`.
* Add a schema-validation spec exercising the line-disabled
  emit path so this drift can't slip past CI again.

Fixtures and the README structural overview pick up `line_coverage`.

Document source_in_json and the coverage.json JSON Schema in the README

The schema branch's README additions were written against the pre-restructure
README. Reintegrate them into the restructured layout: the source_in_json
opt-out lands in the JSON formatter section, and the coverage.json JSON Schema
overview becomes its own subsection under Formatters. Content is unchanged
from the schema work, only rewrapped to match the surrounding prose.

Record the git commit SHA in coverage.json meta

Add a `commit` field to coverage.json's `meta` holding the full git SHA
of SimpleCov.root's HEAD, or null outside a git checkout or when git
isn't available. When `source_in_json false` omits the per-file source
arrays, the commit lets downstream tools recover the exact source from
repository history. The lookup captures git's stderr rather than
forwarding it, so a non-git project doesn't print git diagnostics.

Add a maximum_coverage case to the coverage schema spec

The end-to-end validation exercised every `errors` shape except
maximum_coverage, which is how the earlier maximum_coverage drift went
unnoticed. Cover it alongside maximum_coverage_drop.

Clarify the per-file source description in the coverage schema

`source` is emitted independently of line coverage, so it is not always
the same length as the `lines` array (which is absent when line coverage
is disabled). Describe it as one entry per physical line instead.

Forbid null for branch and method coverage values in the schema

Branch and method `coverage` values are always an integer hit count or
the string "ignored". Only line coverage uses null, for non-executable
lines. Give branch and method coverage their own definition so the
schema no longer permits a null that never occurs for them.

The JSON fixtures hard-coded the gem version, so the fixture-equality

Cut the first release candidate for 1.0.0 and relabel the CHANGELOG

Route releases through the Push Gem workflow

`rake release` published the gem from the developer machine, which is what
prompts for a RubyGems OTP. Releases are meant to run in CI via the Push
Gem workflow (.github/workflows/push_gem.yml) using trusted publishing,
which needs no API key and no OTP. Outside CI, replace `rake release` with
a pointer to that workflow so a local invocation cannot tag, push, or
publish by accident. GitHub Actions sets CI=true, so the real release task
still runs there unchanged.

Create a GitHub Release when pushing a gem

rubygems/release-gem pushes the version tag and publishes to RubyGems but
does not open a GitHub Release, so the Releases page had to be updated by
hand after each release. Add a step that creates a Release for the tag it
just pushed, with notes generated from merged PRs. Prerelease versions
(like 1.0.0.rc1) are flagged with --prerelease via Gem::Version#prerelease?
so they do not show as Latest or steer gem install users toward them.

Trigger the release workflow from `rake release`

Match the release flow used across the other gems. `rake release` now
builds the gem and pushes the version tag (build, guard_clean,
source_control_push) without pushing the gem, so there is no OTP prompt.
The Push Gem workflow triggers on the pushed `v*` tag instead of
workflow_dispatch and publishes explicitly: configure trusted publishing,
build, sign with Sigstore, push with attestation, then open the GitHub
Release. This replaces rubygems/release-gem, which ran the full `rake
release` in CI and would have tried to re-create the already-pushed tag.

Only warn about expired results in the reporting process

When the suite runs with forked workers (merge_subprocesses), each
worker calls SimpleCov.result to store its slice, which merges the
resultset and so reaches the expired-results check. The default
at_fork sets print_errors false for those workers, but unlike every
other SimpleCov warning, warn_about_expired_results did not honor it.
The result was one copy of the merge_timeout warning per worker, e.g.
eight identical lines for an eight-worker run.

Gate the warning on print_errors so only the reporting process emits
it, matching warn_about_incomplete_parallel_results and
warn_about_deferred_report.

Deduplicate legacy-API deprecation warnings by call site

Each legacy configuration alias (track_files, add_filter, add_group,
minimum_coverage_by_file, and the rest) warned on every call with no
deduplication. A deprecated method called in a loop, or a config block
re-evaluated once per parallel worker or spec file, flooded stderr with
the same notice until unrelated output was unreadable. See issue #1204.

Introduce SimpleCov::Deprecation.warn, which prepends the location and
`[DEPRECATION]` tag the call sites used to build inline, and emits each
notice at most once per source location. Keying on the caller location
collapses a deprecated call in a loop to a single line while still
warning separately about each distinct call site the user has to fix.

Route the twelve config/source_file aliases through it. The already
deduplicated `:nocov:` and `.simplecov`-start warnings keep their own
once-only guards.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1204.

Name forked subprocesses by a stable serial, not the pid

The default at_fork built each worker's command_name from the child's
OS pid: "Minitest (subprocess: 12345)". Because the pid changes every
run, a re-run's workers were always named differently from the previous
run's, so their resultset entries never overwrote the old ones. They
accumulated in .resultset.json until merge_timeout dropped them, and
while several runs sat in the window together SimpleCov merged their
results. When the file set had drifted between those runs (a deleted
file, a changed filter), stale files leaked into the report and the
denominator — and therefore the coverage percentage — changed from run
to run. See issue #1171.

Assign each forked subprocess a process-local serial instead. The
parent bumps the serial before each fork (so the child inherits its own
ordinal via copy-on-write) and the default at_fork names the worker
from it. The serial sequence is identical from one run to the next, so
a re-run's workers overwrite the previous run's entries and the
resultset stays bounded.

Within a run the serials are still distinct, so workers don't clobber
each other, and the #581 combine-on-concurrent-write logic continues to
protect against an empty parent result overwriting a worker's data.
Custom at_fork blocks still receive the real pid argument.

finds the primary column by its cell--<type>-pct class and falls back to
the first coverage column when the value is absent (older reports).

The default sort runs during the initial render, while the loading overlay
is shown, so it doesn't block interaction.

After a native wait confirms every sibling process has exited, no
further resultset can appear. A count below the expected worker count
then just means some workers produced none, which happens when a
runner spawns one worker per core on a machine with more cores than
test files. Those idle workers load nothing and write no resultset, so
the reporting worker blocked for the full parallel_wait_timeout (60s by
default) on every run.

short settle window, accept it as final instead of waiting out the
timeout. GenericAdapter has no process-exit signal and cannot tell an
idle worker from a slow one, so it keeps waiting the full timeout as

cores than spec files the extra workers get no file and write no
resultset, which the reporting worker now handles gracefully but still
has to detect. Passing -n 2 matches the worker count to the number of
spec files so the run stays fast and deterministic across machines

and absorbs clicks while the sort runs. Smaller tables still sort inline.

takes a moment, but it is now communicated and non-interruptible.

Cell contents never change after render, so sort values are now cached
per row instead of re-read from the DOM on every sort, and re-clicking
the active sort column reverses the current order outright rather than

The bar width equalizer wrote inline styles on every bar sizer for each

load and on every filter keystroke. The width is uniform per table, so

simplecov 1.0.0 broke a formatter configuration pattern the README documented for years:

```ruby
SimpleCov.formatters = SimpleCov::Formatter::MultiFormatter.new([
  SimpleCov::Formatter::HTMLFormatter,

])
```

`MultiFormatter.new` returns a `Class`, not an `Array`, so the 1.0.0 setter raised `NoMethodError` on

whose internal `Array()` call normalized single formatters transparently.

This surfaced in ruby/ruby CI, where net-imap's test helper still uses the pattern above:
https://github.com/ruby/ruby/actions/runs/29193505325/job/86652245625?pr=17830

exe/simplecov loads only simplecov/cli, not the full library, to stay
lightweight. But Color.enabled? read SimpleCov.color unconditionally,
and that method is only defined once simplecov/configuration is loaded.

in any project without a .simplecov file. A dotfile masked it (reading
it lazily requires the full library, which incidentally defines
SimpleCov.color), and the in-process specs never saw it because
spec/helper always loads all of simplecov. NO_COLOR could not work
around it either, since it was checked after the failing line.

as its :auto default (fall through to NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR, then tty?),
so the documented precedence holds and the CLI stays lightweight.

directory with no .simplecov, covering all four colorizing subcommands.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1231.

SimulateCoverage backfills branch data for tracked-but-unloaded files
using StaticCoverageExtractor. emit_safe_navigation keyed the &. branch
on the CallNode's whole location, which extends through an attached
block. Ruby's Coverage ends the branch at the call itself and never
includes the block, so for x&.foo { ... } (and the second link of a
chain like x&.foo&.bar { ... }) the synthesized tuple's end position
drifted past the real one. BranchesCombiner keys arms on
[type, start_line, start_col, end_line, end_col], so a simulated
resultset never combined that arm with the real one, leaving a phantom,
permanently-missed branch on merge. Same class of bug as the elsif
mismatch fixed in 1.0.1, different construct.

Resolve the end position from closing_loc (closing paren), else
arguments (paren-less args), else message_loc, matching what Coverage
uses. Verified byte-for-byte identical to Coverage.result on both Ruby
3.3 and 3.4 across bare, parenthesized-args, paren-less-args, block,
args-plus-block, and chained forms, so no version-conditional branch is
needed. Pin the block-bearing forms in the differential tuple-equivalence
harness, where they failed before this change.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1233.

Skip synthesizing branches for constant-folded conditions

An `if` / `unless` / ternary whose condition is a compile-time literal
(if true, if false, if nil, if 1, if :x, 1 ? a : b, and the same through
parentheses) is folded by the compiler, so Coverage emits no branch for
it. StaticCoverageExtractor emitted one anyway, and since SimulateCoverage
merges simulated entries into real ones by tuple identity, that arm has
no real counterpart to combine with. It survives as a phantom branch that
no loaded run can ever hit, the same unmergeable-tuple failure mode as
the elsif (1.0.1) and safe-navigation-block fixes.

Skip if-like emission when the predicate is a static literal, seeing
through parentheses. while / until are left alone (while true is a real
branch, never folded), as are Regexp and Range conditions (they mean
=~ $_ / flip-flop, which Coverage does branch on). Compound folds
(!true, true || x) are out of scope: negation never folds and &&/||
constant-propagation diverges across Ruby versions.

Verified byte-for-byte against Coverage on Ruby 3.3 and 3.4 via a
differential fuzzer, and pinned with focused specs plus cross-version
fixtures in the runtime tuple-equivalence harness.

Match Coverage's legacy branch conventions and survive stdlib Prism

A differential audit of StaticCoverageExtractor against real Coverage
(fuzzing thousands of small programs on Ruby 3.3 and 3.4, diffing the
branch tuples) surfaced four more mismatches of the same phantom-branch
class as the elsif (1.0.1) and safe-navigation-block fixes. All four are
Ruby 3.3 specific. Ruby 3.4 was already exact.

Prism accessor crash. UnlessNode, CaseNode, and CaseMatchNode expose
their else clause as consequent on the Prism 0.19 that ships in Ruby
3.3's stdlib, renamed to else_clause in Prism 1.3. The extractor reached
straight for else_clause, so on a 3.3 without the prism gem it raised
NoMethodError, which call swallowed, dropping simulated data for every
file containing unless/else or an empty-arm case. Resolve the accessor
once, the same way IfNode's subsequent/consequent split already is.

do-while body. begin ... end while/until parses as a loop whose one
statement is the begin block. Coverage attributes the body to the whole
span on 3.4 but to the begin's inner statements on 3.3.

Empty arm position. On 3.3 the range Coverage gives an empty then, else,
or when arm depends on whether the construct is in value (method-return)
position, where it keeps the whole range, or void position, where it
collapses to a point at the arm header's end. 3.4 dropped the
distinction. A new ValuePositions pass marks value position, which
reaches a node only through statement tails and if/unless/when arms and
is discarded by assignments, blocks, case/in arms, and loop bodies.

One-line pattern matching. x => pattern and x in pattern emit a :case
branch on 3.3 and nothing on 3.4; the extractor had no visitor for them.

The condition-folding literals move to their own ConditionFolding module
and the value-position pass to ValuePositions, keeping the visitor and
conventions files focused. Regression fixtures for every case are pinned
in the runtime tuple-equivalence harness, which runs against real
Coverage on each CI Ruby.

Add a differential fuzzer for the static coverage extractor

The extractor has to reproduce, tuple for tuple, the branch data
Coverage would emit for a file, because SimulateCoverage merges the two
by position and any drift becomes a permanently-missed phantom branch.
Four separate reports (elsif, safe-navigation blocks, and the four in
the preceding commit) show how easily a construct or nesting slips
through the hand-written fixtures.

This adds a seeded generator (BranchFuzzer) that builds small def bodies
nesting every branch construct Prism emits, and an opt-in spec that runs
each through real Coverage in a subprocess and through the extractor,
asserting the id-stripped tuples match. It compares against the running
Ruby's Coverage, so it pins version-specific conventions on whichever
Ruby and Prism CI runs. It's randomized and shells out per sweep, so it
only runs under SIMPLECOV_FUZZ=1, with SIMPLECOV_FUZZ_SEEDS and
SIMPLECOV_FUZZ_PER_SEED tuning the volume; a failure prints the offending
source to copy into the deterministic spec.

Drop a simulated file's branches when a real run covered it

SimulateCoverage backfills branches and methods for tracked-but-unloaded
files by static analysis, and the merge unions those tuples into the real
ones by position. If a synthesized tuple's location drifts from what
Coverage emits (the class of bug behind the elsif, safe-navigation, and
Ruby 3.3 fixes), the drifted tuple has no real counterpart to combine
with and survives the merge as a phantom, permanently-missed branch on a
file that was actually fully covered.

Reconcile at the point two file coverages combine: when exactly one side
was actually executed (has a covered line, which a simulated file never
does), treat its branch and method tuples as authoritative and drop the
other side's. This contains any future extractor drift to denominator
inflation for files no process loaded, rather than a false miss on a
covered file. Lines still combine from both sides, so a simulated file
keeps contributing the unloaded-file line denominator.

When both sides ran, or neither did, nothing changes: the tuples combine
by union as before.

Aggregate runtime-duplicated coverage entries by source location

Ruby's Coverage reports two kinds of entries that are finer-grained than
source locations, and reporting them verbatim creates phantom misses on
fully-covered code.

Methods are recorded once per RECEIVER. A block handed to define_method
or define_singleton_method from a shared code path (a module's included
hook, a builder) yields a separate [receiver, name, location] entry for
every class it lands on, all pointing at the same source. A receiver
whose copy is never called contributes a permanently-zero entry, so a
line with 100% line coverage shows an uncovered method. The existing
address normalization merged same-shaped anonymous receivers by accident
but not named ones or differing wrappers (Class vs Module singletons).
Aggregate method entries by (name, location) in ResultAdapter, summing
hits, and match on the same source identity in MethodsCombiner so
cross-process merges cannot resurrect per-receiver duplicates.

Branches under eval coverage are recorded once per COMPILE. Rendering
the same template through several view classes (hanami-view compiles per
view) emits several conditions at identical coordinates in the same
file, each counting only its own renders. That inflates the branch
denominator, and when different specs exercise different sides through
different compiles, each side shows a phantom miss even though both ran.
It also makes ignore_branches :implicit_else swing the report wildly,
since it strips only the synthetic-else halves of every duplicate.
Aggregate conditions by location in ResultAdapter via
BranchesCombiner's existing identity merge. Regular source can never
emit two conditions at one location, so this is a no-op outside eval.

Verified against the reporting user's actual suites: Inspectable's
method coverage goes from a phantom 24/25 to a correct 24/24, and
Milestoner's ERB templates drop from 14 duplicated branch conditions to
zero with line coverage unchanged.

The extractor audit and aggregation work added two modules and changed

Survive user code that breaks receiver name rendering

Adapting a raw coverage result renders each method coverage key's
receiver with to_s. A singleton class's to_s renders its attached object
via #inspect, which user code can shadow with an incompatible signature.
Liquid's Utils module defines inspect(value, max_depth = 2) as a
module_function, so any suite whose coverage universe includes Liquid (a
vendored bundle under the project root survives UselessResultsRemover)
raised ArgumentError from the at_exit hook and lost its report. The
exposure predates 1.0.2, which only moved the call.

Rendering now falls back on failure to rebuilding the singleton wrapper
from Module#name via bound methods, which cannot be shadowed, and then
to the address form, which the existing address normalization collapses.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1236.

Aggregate method coverage by source location alone

Ruby records one method coverage entry per defined method, so a builder
looping `container.each_key { |key| define_method(key) { ... } }` yields
an entry per generated name, all at the block's source location. The
1.0.2 aggregation keyed entries on (name, location), which merged
per-receiver copies but kept per-name copies apart, so every name whose
generated wrapper no test happened to call showed as an uncovered method
on a line with full line and branch coverage.

Key the aggregation on location alone, in the adapter and in
cross-process merging. A source location is the unit a file-based report
can express, and regular defs map one location to one name, so they are
unaffected. Verified against Pipeable, where the report previously
showed thirteen phantom uncovered methods at the builder's define_method
block and now shows full method coverage with the gem's
simplecov:disable workaround removed.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1234.

Assert engine-independent invariants for receiver name fallbacks

The two singleton-wrapper fallback specs pinned CRuby's exact rendering
and failed on JRuby and TruffleRuby, which render a singleton class from
the class name chain without calling the attached object's inspect, so
the rescue path never fires there and the strings differ (both engines
produce variants like "#<Class:#<Module:0x0>>"). The production behavior
is correct on every engine.

Accept formatter instances in formatter configuration

SimpleCov unconditionally called .new on the configured formatter, both
in Result#format! and inside MultiFormatter, so there was no way to
reach constructor options like silent: true. Passing an instance
crashed with NoMethodError at report time.

Formatters configured as classes are still instantiated fresh for every
report. Anything else is treated as a ready-built formatter instance
and used as is, in both the single formatter setting and formatters
lists.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1240.

fix: memoise key parsing in RubyDataParser to fix combiner performance regression

Measured on a real 66-worker CI merge (~21k files, ~46k branches, branch coverage enabled): the collate step (which merged 66 reports) regressed from ~29s under `0.22` to ~145s (5x slower) under `1.0.0`.

A wall-clock stackprof attributes main time to `Ripper#parse` under `RubyDataParser.parse_array_string`.

Resultset JSON stores keys as stringified Ruby literals (`"[:if, 0, 14, 4, 14, 30]"`), and RubyDataParser walks them back into arrays with a Ripper parse. That parse sat on a hot path: `BranchesCombiner` and `MethodsCombiner` derive a merge identity from every key of *both* sides on *every* pairwise merge. Folding N resultsets therefore parsed each key string N-1 times.

This PR adds memoisation to `RubyDataParser.call` to avoid parsing strings that have already been parsed.

Notes:

- The set of unique keys is bounded by the project's branch and method count, so the cache stays reasonably small and needs no eviction.
- Cached arrays are frozen and shared. Every caller (both combiners, `BranchBuilder`, `MethodBuilder`, `SourceFile::Method`) destructures the parsed array without mutating it; freezing enforces that any future mutation surfaces as an error instead of silent cross-caller corruption.
- Array inputs still pass through untouched and unfrozen - in-process results never hit the cache, exactly as before.

Add a benchmark for collation

perf: memoise merge identities and reuse combiner tables

Measured with `ruby benchmarks/collate.rb` (160 resultsets, 1836 files,
147,875 lines, 8,205 branch conditions, branch coverage enabled):

    phase        before    after
    merge         8.44s    5.54s   -34.4%
    total         9.21s    6.27s   -32.0%

`BranchesCombiner.combine` dominated the merge either way, but its share
of it fell from 59% to 43%.

Collating N resultsets folds them pairwise, and both branch and method
combining derive a merge identity from every key of *both* sides on every
one of the N-1 merges. The accumulator's keys therefore had an identity
derived for them N-1 times, always to the same answer. `RubyDataParser`
already memoises the string *parse*, but each call still allocated a fresh
location array and then hashed it as a `Hash` key, and `Array#hash` is not
memoised.

Every fold also rebuilt more than it needed to: `combine` stored a
replacement `[tuple, count]` pair for every key it had just merged, and
`merge_branches` allocated a new pair instead of updating the existing one.

So:

- Memoise the derived identity, keyed by the raw key, so a hit skips the
  parse cache lookup as well as the derivation.
- Update the accumulated pairs in place and drop the redundant write-back.

Notes:

- The cache is bounded by the project's branch and method count, the same
  argument that lets `RubyDataParser`'s parse cache live without eviction.
- Cached identities are frozen. They are shared across calls now, and every
  caller only ever uses them as a hash key.
- `tuple_identity` and `source_identity` keep their signatures but are no
  longer the memoised entry point - they are the plain derivation the cache
  calls on a miss.
- Pairs are only mutated where `combine` built them itself, so nothing a
  caller still holds can be reached. `LinesCombiner`'s deliberately
  non-mutating contract is untouched.
- Both the string and array forms of a key still resolve to equal
  identities, so a resultset that has been through JSON merges with an
  in-process one exactly as before.
- Verified no behaviour change: merging all 160 resultsets with branch and
  method coverage enabled produces a byte-identical result before and
  after, in insertion order and canonically sorted alike.

perf: intern merge identities to Integers

Follows on from memoising the identities themselves. Measured with
`ruby benchmarks/collate.rb` (160 resultsets, 1836 files, 147,875 lines,
8,205 branch conditions, branch coverage enabled):

    phase        before    after
    merge         5.54s    4.47s   -19.3%
    total         6.27s    5.41s   -13.7%

Cumulatively the merge is now 4.47s against 8.44s before either change,
-47%.

An identity exists only to be a key of `combine`'s working hash, and
`Array#hash` is not memoised, so keying on the five-element location tuple
rehashed all five elements on every lookup - for every key of both sides of
every one of the N-1 merges. Interning each distinct identity to a
sequential Integer makes those lookups hash an immediate instead.

Notes:

- Two keys are given the same id exactly when their identities compare
  equal, so this is transparent to merging: differing branch ids still
  collapse (issue #1233), and the string and array forms of one key still
  merge together.
- The ids are an internal detail. They are never exposed - `combine`
  returns `merged.values`, so the interned keys are dropped on the way out
  and the retained tuple is still the first one seen.
- `tuple_identity` and `source_identity` are unchanged and still return the
  location tuple; interning happens between them and the working hash.
- Adds a second bounded table per combiner, sized by the count of distinct
  identities rather than of distinct keys.
- Verified no behaviour change: merging all 160 resultsets with branch and
  method coverage enabled produces a byte-identical result before and
  after, in insertion order and canonically sorted alike.

Add mixed-form merge specs for the tuple combiners

The combiner specs covered array-with-array and string-with-string
merges but not the mixed case, where an in-process result merges with a
resultset read back from JSON and the same key arrives in both forms.
That case is exactly the invariant the interning layer introduced in
https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/pull/1244 has to preserve
(two keys share an id exactly when their identities compare equal), and
a regression here would silently double-count branches and methods. Pin
it with one spec per combiner.

Extract shared identity interning into Combine::IdentityInterner

BranchesCombiner and MethodsCombiner carried identical copies of the
interning cache introduced in
https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/pull/1244, differing only in
which identity derivation they call. Move the cache construction into a
small factory that takes the derivation as a block. Call sites are
unchanged and each combiner keeps its own independent cache and id
table, since the factory builds fresh ones per call.

No behavior change. The combine specs, including the new mixed-form
ones, pass, and a run of the collate benchmark against the same fixture
produces byte-identical output at unchanged speed.

Make the HTML report a single self-contained index.html

The HTML formatter previously wrote index.html plus five sibling files
(coverage_data.js, application.js, application.css, and three favicon
PNGs). The compiled template now inlines the viewer's JavaScript and
CSS at build time (rake assets:compile), and the formatter
substitutes the coverage JSON at a marker in the template at report
time, so the whole report is one file. coverage.json is still written
alongside as the sanctioned data artifact.

A single file can be mailed, copied anywhere, or uploaded as a
non-zipped GitHub Actions run artifact (actions/upload-artifact with
archive: false only supports single files) and viewed directly from
the run page. It also makes report updates atomic. A reader can no
longer catch index.html and coverage_data.js from different runs
because the report is replaced in one rename.

Every "<" in the embedded payload is escaped as \u003c (valid JSON,
since "<" can only occur inside strings), so source text containing
"</script>" or "<!--" cannot terminate the surrounding script
element. The asset build refuses to inline a bundle containing such
sequences.

The embedded payload is serialized compactly. Pretty printing puts
every element of every per-line coverage array on its own indented
line, which makes the report roughly a third larger (simplecov's own
dogfood report is 647 KB compact against 947 KB pretty). The sibling
coverage.json stays pretty-printed for human readers.

The asset build also renames the stylesheet's custom properties to
short aliases after minification. The descriptive names repeat at
every use and cost about 3 KB of the compiled template. Properties
that JavaScript reads or writes by name (--bar-sizer-width and the
band colours) are exempt and keep their names.

The favicon (a solid square in the overall coverage band's colour) is
drawn by the viewer on a canvas from the live --green/--red/--yellow
palette values instead of shipping as fixed PNGs, so it matches the
report's colours exactly and follows the light/dark theme, including
the in-page toggle and OS preference changes.

The pre-1.0 simplecov-html formatter offered inline assets behind the
SIMPLECOV_INLINE_ASSETS environment variable. The 1.0 client-side
rendering rewrite dropped that mode. This restores single-file reports
as the default and only mode, with no flag or environment variable.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1241.

Skip synthesizing branch and method tuples nothing will read

Simulating a tracked-but-unloaded file statically enumerates its branch
and method tuples (#1059), and the Prism parse behind that is over half
the cost of simulating a file. It ran even for the default
line-coverage-only configuration, where Combine::FilesCombiner and the
statistics both drop the tuples unread, and it is paid once per tracked
file in every process, which is why it shows up on large parallel runs.

SimulateCoverage.call now takes a synthesize: keyword and the injection
site passes branch_coverage? || method_coverage?. On a 400 file
synthetic project the default configuration's injection pass goes from
0.526 to 0.222 ms per file. Line classification is identical either way,
and suites with either criterion enabled are unaffected.

Reported with measurements by @andriytyurnikov.

Refs https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1250.

Flag never-loaded files in merged results

SourceFile::Statistics reports 0% rather than a misleading 100% when a
never-loaded file has no branch or method data (#902), but the rule keys
off a loaded: flag that only the single-process path set.
ResultMerger.create_result omitted not_loaded_files, so every file in a
merged report claimed to have been loaded and the rule never fired
there. A tracked file no process loaded and that contains no
conditionals, say a constants file caught by a cover glob, reported 100%
branch and method coverage. Only branchless files exposed it, since
#1059's synthesized tuples already give anything with a conditional a
real 0%.

The flag cannot be carried across, since Result#to_hash writes only
coverage and a timestamp, so the merged result re-derives it from the
merged line counts using the same "did any line execute" signal
Combine::FilesCombiner reconciles on. This also matters for the previous
commit, which keeps synthesized tuples out of resultsets written by
line-coverage-only runs: a later collate with branch coverage enabled
now reports those files as 0% rather than 100%.

Line counts only carry that signal when the run produces them. A
branch-only or method-only run gets none from Coverage for the files it
loaded, so judging on their absence would mark every file in the report
not loaded and report 0% for the branchless ones. SimulateCoverage now
omits line data under those criteria too, mirroring Coverage, which
keeps a simulated file from looking like one a sibling process loaded
once the two merge. Nothing is flagged there rather than misflagged.

Reported with an exemplary diagnosis by @andriytyurnikov.

Refs https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1250.

Stop matching the :nocov: regex twice on every classified line

SimpleCov.result simulates coverage at exit for every file a track_files
or cover glob matched that the process never loaded. It is per-process
work, so a parallel run pays it once per worker, and since each worker
loads only a fraction of the code, nearly every worker simulates nearly
the whole project. Skipping the branch and method synthesis takes the
bulk of that out for a line-coverage-only run; classification is what
remains, and it is paid under every configuration.

LinesClassifier#classify ran the :nocov: regex twice per line: once to
toggle skipping and once inside not_relevant_line?. A marker is always a
comment, so the cheaper whitespace-or-comment test now gates the token
match, and a line of real code -- most of a source file -- no longer
pays for it at all.

Measured over SimpleCov's own lib/ (104 files, 8,845 lines), median of
three runs each:

  classify alone                    48.31 -> 43.36 ms   -10%
  simulate, line coverage only      67.58 -> 60.09 ms   -11%
  simulate, synthesis enabled       85.30 -> 79.41 ms    -7%

benchmarks/simulate_coverage.rb covers this path, which had no benchmark
before -- only collate and Result did, so nothing measured the
per-process work at exit.

The rescue in LinesClassifier.no_cov_line? is no longer reachable from
classify, since an invalid byte sequence now fails the whitespace test
first. SourceFile::SkipChunks still calls it directly on raw source, so
it keeps its rescue and gains a direct spec.

The spec added alongside pins that `synthesize: false` skips the Prism
parse outright rather than parsing and discarding it, which is the claim
behind that flag.

Pin the marker/comment invariant classify_line depends on

Gating the :nocov: match behind the whitespace-or-comment test is sound
only while every marker is also a comment. That holds because no_cov_line
is anchored ^(\s*)# , strictly narrower than COMMENT_LINE's ^\s*# , but
nothing said so and nothing tested it.

Loosening the marker to also match a trailing "x = 1 # :nocov:" would
break the gate silently: whitespace_line? is false for that line, so the
toggle would never fire and the block would stop being skipped, with no
test failing. Before the single-pass rewrite the same change would simply
have worked.

Adds specs pinning both directions, and a note on no_cov_line itself,
which is what someone making that change would be editing.

Absorb resultsets into one accumulator instead of folding pairwise

Merging results folded them together pairwise, so every one of the N-1
steps rebuilt the whole accumulated structure: a fresh outer file hash,
a fresh lines array for every file, and a fresh branch/method table for
every file whose keys were re-interned from their tuples each time. A
160-worker run over ~1,800 files did ~290,000 whole-file rebuilds to
produce ~1,800 files of output, which made merging the dominant cost of
collate by a wide margin.

Combine::CoverageAccumulator now absorbs results one at a time into
state it owns outright and updates in place, and the interned branch
and method tables become tuple-keyed hashes once, at the end. Results
are still read and absorbed one at a time, so the memory ceiling
ResultMerger.merge_results is careful about is unchanged: peak RSS on
the benchmark is identical.

On benchmarks/collate.rb -- 160 resultsets, 1,836 files, 147,875 lines,
branch coverage on -- the merge phase drops from 5.85s to 3.38s (-42%)
and the whole collate from 6.65s to 3.87s. Peak RSS is unchanged.

The line merge itself was left alone beyond folding in place. At around
60ns per element it is already at CRuby's floor; a tight index loop
that avoids the block and method call per element measures the same.
Only the redundant re-walking was recoverable.

Combine::FilesCombiner and Combine.combine are gone. Both became
unreachable once the fold stopped being pairwise, and both were
internal API (sig/internal, never sig/simplecov.rbs). FilesCombiner's
spec cases, including the #1233 executed-vs-simulated reconciliation
that MergedFile now performs, move to the accumulator's spec.

The read-and-fold loop is extracted as ResultMerger.absorb_results so
benchmarks/collate can time what ships rather than its own copy of it.
It had one, which silently kept benchmarking the pairwise fold and
reported this change as no improvement at all. The loop only iterates
its paths, so the benchmark's progress reporting rides along on an
Enumerator rather than needing a hook inside the merge.

Coerce the lines table before testing whether a file ran

CoverageAccumulator.executed? reads straight off a parsed resultset,
which is external input: a file written by another SimpleCov version, or
hand-edited, can carry anything under "lines". FilesCombiner coerced with
Array() before testing, and folding that logic into the accumulator
dropped the coercion, so a malformed scalar now raises NoMethodError out
of the middle of reconcile_synthesized rather than resolving to a wrong
answer.

never_executed_files is insulated because it still guards with Array()
first, but reconciliation calls this directly on raw resultset data.

Restores the coercion and pins it, including the malformed-scalar case,
which fails against the uncoerced version.

Read the enabled criteria once per fold, not once per file

MergedFile asked SimpleCov whether branch and method coverage were
enabled every time it was built, which its own comment noted was already
an improvement over asking once per merged pair. One step further: the
answer cannot change mid-fold, so the accumulator reads it once and hands
it down.

branch_coverage? reaches Coverage.supported?, and the collate benchmark
merges 1,836 files, so this drops a few thousand lookups to two. No
behaviour change, and the criteria arrive as keyword arguments so the
merged file no longer reaches for global configuration on its own.

Extract unloaded-file injection into its own module

Discovering tracked files and simulating the ones that were never loaded
lived as private helpers on the SimpleCov singleton, reading root, globs
and criteria straight off it. The next commit moves the injection to the
merge step, which runs on behalf of processes whose configuration it does
not share, so the logic has to take what it needs as arguments.

SimpleCov::UnloadedFileInjector now owns discovery and injection.
SimpleCov.inject_unloaded_files is the seam the merger will call, public
for that reason and marked @api private. No behaviour changes: every
process still injects its own unloaded files exactly as before.

Inject unloaded files once at the merge point

inject_unloaded_files skips only what the current process loaded, so
every worker in a parallel run simulated nearly the whole project and the
merge discarded all but one copy of each file. Only the union of what
every process loaded says what was really never loaded, so the injection
now happens in ResultMerger.create_result. Over 400 tracked files with 40
loaded by no worker, a 16-worker run goes from 6040 simulations taking
3.15s across the workers to 40 taking 0.024s once, flat in worker count.
A single process, and any run with merging false, pays what it did
before, and resultsets shrink from 13.4MB to 800KB at 16 workers.

The merge needs to know which files were tracked, and that configuration
lives in whichever process ran SimpleCov.start. A standalone collate
never ran it, so deferring alone would have left it with no glob to
expand and silently dropped every untested file: 90 files at an inflated
36.88% where there should be 400 at 8.30%. Each process therefore records
the paths it was told to track into its resultset, and the merge unions
those. Discovery costs a Dir.glob per process, 1.26ms over 400 files,
against the simulation it replaces. The key is omitted when empty and
absent from resultsets written by earlier versions, which already carry
the files their process injected and so merge unchanged.

Merged coverage and the not-loaded set are identical at every worker
count. Knowing exactly which files were injected also supersedes the
line-count heuristic for them, so a never-loaded branchless file is now
flagged under a branch-only run, which that heuristic cannot do because
it has no line data to judge by.

ResultMerger::UnloadedFiles holds the merge half. ResultMerger.valid_results
went unused and is removed.

Refs https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1250.

Take the merge's cues from the data, not the merging process

Four places where deferring injection left the merge reading state that
belonged to whichever process produced the resultset. Same shape as the
glob problem the tracked-path list already solved, so they are fixed the
same way: what the producer knew goes in the resultset, and the merge
derives the rest from the data it is merging.

A process records what it was told to track, did not load, and would have
reported. Two things were leaking. Result#to_hash serializes coverage
after filtering, so a file the process loaded and then filtered out was
