absent from the stored coverage while still listed as tracked, and the
merge simulated it back in as never loaded. And a tracked file the
process never loaded but its own filters exclude was recorded too, so a
merge that does not share those filters reported a file the producer
deliberately left out. Filters that decide from the path alone are now
applied when recording. A block filter is handed the source file and may
consult coverage that does not exist yet, so those still fall to the
merging process, which is why Filter#path_only? defaults to false.

Injection read branch_coverage? and friends off the merging process,
which for `simplecov merge` never ran SimpleCov.start at all. An injected
file given fewer tables than the files beside it is what inflates the
percentage #1059 fixed, so the criteria now come from the merged data.
The configuration is consulted only when the merge carried no files and
there is nothing to be consistent with.

Tracked paths were collected before drop_expired_results, so a resultset
dropped for being past merge_timeout still contributed paths and a file
only a stale run ever tracked was simulated in at 0%. merge_valid_results
now yields the surviving entries, and both merge entry points collect
from those.

Each fix has a spec that fails against the behaviour it replaces.

Fix CommandGuesser mislabelling suites from incidental path substrings

The framework patterns were bare substrings matched against
"#{$PROGRAM_NAME} #{ARGV.join(' ')}", so a "test/" anywhere in that
string decided the suite name. A Ruby installed under a "latest/bin"
directory (the layout mise creates) put "test/" in the path of every
binary run through it, and because "test/" is checked before "spec/",
RSpec and Cucumber suites alike came out as "Unit Tests". Arguments were
affected too, so "rspec spec/greatest/foo_spec.rb" was mislabelled the
same way. Under merging the command name is the resultset key, so a
mislabelled suite was filed under the wrong key rather than failing
loudly.

The patterns now match only at a path segment boundary, where a boundary
is the start of the string, whitespace, a forward slash, or a backslash.
Counting only forward slashes would drop matches the bare substrings used
to make on a Windows argument like "spec\foo_spec.rb", and no CI job
catches that: windows-latest invokes with forward slashes, and a
recognized executable short-circuits before the patterns run.

Segment matching alone would have regressed "rspec features", an RSpec
suite whose examples live in features/, which passed before only because
the unanchored "spec" pattern matched the letters inside "rspec". So the
invoked executable is now consulted first. Generic runners are
deliberately absent from that table, letting "ruby test/integration/
foo_test.rb" and rake's test loader still reach the path patterns that
draw the unit, functional, and integration distinction.

The executable is read from $PROGRAM_NAME, recorded separately as
CommandGuesser.original_program_name. Recovering it from the flattened
command by taking the first token would truncate a program path that
contains a space, so "/opt/My Ruby/bin/rspec features" would lose the
executable and be claimed by the features pattern. Assigning the
flattened command clears the recorded name so the two cannot describe
different runs, and callers that set only the command still get the
first-token derivation.

Reported with an exemplary diagnosis by @andriytyurnikov, who also
verified the fix on an affected machine and found the Windows gap.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1249.

Fan the collate merge out across forked worker processes

Collating a large CI matrix spends nearly all its wall clock reading,
parsing and folding the shards in sequence. SimpleCov.collate takes a new
processes: argument that runs that fold across that many forked workers.
Collating 160 real resultsets from a 231k line Rails app on a 4-core CI
node went from 49s to 30s, and on the repository's own benchmark 160
resultsets covering 1,836 files went from 4.53s at the default to 1.35s
across 8 workers.

Each worker folds a contiguous slice of the file list and ships its
[command_names, coverage] pair back over a pipe, and the collating process
folds the slices back in order. Visiting the resultsets in the order a
single-process merge visits them makes the report identical rather than
merely equivalent, and a differential spec checks that against an
independently stated reference merge across different fan-out groupings,
since splitting a fold requires it to be associative and not only ordered.

processes: defaults to the SIMPLECOV_CONCURRENCY environment variable, or 1
when it is unset, so one rake task can serve CI runners of different sizes.
One process never forks, so existing calls take exactly the path they always
have. The count is deliberately not clamped to the core count and not gated
on a minimum number of resultsets, because only the caller knows what a
collate job may use. Anything below 1 is taken as 1, and asking for more
processes than there are files gives one file per process.

Every failure path returns nil rather than a partial merge and the caller
redoes the fold in this process, because reporting a subset of the
resultsets would silently understate coverage. That covers a runtime that
cannot fork (JRuby, TruffleRuby, Windows), a worker that died, and a
truncated payload. Workers are drained on a thread each so every pipe is
read while they are still writing, since a payload larger than the pipe
buffer would otherwise block its worker mid-write while the parent blocked
reaping it. Children end with exit! so they never fall through to the
collating process's inherited at_exit handlers.

Keep branch and method data the resultsets carried

A merge runs on behalf of the processes that produced the resultsets and
does not necessarily share their configuration. `simplecov merge` only
requires the library, so it never runs SimpleCov.start and measures
nothing, and a SimpleCov.collate block need not repeat enable_coverage
:branch. Such a process dropped the branch table from every file that
appeared in more than one resultset, while passing through untouched the
table of any file that appeared in only one:

  merging process branch_coverage? false
    sample.rb      keys=["lines"]              branches GONE
    resultset1.rb  keys=["lines", "branches"]  branches kept

So the merged output was both lossy and internally inconsistent, and
merge_and_store wrote that state back to disk for the next collate to
read.

A criterion is now in play when the merging process measures it or when
tuples that survive reconciliation carried it. Nothing measured is lost,
and a process that does measure a criterion still always gets a table,
even an empty one, which is what lets SourceFile tell "no branches in
this file" apart from "branch coverage was off".

Which tuples survive needs two things said. A simulated side's
synthesized tuples are dropped when the other side ran, and the criterion
goes with them: keeping an empty table there would claim the file has no
branches when the truth is that nobody measured them in the run that
executed it. The side that ran therefore decides which criteria the file
carries, not only their tuples, which is also what keeps the answer
independent of which side is absorbed first.

And a side is only judged when it can be. Absent lines do not mean a side
never ran: a branch-only or method-only run omits them even for the files
it loaded, so judging on their absence discarded the real branch counts
such a run had measured. Unknown now means union, which is already what
happened when neither side carried lines. never_executed_files guards the
same conflation for the same reason.

This predates the accumulator. FilesCombiner gated on the same
configuration before it, so the behaviour goes back well beyond the merge
rewrite.

Judge never-loaded files only by their relevant lines

Re-deriving a merged result's not-loaded set from the merged line
counts flagged any file that never executed a line, but a loaded file
need not have executed anything. A file with no executable lines at
all, such as a comment-only constants stub, reports every line as
nil, so the merge marked it never-loaded and the rule from
https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/902 turned its
branch and method coverage into 0% even though a process really did
load it. That misread can fail minimum_coverage_by_file under those
criteria and renders the file as not loaded in reports.

A file is now judged only when it carries at least one relevant line.
Genuinely unloaded files still carry judgeable data because
SimulateCoverage gives a simulated file a 0 on every relevant line,
and a simulated file with no relevant lines is already flagged by the
injection step reporting it.

This tightens the unreleased fix for
https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1250 before it
ships.

Match each Ruby's constant folding in the static extractor

A statically-known-truthy/falsy condition is folded by the compiler:
Coverage emits no branch for the condition, and the dead arm's whole
subtree is eliminated with it. The extractor synthesized tuples for
both, so a tracked-but-unloaded file with an "if false ... end" block
around disabled code gained phantom, permanently-missed branches and
phantom uncovered methods, the same unmergeable-tuple failure mode
the folding support exists to prevent. The visitor now asks the fold
for a truthiness verdict and visits only the live arm. A falsy
predicate's elsif chain is its subsequent IfNode, so visiting it
emits the plain if branch Coverage keeps.

The folding table matches the compiler literal for literal, verified
against real Coverage. __LINE__, __ENCODING__, and a stabby lambda
fold like the simple literals, while their lookalikes stay tracked on
purpose: a lambda call proves nothing at compile time where the ->
literal proves everything. Parentheses are transparent to the fold
for most literals, but a parenthesized nil, string, or stabby lambda
keeps its real branch while (true), (1), (:s), (__LINE__), and the
rest fold like their bare forms.

The fold is also version-aware, because CRuby 3.4 rebuilt it on the
Prism compiler and the parse.y fold it replaced differed in three
observable ways, verified against real Coverage on 3.2 and 3.3.
__FILE__ folded there but no longer does, being a string to everyone
but the modern compiler. Parentheses were transparent for every
literal on 3.2, so (nil), ("x"), and (-> {}) all fold there, and
(__FILE__) is opaque like other strings from 3.3 on. And on 3.2 a
folded condition's dead arm keeps its nested branch table entries,
even inside dead def bodies and lambdas, because parse.y instrumented
branches before eliminating dead code. Dead defs never register on
any version, so 3.2 visits the dead arm with method collection
suppressed.

The runtime tuple equivalence battery pins all of this against the
running Ruby's Coverage across the CI version matrix, and the
fuzzer's if-like sites (if, elsif, unless, ternary, and the modifier
forms) now draw a compile-time literal a quarter of the time so fold
verdicts and dead-arm elimination are exercised under random nesting.
Loops and case subjects keep the never-constant pool, since loops do
not fold regardless. The sequential id assignment spec had also been
asserting nothing since folding landed: its "if true" conditions fold
away, so the id list it checks was empty and both expectations passed
vacuously. Its conditions are non-literal now, and it pins the
expected tuple count so it cannot go quietly vacuous again.

Keep the accumulator to its documented merge promises

The comment on CoverageAccumulator.executed? says the Array() coercion
keeps a malformed lines entry to a wrong answer instead of a
NoMethodError out of the middle of a merge, but it only delivered that
for nil and scalar numbers. A Hash coerces to pairs and a String to
itself, and neither responds to positive?, so exactly the hand-edited
or foreign resultset the comment worries about still crashed the
merge. Counting only Numeric values delivers the promise and treats a
JSON float like an integer while it's at it.

The accumulator also documents that method coverage stays nil until
some resultset actually carries methods, and the union path honors
that, but the two executed-vs-simulated reconcile paths promoted to an
empty table whenever method coverage was merely measured. An
executed-plus-simulated pair with no methods anywhere answered {}
where the same data all-executed answered nil, and since the merged
shape is persisted into .resultset.json and the fold does distinguish
nil from {} on later absorbs, the inconsistency fed forward rather
than washing out. The drop path now promotes only when the discarded
side carried a methods table, and the replace path keeps an empty
table only when the replaced side had carried one, so the answer no
longer depends on which side was absorbed first. Branch tables are
untouched, they always materialize once branch coverage is measured.

Let formatters= opt out with false like formatter does

The formatter setter documents false as the way to skip formatting
entirely, and normalizes it to nil. The plural setter's Array
normalization from 1.0.1 turned the same false into [false], quietly
configuring a MultiFormatter over a value that can only fail, so every
report printed "Formatter false failed with NoMethodError" instead of
skipping formatting. Normalize false to empty before wrapping, so nil,
false, and [] all mean the same explicit opt-out on both setters.

Scope the resultset lock flag reset to the acquiring call

ResultsetStore.synchronize reset its reentrancy flag in a method-level
ensure, which also runs when a nested call early-returns. The first
nested call therefore cleared the flag while the outer call still held
the flock, and a second sibling nested call would re-enter the flock
path, open a second fd on the lock file, and block forever against its
own process. Nothing nests twice today, so the deadlock was latent,
and the existing reentrancy spec exercised only single nesting so it
could never catch it.

The reset now lives in an ensure around only the acquiring branch, and
the reentrancy coverage gains the sibling-nesting shape, which
deadlocks in under a second on the previous code.

Read the HTML template and report JSON as UTF-8 explicitly

File.read without an encoding tags what it reads with the locale's
Encoding.default_external, which minimal CI containers resolve to
US-ASCII and Windows to a code page. For format_from_json that is a
live crash: a coverage.json carrying non-ASCII source ("135°C") hits
Encoding::InvalidByteSequenceError in JSON.parse before the template
is even touched. For the template read it is a trap primed for the
first non-ASCII character a frontend build ships: substituting the
UTF-8 payload into a template tagged with a non-UTF-8 encoding raises
Encoding::CompatibilityError inside the at_exit hook, and it works
today only because the compiled template happens to be pure ASCII.

Both reads now pass encoding: Encoding::UTF_8, and the specs exercise
format and format_from_json under a US-ASCII default external.

Clear a pre-1.0.4 report's sibling files when formatting

A coverage directory written by 1.0.0 through 1.0.3 keeps its
coverage_data.js, application.js, application.css, and the three
favicon PNGs after upgrading to the single-file report, since nothing
ever wrote over or removed them. The stale coverage_data.js is worse
than clutter because simplecov serve happily serves it next to the new
report. Formatting now deletes those six known names from the output
directory, leaving anything else in it alone.

Tolerate malformed resultset data in parsing and merging

ResultsetFile tolerates a missing, empty, or unparseable
.resultset.json by warning and returning an empty hash, but valid JSON
of the wrong shape sailed through. A top-level array or string parses
fine and then crashes merge_valid_results, which iterates
command => data pairs, with a NoMethodError out of the middle of a
merge. A non-Hash now gets the same warn-and-continue treatment as a
parse failure, and a "null" file keeps its long-standing meaning of an
empty resultset with no warning.

The merge hot loop had the same gap one layer down. LinesCombiner has
two entry points with different tolerance: combine's
merge_line_coverage coerces a malformed count with to_i, while the hot
loop the accumulator actually uses did raw addition, so a "3" from a
hand-edited or foreign resultset concatenated strings or raised
TypeError mid-merge depending on the other side. The loop now coerces
anything that isn't already an Integer, keeping the well-formed fast
path branch-for-branch what it was, and merge_into gains the unit
specs it never had.

Delegate the parallel merger's serial fallback to ResultMerger

When absorb_results answers nil the fan-out never ran and the serial
path is exactly ResultMerger.merge_results, but merge_results
re-implemented its absorb-plus-collector wiring inline. Delegating
keeps one authoritative spelling of the serial merge and leaves the
parallel path's create_result call the only thing this method owns.

Close the failing spawn's own pipe when fork raises

spawn_workers cleans up the workers it already spawned when a later
fork raises, but the pipe created for the very spawn that failed
belonged to nobody: both descriptors were abandoned to the GC while
EAGAIN propagated. An ensure now owns the pair, always closing the
parent's writer end and closing the reader too when no child was
spawned to feed it. Steep cannot type body locals inside an ensure,
hence the ignore markers, following the Marshal.load precedent in
read_payload.

The ensure's nil-safe arms also cover the case where IO.pipe itself
raises (EMFILE) and there is no pair to close. Nothing exercised that
arm, which the dogfood's 100% branch enforcement rightly flagged, so
a spec now drives spawn_worker through a failing IO.pipe and expects
the original error to surface unmasked.

Keep the nocov toggle in the classify call, not the instance

LinesClassifier carried its :nocov: skip toggle in an ivar, so a
classifier instance shared between concurrent classify calls would
interleave their toggles. Every current call site instantiates per
call, making the hazard latent, but nothing enforced that. The state
now lives in a one-slot box each call owns, one allocation per file
rather than per line, so the hot loop's shape is unchanged and the
instance is safely reusable.

Apply small cleanups from the pre-1.0.4 review

IF_NODE_SUBSEQUENT_METHOD and ELSE_CLAUSE_METHOD were defined in
visitor.rb after it had already required location_conventions and
value_position, both of which reference them. That worked only
because every reference happens at call time, a load-order trap for
the next editor. They now live in PrismCompat, required first by each
consumer, together with the subsequent and else_clause helpers that
LocationConventions and ValuePositions had each spelled out for
themselves.

The rationale for printing formatter status lines with $stderr.puts
rather than warn lived as a verbatim comment-plus-rubocop-disable
pair in both HTMLFormatter#format and JSONFormatter#format.
Base#emit_status now owns the guard and the explanation, each
formatter's format ends with one call, and the stderr contract specs
cover both unchanged.

Nothing in lib has called LinesCombiner.combine or
merge_line_coverage since the accumulator took over the fold, only
their own specs did. The relevance-rule documentation (nil + nil =
nil, nil + int = int, int + int = sum) moves onto merge_into, the
entry point that actually runs, and the specs now pin those rules
there, including the non-mutation of the source array.
BranchesCombiner.combine and MethodsCombiner.combine stay: the branch
one has a live caller (ResultAdapter's eval-duplicate dedup) and both
are the pairwise unit-spec seam. Their stale "built by combine above"
comments now name absorb, which is what builds those tables on every
path.

MergedFile#new_table was public but purely internal, so it moves
below private. Three sites in LocationConventions hand-built the same
"start of A through end of B" PointLocation and now share a span
helper. And UnloadedFileInjector (the mechanism: expand globs,
simulate files) and ResultMerger::UnloadedFiles (the merge-time
policy: when to inject, which criteria simulated files carry) are
easy names to confuse, so each module's comment now points at the
other and says which half it owns.

The review also found redundant specs. The HTML formatter's bare
"embeds a window.SIMPLECOV_DATA script" example was fully subsumed by
the parseable-JSON one, and the self-contained assertions were split
between two examples in two describe blocks. One example now pins the
whole self-contained property (DOCTYPE, inlined style and script, no
sibling-file references). The results_combiner "reconciling a
simulated file against an executed one" block re-tested exactly what
coverage_accumulator_spec pins in both absorption orders and is gone.
Also swaps the two shell-outs to rm for the FileUtils.rm_f the rest
of the file already uses.

Share one differential harness between the battery and the fuzzer

The deterministic construct battery and the opt-in fuzzer each carried
a private copy of the same machinery: write programs to files, load
them under Coverage(branches: true) in one subprocess, parse the
payload, and strip process-local ids for comparison. The copies had
already drifted (the fuzzer silenced $VERBOSE and tolerated programs
with no branch entries, the battery did neither). Both now use
CoverageDifferential in spec/support, keeping the fuzzer's more
robust variants, so a divergence found by one can be replayed verbatim
in the other and the next convention fix edits one harness.

The harness also stops discarding the subprocess's stderr. A fixture
that raises while being loaded under Coverage reports its error there,
and the harness captured that output and then dropped it, leaving a
failure message with no cause in it. It is appended to the failure
message now.

Speed up the cucumber suite

The merge_timeout scenario proved a resultset expires by really
waiting five seconds, which was a twentieth of the whole suite's wall
clock spent in a sleep. The merge only ever compares the timestamps
recorded in .resultset.json against merge_timeout, so aging those
timestamps is equivalent and instant. The scenario backdates by six
seconds to sit safely past the five second timeout, and the
now-unused wait step is gone.

The install step was the other standing per-scenario cost. It
unconditionally deleted the sandbox's Gemfile.lock and ran a full
bundle resolve. bundle check against the shipped lock answers in
under a third of the time when the installed gems already satisfy it,
which is every run after the first. A miss, including a lockfile
written by a conflicting bundler on another Ruby version, still falls
back to the original drop-the-lock-and-resolve path.

What remained was almost entirely subprocess and browser time: 135
child test-suite runs at under a second each, plus headless Chrome
assertions, executed one scenario at a time. That parallelizes nearly
linearly, so rake cucumber now runs parallel_cucumber, which splits
the 51 feature files across CPU-count workers and brings the suite
from 90 to 17 seconds on a 14-core machine while CI runners get a
proportional win. rake cucumber:serial keeps the old single-process
runner for debugging without worker interleaving, and JRuby's
cucumber-less fallback still just warns.

Two pieces make the workers safe. Each gets its own Aruba sandbox,
tmp/aruba for the first and tmp/arubaN beyond it, with the Capybara
rack app serving the report out of that same per-worker directory.
And parallel_tests' worker environment is scrubbed from the commands
the scenarios spawn, because SimpleCov inside the spawned projects
reads the same TEST_ENV_NUMBER convention and would defer its report
to a final parallel_tests process that never runs, failing every
scenario that expects a report. Scenarios that exercise
parallel_tests for real set those variables explicitly and are
unaffected.

The retry safety net is gone at the same time. The suite ran with
--retry 3 --no-strict-flaky, which reruns a failing scenario up to
three times and counts an eventually-green one as a pass instead of
reporting it flaky, hiding real intermittent failures behind silently
slower runs. Every scenario now has to pass on its first attempt,
verified with five parallel runs and three serial ones, all 105
scenarios passing each time. The comment on Aruba's exit_timeout
keeps the history of why retries were the wrong tool for cold-cache
slowness.

Update the Rails test project dependency to ~> 8.1

Bump the rspec_rails test project from Rails ~> 7.2.3.1 to ~> 8.1 and
Puma from ~> 7.0 to ~> 8.0, along with the routine lockfile refresh
that regenerating the locks brings in.

Refuse unsafe simplecov clean targets

simplecov clean removes the coverage directory wholesale, so a
coverage_dir that resolves to ".", the project root, or an ancestor
of either (a stray relative path or misconfigured dotfile is enough)
would delete far more than a coverage report. clean now canonicalizes
its target through realpath and refuses to run when the target is the
current directory, the project root located through .simplecov, or an
ancestor of either, printing the refusal to stderr and exiting 1
before touching anything.

Identify workers in current parallel runs

The final parallel worker decides that its siblings have all reported
by counting entries in .resultset.json, but that count is a guess. An
entry left by an earlier invocation inside merge_timeout can satisfy
the wait early, and the settle heuristic can declare a run complete on
stale data. Each stored result now carries the invocation's run id and
its worker's id, the wait counts the distinct workers that have
written for the current run rather than raw resultset entries, and
merging recognizes a concurrent runner by shared run id instead of
only by timestamp freshness.

The run id comes from SIMPLECOV_RUN_ID when set, from parallel_tests'
per-invocation pid file, from the parent pid for other local adapters,
or is freshly random. Whether the id alone proves same-run membership
depends on that provenance (a parent-pid id is shared by consecutive
runs launched from one long-lived parent), so the answer is decided
where the id is generated and memoized alongside it, never re-inferred
from the id's string shape, and a non-authoritative match still
requires a fresh timestamp. Distributed or custom runners whose
workers do not share a launcher process should export the same
SIMPLECOV_RUN_ID in every worker.

A mismatched run id alone does not prove an entry is leftover state,
though. A shelled-out test runner (fork+exec, like system("rspec"))
does not inherit the parent's memoized run id, and SIMPLECOV_RUN_ID
is not exported to child environments, so the child stores its entry
under a random id of its own. Treating that entry as stale would let
the parent's near-empty result overwrite the child's real coverage,
the exact data loss the merged_entry guard exists to prevent. See
https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/581.
concurrent_runner_entry? therefore falls back to the timestamp when
run ids do not match, using a strictly-after comparison so an entry
stamped at the exact instant we started still counts as leftover from
a previous run. Worker counting keeps the strict id match, where
admitting a stale entry would end a sibling wait early.

Worker identities read back from a resultset are namespaced pairs,
[:worker, id] for entries that carry a worker id and [:legacy, command
name] for fresh entries written without one, so a resultset mixing
entries written with and without worker ids can never alias a real
worker id to a synthesized legacy identity.

Correct per-file statistics across criteria

Strength, the average number of executions per coverable unit, was
only computed for line coverage. Branch and method statistics never
passed a total_strength, so their strength was a constant 0.0, and
the line sum ran over every line in the file, letting hits on ignored
lines inflate the average of the lines that actually count. One
shared helper now builds the CoverageStatistics for all three
criteria, summing hit counts across the relevant items only and
dividing by covered plus missed, so branch and method strength carry
real values and ignored lines no longer contribute. Never-loaded
tracked files keep their pinned 0% branch and method coverage, and
the schema descriptions now spell out the formula.

The JSON formatter's per-file total_methods had the same blind spot
for ignored items: it counted every parsed method, ignored ones
included, so a file with an ignored method reported a total that
neither covered_methods plus missed_methods nor
methods_covered_percent agreed with. The total is now the sum of
covered and missed, matching how the percent is computed, while the
per-method array still lists every method.

Make configuration block context explicit

Evaluating a configuration block used to copy the caller's instance
variables onto the configuration object and copy them back when the
block finished. That mingles two unrelated sets of state. A caller
variable such as @root shadows the real configuration while the block
runs, so cached values like coverage_path derive from the caller's
data, anything the block assigns travels back out to the caller
instead of remaining configuration state, and the copying rejects
frozen and immediate-value owners, breaks overlapping and nested
evaluations, and leaks state between threads touching the caller
during evaluation.

Configuration block context is now explicit. A zero-parameter block
runs via instance_exec with self bound to the real configuration
target, preserving normal Ruby identity, binding, require_relative,
__dir__, nesting, and backtraces, so idioms like root __dir__
evaluate from the file that defines the block. A block that needs
caller helpers or instance variables accepts the target as an
argument and keeps its lexical self, as in
SimpleCov.configure { |config| config.add_filter @filter }. Caller
state is never copied onto SimpleCov, and configure raises
ArgumentError when called without a block.

Serialize resultset access across threads

The resultset store guarded reentrancy with a single module-level
@locked flag, and that flag is shared by every thread in the process.
Once one thread set it and took the file lock, any sibling thread saw
@locked as true and walked straight into the critical section with no
lock at all, so two threads in one process could read and rewrite
.resultset.json concurrently.

A Monitor now serializes threads ahead of the process-wide flock.
Reentrancy keys off mon_owned?, so only the thread holding the lock
bypasses a nested flock (which would deadlock on a second descriptor
for the same lock file) while sibling threads block until the owner
releases it. The specs exercise the new behavior deterministically
with queues and a pipe-driven child process instead of sleeps,
covering nested and sibling calls, blocked sibling threads, lock
release when the critical section raises, and cross-process blocking.

Fail diff on any coverage regression

The --fail-on-drop flag only inspected each row's line delta, so a
change that held line coverage steady while losing branch or method
coverage still exited zero and sailed through the very CI gate the
flag exists to provide. The exit code now trips when any reported
criterion slipped, taking the minimum of a row's line, branch, and
method deltas. The single-call emit_json wrapper is inlined along the
way.

Switch between line coverage modes

Enabling :oneshot_line already evicted :line, since Ruby cannot
measure both at once, but the replacement only worked in that one
direction. Enabling :line after :oneshot_line kept both criteria, and
starting coverage then passed both incompatible modes to
Coverage.start, which raised RuntimeError: cannot enable lines and
oneshot_lines simultaneously.

The two line modes now replace each other in either direction, so the
last requested mode wins, including within a single variadic
enable_coverage call. Replacing the mode that also serves as the
primary criterion resets the primary to an enabled default rather
than leaving it pointing at a criterion that is no longer enabled.

Reserve implicit Ungrouped group name

Files that match no configured group land in an implicit "Ungrouped"
bucket, and a user-defined group with that same name was silently
overwritten during result processing, discarding whatever files it
had matched. Configuring a group named Ungrouped now raises
SimpleCov::ConfigurationError, and result processing validates the
group keys it receives, so an assigned groups hash cannot smuggle the
name in either.

Group names are also normalized when configured. A name is a Hash
key, a report label, and a JSON object key all at once, so a Symbol
name now means the same group as its String spelling (group
:Ungrouped is rejected like the string form, and a symbol-named group
can no longer produce a duplicate JSON key next to a string-named
one), and a name that is neither a String nor a Symbol raises
SimpleCov::ConfigurationError. Group configuration moves out of the
filters file into its own configuration/groups.rb alongside the new
GroupNames module.

Regenerate frontend with locked esbuild

The checked-in template drifts from the html_frontend sources when it
is built with whatever esbuild happens to be installed, and then every
source change diffs as a wholesale rewrite of the minified bundle.
Rebuilding with the lockfile's esbuild makes the template
byte-for-byte reproducible, so future diffs show only what the source
change actually did.

Keep user groups distinct from built-in report sections

The viewer derives each file list's DOM id from its display title,
and that mapping leaked collisions in two ways. The hex encoding that
fixed https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1038 uses
underscores to delimit escaped characters but left literal
underscores unescaped, so a group named with the literal escape
spelling of another's punctuation (By/group next to By_2f_group)
produced the same id and one tab opened the wrong file list. And
because the overall All Files section was encoded through the same
title-to-id path as user groups, a configured group named All Files
shared the overall section's id and tab target outright.

toHtmlId now escapes underscores too, so every distinct title yields
a distinct id, and renderFileList takes an explicit containerId
instead of deriving one from the title. The overall section gets the
fixed id g-total while groups encode under a group- prefix, so the
built-in section and a like-named group keep separate identities. The
cucumber group step no longer mirrors the encoder to reconstruct ids,
it walks the containers in document order instead, and a new step
clicks every tab and asserts each one reveals exactly its own file
list, so the scenarios check behavior rather than the encoding
scheme.

simplecov report --json had the same collision one surface over: it
flattened the overall "All Files" entry and every configured group
into one JSON object keyed by section name, so a user group that
happened to be named All Files silently overwrote the overall totals.
The payload now keeps separate namespaces, emitting
{"total": {...}, "groups": {...}}, which preserves both sections no
matter what a group is called. The text report keeps its flat listing
but labels the colliding user section "All Files (group)" so the two
lines are distinguishable there too.

Scope sort state to each report table

The sorter keyed its remembered column and direction on the table's
id, but the report's file-list tables have no ids, so every table fell
through to the same "default" key and shared one sort state. Clicking
a column already selected in another group then took the toggle
branch, reversing rows that were never sorted while displaying an
ascending indicator. The state now lives in a WeakMap keyed on the
table element itself, so each group's table tracks its own sort and
the id-or-attribute fallback naming goes away.

A new cucumber scenario sorts one group, switches to another, sorts
the same column there, and asserts both the resulting row order and
the ascending indicator, exercising exactly the cross-table bleed.

Handle invalid coverage JSON in CLI commands

The read-only CLI commands only guarded against a missing input file.
A malformed or unreadable coverage.json, or one whose root or
"coverage" field is not an object, escaped as a raw JSON parser or IO
backtrace, and uncovered borrowed report's loader, so its input
errors were labeled "simplecov report".

A shared CLI::CoverageFile boundary now loads the document for
coverage, report, uncovered, and both inputs to diff. Each failure
returns status 1 with one diagnostic line naming the command that was
actually run, and the boundary validates only the stable outer shape,
so coverage.json files from older schema versions remain readable.

Harden the frontend asset build and verify it in CI

The asset rake tasks shelled out to whatever esbuild happened to be on
PATH, and the CSS minifier's IO.popen never checked the subprocess's
exit status, so a rejected stylesheet quietly yielded empty output and
a "successful" build replaced the checked-in report template with a
stylesheet-free page. The build now resolves esbuild from
html_frontend/node_modules/.bin (raising with a bun install hint when
it is missing) so the version comes from bun.lock rather than the
environment, and minify_css runs through Open3.capture3 and raises
with the exit status and stderr when esbuild fails. A spec drives
minify_css against a stub esbuild that exits 42 to prove the failure
surfaces.

A new assets:check task recompiles the frontend and fails on any git
diff against the checked-in template, and the typecheck workflow runs
it (with a frozen bun lockfile), so a dependency update or source
change can no longer leave the compiled index.html stale. The
workflow pins setup-ruby to the latest stable Ruby, since the
repository has no .ruby-version file for the action to discover.

Honor primary coverage in SimpleFormatter

SimpleFormatter always printed line coverage because its no-argument
covered_percent call reads the line statistic, so a project configured
with primary_coverage :branch or :method got a per-file listing of the
wrong criterion despite the documented primary-criterion behavior.
Each file's percentage now comes from the configured primary coverage,
routed through SimpleCov.coverage_statistics_key so an :oneshot_line
primary correctly reads the normalized line statistics it is folded
into.

Streamline the JSON formatter's internals

The "is line coverage being reported" question was spelled as a pair
of coverage_criterion_enabled? calls for :line and :oneshot_line in
three places (FileList's reporting criteria, the result hash's
meta.line_coverage flag, and SourceFileFormatter's emit decision),
each with its own comment explaining the oneshot synonym. All three
now ask the existing SimpleCov.line_coverage? predicate, which already
encodes that synonym, so the emit decisions cannot drift apart and the
specs stub one predicate instead of two criterion queries.

The three JSON formatter helpers (ResultHashFormatter,
SourceFileFormatter, and ErrorsFormatter) held their inputs in
instance variables only to thread them between private methods, and
ErrorsFormatter's memoized @errors hash meant a reused instance would
keep accumulating violations across calls. They become stateless class
methods that take the result or source file as an argument, callers no
longer construct throwaway instances, and every serialization builds a
fresh errors hash, which a new spec pins down.

Disambiguate colliding HTML file IDs

The viewer identifies each source file by its SHA-1 truncated to 8 hex
characters, and with enough files two paths can truncate to the same
id, leaving one file's detail link opening the other's source. The id
allocator now buckets filenames by their truncated hash and, within a
colliding bucket, sorts the names and appends a deterministic numeric
suffix to every entry after the first. Non-colliding files keep the
exact fragment they had before, so existing bookmarked links stay
valid, and fileId now raises on a filename that was never precomputed
instead of silently returning undefined.

A new cucumber feature covers two files whose names truncate to the
same hash and walks the report's detail view for each, proving every
source link opens its own file.

Support HTML reports without line coverage

The viewer assumed every report carries line statistics, so a run
configured with disable_coverage :line crashed while dereferencing
absent line data (the overall percentage read data.total.lines, every
file list rendered a Line Coverage column from stats.lines, and the
source renderer indexed data.lines unconditionally). The types now
admit their real shape, StatGroup and FileCoverage mark all line
fields optional, and a new coverage module picks the active criterion
from the report metadata, preferring the configured primary criterion
when its data is present and falling back to whichever of line,
branch, or method coverage exists.

Rendering keys off that selection everywhere line coverage used to be
hardwired. Tab percentages, the favicon color band, and each group's
covered_percent come from the primary criterion's stats, the line
column, its data attributes, the covered and missed source legend
entries, and the per-line hit annotations all appear only when line
coverage is enabled, and the file summary shows line coverage as
disabled rather than 0 of 0.

New criterion-only cucumber scenarios drive a branch-only and a
method-only report through the full page, guarded by a
method_coverage_supported? hook. The step helpers are aligned with
the viewer's data shape along the way: the source-files step reads
line and method columns only when the table asks for them, the
summary step's data-attribute map gains the method criterion entry
renderFileRow emits, and the skipped-lines helper tolerates coverage
entries without a lines array.

Share and harden coverage JSON parsing

The CLI's coverage-file boundary and HTMLFormatter#format_from_json
each parsed coverage.json on their own, and each missed something.
The CLI tagged the bytes as UTF-8 without checking them, so invalid
input sailed through parsing and surfaced later as a
JSON::GeneratorError backtrace, while format_from_json accepted any
well-formed JSON regardless of shape and created its output directory
before checking anything, so a viewer-less document failed only at
view time.

A shared SimpleCov::CoverageJSON.load now reads the bytes, rejects
invalid UTF-8, and requires an object root, converting parser
failures into one domain error both consumers rescue.
format_from_json also validates the viewer's required sections and
each coverage entry's source array before creating the target
directory or replacing an existing index.html, so a bad input can no
longer destroy a good report.

Build missing HTML reports before serving

simplecov serve only checked that the coverage directory existed, so a
directory holding just coverage.json (a run that never produced the
HTML report) bound a server that could only 404 the index. A new
ReportPreparer now runs before the socket binds. An existing
index.html is served untouched, keeping a self-contained report usable
even when its optional sidecar JSON was later removed or damaged. When
the index is missing but coverage.json is present, the preparer builds
the self-contained report from the JSON. When neither artifact exists,
or the JSON cannot produce a usable report, serve exits with one
diagnostic instead of binding at all.

Publish merged results only from final processes

With merging enabled, every parallel worker stored its slice and then
read the resultset back, waiting on its siblings and caching whatever
partial merge existed at that moment. Only the exit path also checked
final_result_process?, so merge ownership was split across two
predicates that each call site had to combine correctly.

merge_finalization_owner? now folds final_result_process? in, so a
non-final worker stops after storing its own result and the adapter's
selected final process alone waits for siblings, merges, formats,
enforces thresholds, and writes .last_run.json. An explicit
SimpleCov.collate keeps ownership regardless of worker identity.

Share atomic artifact writes

Artifact writing was spelled four ways: the HTML formatter carried
its own temp-and-rename helper, .last_run.json and the resultset
store each built a temp name from the process id alone, which two
threads in one process share, and the JSON formatter and simplecov
merge wrote in place, so a concurrent reader could catch a partially
written document.

A shared SimpleCov::AtomicFile.write now backs all of them. It stages
content in a Tempfile.create name in the destination directory, so
concurrent writers cannot collide, then renames over the target, so
readers see either the old file or the complete new one. Existing
Unix permission bits are carried over to the replacement (a fresh
file gets 0666 masked by the umask), and each artifact keeps its
historical byte format, including the trailing newline the puts-based
writers emitted.

Build source-less HTML data in one pass

With source_in_json false the HTML formatter called
JSONFormatter.build_hash twice, once with source for the embedded
viewer payload and once without for coverage.json, so it traversed the
whole result and queried Git a second time solely to omit each file's
source field. The source-less payload is now derived from the
source-bearing hash by stripping the :source entry from each coverage
value into a fresh hash, leaving the viewer payload untouched. The
spec asserts build_hash runs exactly once and that coverage.json
equals the embedded payload minus source.

Reorganize the formatter, serve, and CLI specs

The HTML and JSON formatter specs, plus stderr_output_spec, each
re-tested Formatter::Base behavior through their own subclass, so the
status line's stderr contract, criterion ordering, zero-total
suppression, percent flooring, colorization, and the
displayable_output_path relativization fallbacks were all specified
two or three times over. A new spec/formatter/base_spec.rb now
exercises Base directly through a minimal subclass, and the subclass
specs keep only what they own, the entry point named in the HTML
status line and the JSON prefix on the JSON one.

The serve coverage had two end-to-end specs that both spun a real
server and asserted a 200 body, one through the run entry point and
one against serve_loop alone. The serve_loop spec folds into the
run-level spec, which now also asserts the 404 path, and a focused
with_server spec doubles TCPServer to pin close-on-raise without
binding a socket. cli_spec also requires "coverage" itself instead of
depending on another spec file having loaded it first, so it passes
when run in isolation.

Centralize formatter dispatch

Result#format! and MultiFormatter both spelled the same two-step,
normalize the configured formatter through Formatter.instance_for and
then call #format on it. A new Formatter.format owns that pairing, so
both call sites dispatch through one spelling. The README now also
documents that a ready-built formatter instance receives #format
directly, which is what lets constructor options carry through to
report generation.

Validate HTML viewer data before rendering

HTMLFormatter#format_from_json only checked that the four top-level
sections were objects and that each coverage entry carried a source
array, so a coverage.json with broken metadata, missing totals for an
enabled criterion, or non-string source lines embedded cleanly and
crashed later in the browser viewer, which dereferences those fields
without defensive fallbacks. The checks move out of the formatter into
a dedicated ViewerDataValidator that covers everything the viewer
touches, the meta strings and ISO 8601 timestamp, boolean coverage
flags, numeric statistic fields for every enabled criterion in the
total and in each group, string filename lists on groups, and string
source lines per file.

Validation still runs before the output directory is created or an
existing report is replaced, and each rejection names the offending
key with a located message such as total.lines.covered must be a
numeric.

Restrict filename relaxation to bare StringFilter arguments

A StringFilter argument containing a dot always took the filename
substring branch, which prepends [^/]* to the pattern. For a
multi-segment argument such as "app/models/user.rb" that relaxation
made the first segment match as a suffix of a longer segment, so
skipping "app/models/user.rb" also silently dropped files like
"webapp/models/user.rb". The relaxation also lacked a trailing
boundary, so "test.rb" matched a "test.rbx" segment.

Apply the substring relaxation only to bare filenames (arguments
without a slash) and anchor its tail to a dot, slash, or end of
string. Multi-segment dotted paths now use the exact segment-boundary
pattern, and the trailing-slash directory check runs first so dotted
directory arguments keep directory semantics.

Honor enabled: false for oneshot and eval coverage

The oneshot and eval branches of enable_coverage_criterion returned
before consulting the enabled keyword, so a config like
"coverage :line, oneshot: true, enabled: some_flag" or
"coverage :eval, enabled: some_flag" always enabled the criterion,
the opposite of what was written when the flag is false.

Resolve the criterion variant first, then route through the shared
enable or disable path. That also requires disable_coverage(:eval),
which previously raised a misleading "Unsupported coverage criterion"
error for an API that enable_coverage had just accepted, leaving eval
coverage impossible to turn off once enabled. It now switches the
toggle back off, mirroring enable_coverage.

Move the eval toggle into configuration/eval_coverage.rb. It is a
boolean toggle, never a member of the enabled-criteria set, so it gets
its own file in the one-concern-per-file configuration layout.

Harden the CLI against bad dotfiles and arguments

The defensive fallback around reading coverage_dir from a project
dotfile rescued LoadError and StandardError, but a dotfile with a
syntax error makes load raise SyntaxError, a ScriptError that neither
clause catches. That parse error is the very case the fallback's
comment claimed to handle, and it crashed every CLI command in the
affected project with a raw backtrace. Rescue ScriptError instead,
which covers both SyntaxError and LoadError, and restore the
coverage_dir snapshot in an ensure block so a dotfile that raises
after setting coverage_dir cannot leave a host process's configured
dir clobbered.

Argument errors got the same treatment. The CLI had no
OptionParser::ParseError handling anywhere, so a typo'd flag
(simplecov uncovered --bogus) or a malformed typed argument
(simplecov serve --port foo) aborted with an unhandled exception
backtrace. One rescue in the dispatch path now covers every
subcommand and prints a single error line plus a help pointer,
exiting 1. Two adjacent crashes are also gone: simplecov serve
reported bind failures (port already taken, privileged port,
unresolvable host) as raw Errno backtraces and now reports a clean
error, and simplecov uncovered --top -1 raised from Array#first and
now reports an invalid argument.

Tolerate malformed entries in resultset and last-run files

ResultsetFile.decode warned and returned an empty set for a file
whose top-level JSON was not an object, but individual entries were
trusted blindly. A truncated or hand-edited entry (null, missing
timestamp, non-object coverage) crashed the at_exit merge with
NoMethodError or KeyError from within_merge_timeout? or the coverage
fold. Malformed entries are now warned about by command name and
dropped, and well-formed ones still merge.

LastRun.read had the same gap: corrupt JSON raised JSON::ParserError
straight out of the maximum_coverage_drop check, and a valid but
non-object payload raised TypeError from Hash#dig later. Both now
warn and count as no previous run.

Share the coverage.json write between formatters

JSONFormatter and HTMLFormatter each wrote coverage.json their own
way. The concurrent-overwrite warning for issue 1171 lived only in
JSONFormatter, so under the default configuration (HTMLFormatter
alone) a slower parallel worker silently clobbered a sibling's report
even though the guard exists precisely for that case. The two writers
also disagreed on file mode, text for JSON and binary for HTML, which
made the bytes of coverage.json depend on which formatter wrote last
on Windows.

Extract Formatter::CoverageJSONWriter as the single writer: one
pretty-printed binary write plus the overwrite warning for both
formatters. The check also no longer parses the entire previous
report, which by default embeds the project's full source text, just
to read two meta fields. The meta object is flat and sits at the head
of every file the writer produces, so a bounded head read parses just
that slice and falls back to a full parse for foreign key orders.

Serve each connection on its own thread with a read timeout

The serve loop handled connections serially and read requests with
unbounded blocking readline calls, so one stalled connection blocked
every other request. Browsers routinely open speculative sockets that
send no bytes, which made multi-second stalls easy to hit even
without a misbehaving client.

Each accepted connection now gets its own thread, and connection
reads carry a five second idle timeout so abandoned sockets release
their threads instead of pinning them forever.

The HTTP mechanics (request parsing, traversal-safe path resolution,
response writing) move to Serve::StaticFileHandler, leaving Serve
itself as the CLI wiring: option parsing, binding, and the accept
loop.

Align diff threshold and fail-on-drop with their documentation

The usage text promises that --threshold N lists files whose absolute
delta is at least N%, but the filter used a strict comparison, so a
file that moved exactly N% was silently dropped. The threshold is now
inclusive while the epsilon noise floor stays strict.

--fail-on-drop also failed CI when a file was deleted: a removed
file's deltas are all -baseline%, so removing a fully covered file
(dead code cleanup) tripped the gate even though no remaining file
regressed. Removed rows are still listed but no longer count as
drops, and the usage text says so.

Consolidate the CLI subcommands' shared plumbing

The mapping from a coverage criterion to its coverage.json fields
(lines_covered_percent, covered_lines, total_lines, and the branch
and method equivalents) was maintained three times in three shapes:
Coverage::CRITERIA, Uncovered::CRITERION_KEYS, and
Diff::CRITERION_FIELDS. A schema change needed three coordinated
edits. CoverageFile, the shared input boundary all three subcommands
already load through, now carries the single CRITERIA table and the
three local copies are gone.

The subcommands also re-declared the same --input/--json/--no-color
option trio four times, defined an identical one-line error helper
three times differing only in the command name, and printed the
human-readable stats row from the same format string in two places.
All three now live in CommandHelpers, which subcommand modules
extend. The error prefix derives from the module's own name, so a new
subcommand gets correct messages for free, and the uncovered parser
sheds its Metrics/AbcSize disable along the way.

Deduplicate configuration setters and artifact paths

minimum_coverage, maximum_coverage, and maximum_coverage_drop each
carried their own copy of the normalize-Numeric/validate/assign
sequence, and minimum_coverage_by_group inlined the same steps once
more per group. The four now share normalized_threshold, so the
setters stay behaviorally identical by construction and a future
change to the normalization lands in one place.

use_merging and enable_for_subprocesses duplicated the bodies of
merging and merge_subprocesses instead of delegating the way the
other deprecated aliases do, so a behavior change in the replacement
could silently diverge from its alias. Delegating also fixes
use_merging's return value: with merging disabled its final
expression was the skipped guard assignment, so it returned nil where
merging returns false.

existing_report_newer_than_us? built the .last_run.json path by hand
next to the LastRun helper that owns it, so a change to the file's
location would have to land twice to keep the deferred-report check
working. It now asks LastRun.last_run_path.

Make FileList empty-list behavior consistent

least_covered_file crashed with NoMethodError on an empty list
because the min_by result was cast and dereferenced unconditionally.
Result delegates the method publicly, so any caller holding a fully
filtered result hit the crash. It now returns nil.

never_lines and skipped_lines carried dead empty-list guards: sum
over an empty collection already returns 0, and the guards returned a
Float where the sum returns an Integer, so the return type depended
on whether the list was empty.

Fix comments that no longer match the code

The nocov chunk comment claimed the ranges were zero indexed, but
build_nocov_chunks numbers lines from 1 and the consumer subtracts 1.
The ResultsetFile doc said an empty file warns, but only the
unparseable case does, and it now also drops malformed entries. The
static extractor's visitor comment claimed its tuple ids match
Coverage's conventional shape, but the numbering order differs for
case/when and chained safe navigation. That is harmless since the
combiners intern on source span and reports drop ids, so the comment
now says exactly that.

Prune dead weight from the test suite

Eight of the thirteen step definitions in web_steps.rb are referenced
by no feature file: am on, go to, press, the regex variants of should
see, both should-not-see forms, show me the page, and print the page.
They came along with the generic capybara steps template. Removing
them also removes the file's only Lint/Debugger disable, and a
cucumber dry run confirms every step in the suite still resolves.
spec/fixtures/iso-8859.rb goes too: no spec, feature, or build script
mentions it, and the encoding examples in source_file_spec.rb
exercise the euc-jp and utf-8 fixtures only.

In the CLI specs, the --no-color assertion was copy-pasted across the
coverage, report, uncovered, and diff subcommands. It is now one
shared example that each colorization context feeds its argv, and it
additionally asserts the command produced output at all. The merge
examples each rebuilt the same a/b/merged/fixture paths inline, which
move to lets, and two minimum_coverage_by_group examples re-stubbed
warn on the config even though the describe's before block installs
exactly that stub.

Replace invalid UTF-8 bytes at source load time

A source file with no encoding magic comment is read as UTF-8-tagged
lines, and a stray high-bit byte (a Latin-1 comment in an otherwise
ASCII file, say) left the line invalid. The first regex to touch it,
the loader's own shebang check or any of the lines classifier's
patterns, raised ArgumentError: invalid byte sequence in UTF-8 and
took the whole report down.

The loader now scrubs invalid bytes to the Unicode replacement
character before any regex sees a line: the first-line reads are
scrubbed ahead of the shebang and magic-comment checks, and
ensure_remove_undefs scrubs UTF-8-tagged lines the same way it
already transcoded lines in other encodings. Every line therefore
leaves the loader as valid UTF-8, which classification, the JSON
payload, and the HTML viewer embedding all rely on.

With that guarantee in place, the JSON formatter's per-line
re-encoding became redundant work. It ran every line of every file
through an encoding converter, allocating a converted copy per line
on top of the chomp copy, the single biggest allocation source in
payload building for a large report. The formatter now embeds the
chomped line directly, and the invalid-bytes spec pins that
replacement characters still reach the JSON payload through the
loader's scrub.

Found by a large-project benchmark run whose formatter spec fed a
file with raw Latin-1 bytes through the pipeline.

Write the resultset cache as compact JSON

.resultset.json is a machine-read cache that every parallel worker
rewrites wholesale, and pretty printing nearly doubled the bytes
written, read back, and parsed on each of those store-merge round
trips. On a synthetic 100,000-file project the file shrinks from 89MB
to 51MB and serialization halves. Any JSON parser reads the compact
form, and jq covers the rare need to inspect it by eye.

Add a report pipeline scaling benchmark

Generates a synthetic project of N small files, runs SimpleCov over
it end to end in a child process, and prints per-phase wall-clock and
GC timings as JSON. Comparing two sizes an order of magnitude apart
should show phase ratios tracking the size ratio: at 10,000 versus
100,000 files every phase lands between 9.7x and 10.3x once GC time
is subtracted, so per-file cost is flat and the drift above 10x in
raw wall clock is garbage collection over the larger heap.

This is the harness that found the invalid-UTF-8 loader crash, the
per-line encoding converter copies in the JSON payload build, and the
pretty-printed resultset cache addressed in the preceding commits.

Make the serve handler and specs work on JRuby and TruffleRuby

Neither engine implements IO#timeout=, so the serve handler's first
line raised NoMethodError into the wide client rescue and every
connection closed with an empty response. Guard the call with
respond_to? and accept that an idle connection pins its thread on
those engines, which only leaks a thread in an interactive dev
server.

The cross-process lock spec gave the child one second to boot, but
JRuby and TruffleRuby take several seconds to start a subprocess.
Raise the boot timeout to 30 seconds and the warm reads to 10. The
spec also spawns its child with RbConfig.ruby instead of bare "ruby",
which resolves through PATH and can point at a different interpreter
than the one running the suite (for example a version manager shim
while the suite runs under JRuby). A mismatched child boots against
the suite's bundler environment and dies before printing its ready
line, while RbConfig.ruby always names the running interpreter,
matching what coverage_differential.rb already does.

The require_relative configuration spec eval'd its block with a
synthetic source file that does not exist. CRuby resolves
require_relative from the path string alone, but JRuby resolves it
through realpath and raised ENOENT. Use lib/simplecov.rb, a real file
that still lives outside spec/, so the assertion keeps its bite.

Fix the Windows spec failures and clean guard gap

The clean subcommand's safety guard only protected the cwd and the
project root by prefix comparison. On Windows the filesystem-root
spec stubs the coverage directory as "/", which canonicalizes to a
drive root the prefix comparison can miss, and the spec then really
executed rm_rf from the root of the runner's disk. That deleted the
checkout mid-run, which is why most other Windows failures showed
RSpec unable to read its own spec files. The guard now refuses any
path that is its own dirname (a filesystem root on every platform),
and the spec passes --dry-run as defense in depth so a future guard
regression fails loudly instead of destructively. With roots refused
up front, the trailing-separator ternary in descendant_of? became
dead code and is gone.

The remaining failures were genuine Windows semantics. AtomicFile
retries a rename that fails with EACCES on Windows, where a
destination open in a reader or mid-replacement by a concurrent
writer is not replaceable, matching what the concurrent-writers spec
exercises. The permissions spec now asserts against the mode chmod
actually recorded, since Windows widens 0400 to 0444. Two
configuration specs expand their expected paths because expand_path
prefixes a drive letter there. The failing-esbuild spec skips on
Windows, where its fake minifier (a POSIX shell script) cannot run.

Cut reflows in the HTML viewer's bar-width fit

equalizeBarWidths sized the coverage-bar column with a 1px-precision
binary search over a 80px range, ~7 iterations each forcing a full
table reflow. A reflow of a large file list is expensive, and on a
100,000-file report this was the single biggest cost of finishing the
load, close to a second on its own.

The table's width is not a clean function of the bar width (three bar
columns share the width variable and column min-widths make it step
irregularly), so the fit still has to be found by probing rather than
solved. Stopping the search once the bracket is within 8px instead of
1px roughly halves the reflows. 8px is imperceptible on a 160-240px
bar, and the search still returns a width that fits, so the table
never overflows any more than it already would when long file names
force it to the minimum. Verified across a viewport sweep that the
coarse result never exceeds the exact search's width (so never
overflows) and lands within 8px of it.

At a fixed 1440px viewport the finalize phase of a 100k-file report
drops from ~1000ms to ~855ms.

Keep the CSS mangler off BEM class modifiers

The HTML report's Covered column (line, branch, method) rendered
left-aligned with a wide gap before the Lines/Branches/Methods column,
so "5/" and "6" read as "5/    6" instead of the intended fraction
"5/6". The stylesheet had the right rules all along
(td.cell--numerator right-aligned, td.cell--denominator left-aligned),
but they never reached the page.

The asset build shortens CSS custom-property names to save bytes, and
its token regex /--[a-zA-Z][\w-]*/ also matched the --modifier suffix
of BEM class names. It rewrote the .cell--numerator / .cell--denominator
selectors (and .cell--coverage, .cell--number) to short aliases in the
CSS, but the mangler only touches CSS — the JS keeps emitting
class="cell--numerator" — so the renamed rules matched nothing and the
alignment (and a few other class rules) silently vanished.

Anchor the token to genuine custom properties with a negative lookbehind:
a custom property's -- always follows a separator, while a BEM modifier's
follows an identifier character. Real properties still mangle; class
modifiers are left verbatim so their rules keep matching. A spec pins the
split so the mangler can't eat class names again.

Add a cucumber feature for no-defaults mode

Requiring 'simplecov/no_defaults' before 'simplecov' sets
SIMPLECOV_NO_DEFAULTS so defaults.rb never loads, leaving a clean
slate. Nothing verified that it actually behaves that way. Two
scenarios pin the two observable effects against the faked_project:

- No default formatter: with only SimpleCov.start and no formatter
  configured, the run writes .resultset.json but no index.html and
  prints no "Coverage report generated" line.
- No default filters: the report keeps the two test files the default
  test_frameworks filter would drop (six files rather than four). The
  formatter has to be required explicitly too, since defaults.rb is
  what normally loads it.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/217.

Serialize live results with string criterion keys

A live result's coverage keeps Ruby's Symbol criterion keys while
entries parsed back from .resultset.json carry Strings, and the
combiners read only String keys. When two concurrent runners shared a
command name, the later writer's counts were silently dropped for every
file both sides carried, defeating the clobber-prevention merge from
https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/581. Stringify the
criterion keys in Result#to_hash so the stored and live shapes match.

Parse nested inspect segments in stored method keys

A singleton method defined on a plain instance (def obj.greet) records
its class as the nested inspect form #<Class:#<Object:0x...>>. The
quoting regex stopped at the first closing angle bracket, leaving a
dangling one that failed both Ripper passes, so merging or collating
stored resultsets with method coverage raised ArgumentError and crashed
the run. Recurse the pattern so nested segments are quoted whole.

Keep line-only directives out of method coverage

Method#skipped? fell back to asking whether all of the method's lines
were skipped, so wrapping a def in a simplecov:disable line block (the
README's own line-directive example) silently removed the method from
method totals. Route the deprecated :nocov: chunks through
SkipChunks#for(:method) like every other criterion, so MethodBuilder
marks those methods explicitly, and reduce the fallback to the
no-line-info case.

Require a word boundary after directive categories

The directive pattern matched a category name as a prefix of a longer
word, so a free-form reason like linear algebra reasons parsed as the
category line with the rest as reason. That narrowed the directive to
line coverage, the opposite of the documented behavior where
unrecognised text falls into the reason bucket and the bare form
over-disables everything.

Normalize group names in per-group threshold stores

group :Models normalizes the name to the String Models, but
minimum_per_group 95, only: :Models stored the Symbol untouched, and
the deprecated minimum_coverage_by_group setter kept Symbol keys too.
The check-time lookup then missed and the threshold was silently
unenforced, with only a confusing warning that the group does not exist
among available groups listing that very name. Run both stores through
GroupNames.normalize.

Gate diff --fail-on-drop on the same epsilon as display

Row inclusion and delta display both suppress deltas below EPSILON as
float noise, but coverage_drop? used a bare negative? check. A file
listed for a gain in one criterion could exit 1 over a 1e-14 drift in
another criterion, failing CI with only gains visible in the output.
Treat a drop as real only when it exceeds EPSILON.

Fold multi-statement paren conditions like the compiler

CRuby folds a multi-statement paren condition by its last expression
(Coverage emits no branch for if (1; 2)), but the extractor stopped
unwrapping at multi-statement bodies and synthesized a then/else pair
no run can ever hit. That is the permanently-missed phantom-tuple
failure mode the condition folding module exists to prevent.

The fold only happens when the compiler can eliminate every leading
statement of the sequence. Pinned against real Coverage on 3.2, 3.3,
3.4, 3.5, and 4.0: parse.y (3.2) eliminates only pure literals, the
3.3 compiler also eliminates side-effect-free reads and containers of
them, and the Prism compiler (3.4+) narrows containers to fully static
literals. Paren opacity applies to the last statement of a sequence
exactly as it does to a single wrapped literal. The new shapes are in
the runtime tuple equivalence battery and the fuzzer pool, so CI pins
them per version.

Skip the global config when HOME is set but empty

Some container and CI images export HOME as an empty string. That
passed the set-at-all guard, and File.expand_path then raised
ArgumentError (non-absolute home) out of require simplecov, so the gem
could not be loaded at all in those environments. Treat an empty HOME
like an unset one, keeping the ENV-based check because Dir.home raises
on JRuby when HOME is missing.

Harden the CLI subcommands' input validation

Three crashes become one-line errors. merge on a directory or
unreadable file raised EISDIR or EACCES with a backtrace because only
missing files and bad JSON were rescued, and the exist?-then-read pair
was racy besides. report crashed its emitters on valid JSON whose
total or groups had the wrong type. coverage crashed print_human when
the matched per-file entry was not an object.

Also consolidates the parse scaffolding the four read-only subcommands
each rebuilt (defaults hash plus OptionParser around common_options)
into CommandHelpers.parse_common.

Count dotfiles in clean's dry-run and reuse CommandHelpers

The dry-run entry count used a bare Dir glob, which skips dotfiles, so
a coverage directory holding .resultset.json and .last_run.json
undercounted what rm_rf would actually delete. Glob with FNM_DOTMATCH
and skip the directory's own dot entry. Clean also now extends
CommandHelpers instead of hand-writing its simplecov clean prefixes.

Polish the serve handler's edge responses

A malformed request line (missing the path token) raised inside the
wide rescue and closed the connection with an empty response, leaving
the defined 400 status text unreachable. Answer 400 explicitly. The
announced URL now brackets IPv6 hosts so --host ::1 prints a valid
address, and the deliberate non-percent-decoding of request paths is
documented as part of the traversal defense.

Guard against unusable PARALLEL_TEST_GROUPS values

Both built-in adapters computed the expected worker count with
ENV[...]&.to_i || 1, which returns 0 for a set-but-empty or
non-numeric value because 0 is truthy. A 0-worker expectation makes
the reporting worker's sibling wait return immediately, so it could
format before its siblings stored their results. Parse with
Integer(..., exception: false) and fall back to 1 for anything
non-positive.

The parsing and the parallel_tests-off opt-out guard both lived
identically in the two adapters; they now sit once in Base.

Close small robustness gaps in simulation and enforcement

SimulateCoverage rescued only ENOENT in read_lines and coverage_stub,
so a track_files glob sweeping up a directory named like a Ruby file
or an unreadable file crashed the merge step with EISDIR or EACCES.
Both now degrade to an empty file like a missing one.

CoverageViolations.compute_drop subtracted whatever type a hand-edited
.last_run.json carried, raising mid-at_exit for a string percent, and
lookup_group's misconfiguration notice went through Kernel#warn, which
-W0 swallows and Warning hooks intercept. The drop check now treats a
non-numeric value as missing, and the notice routes through
ExitCodes.print_error gated on print_errors like every other
enforcement message.

ResultsetFile.read swallowed files truncated to a single byte under a
length check, hiding exactly the corruption the module warns about. A
blank file still quietly means no results, but any other content flows
through decode, and the exist?-then-read race is gone.

Extract a shared base class for the exit-code checks

The five threshold checks each repeated the same skeleton: stash the
result and threshold configuration, fail when any violation exists,
memoize the violations, and loop them through a reporter. The new
ExitCodes::Check carries that shape once, so each check now declares
only its exit code, its CoverageViolations query, and its message
format. Also declares the RBS that the earlier CLI consolidation
commits should have carried.

Share the interned count-merge loop between combiners

BranchesCombiner.merge_branches and MethodsCombiner.merge_methods were
the same loop: intern each tuple, sum counts into [raw_key, count]
pairs, keep the first-seen raw key for display. It now lives once in
Combine::InternedCounts. The structural differences that are real
behavior (the nested condition-to-arms tables, the nil-preserving
method table) stay where they were.

Route cover filters through Filter.build_filter

build_cover_filter re-implemented the whole filter dispatch when its
only real difference from add_filter is glob semantics for bare
Strings. Filter.build_filter now takes a string_filter parameter that
also threads through Array elements, so the deliberate glob-vs-
substring divergence lives in one line and cover keeps its specific
error message by rescuing the generic one.

Clarify the eval threshold error and two stale comments

coverage :eval, minimum: 100 raised Unsupported coverage criterion
eval even though coverage :eval by itself is supported. The refusal
now says thresholds are the problem, and primary_coverage :eval gets
the same clear message. The defaults.rb comment claimed .simplecov
start calls are intercepted when they only draw a deprecation warning,
and the frozen /o interpolation of the nocov token is now documented
at its regexp.

Make the clobber-prevention backstop see failed child reports

The backstop that keeps an empty parent process from formatting over a
child's report keyed its freshness check on .last_run.json, which only
fully successful runs write. A rake parent therefore clobbered the
child's report exactly when the child's tests or coverage checks had
failed, which is when that report matters most. Result#format! now
touches coverage/.report_stamp no matter how the run ends, and the
backstop accepts either file as evidence. The exist-then-mtime race is
gone too, replaced by a rescue.

That rescue exposed a subtle at_exit hazard this commit also guards:
completing any rescue inside an at_exit handler resets $ERROR_INFO to
nil, so at_exit_behavior now captures the suite's exit status before
the deferral probe runs and hands it to run_exit_tasks!. Without that,
a failing suite read as clean after the probe and its failure exit
status was swallowed (caught by the return-codes fixture specs).

Restructure the documentation around a trimmed README

The README had grown to 1,617 lines. It now holds what a newcomer
needs (intro, getting started, example output, a configuration taste,
and a documentation index) in under 180 lines, written in a plain
voice without rhetorical flourishes. Everything else moved into topic
guides in a new docs/ directory: Configuration, Parallelism,
Formatters, CLI, and Troubleshooting.

The meta documents join them, clearing the project root down to
README.md and LICENSE: both changelogs, the contributing guide, the
code of conduct, the issue template, and the three link lists that
lived in doc/. Filenames follow one scheme, Title Case with lowercase
particles and underscores between words (Code_of_Conduct.md,
Alternate_Formatters.md, CLI.md). Underscores rather than hyphens
because GitHub matches community health files and issue templates by
those exact names apart from case, and it recognizes docs/ as a
location for them, so the code of conduct link, contributing prompt,
and new-issue template all keep working. LICENSE deliberately stays
at the root: GitHub license detection only scans root-level files,
and the gem packages it from there.

The alternate formatters catalog was rebuilt against the RubyGems
search results for simplecov (112 gems). Twenty formatters join the
twelve that were listed, organized by output type: terminal output,
HTML reports, machine-readable formats for CI and tooling, coverage
badges, and the build-your-own ERB route. The most notable addition
is simplecov-console, at twelve million downloads the most-used
formatter that was missing. Every entry was verified against
RubyGems and all new links checked live; simplecov-cobertura's moved
repository is also fixed.

Nothing under docs/ ships in the gem. The old doc/* glob is gone from
the gemspec, which drops the package from 197KB to 176KB, and the
