Add `patch` command for per-change coverage

`simplecov patch` answers the question `diff` does not: is the code in
this change tested? It reads `git diff --unified=0 <base>...HEAD`,
intersects the added and modified line numbers with the current report
(--input), and prints line coverage — and branch coverage over the
branches those lines carry, when the report measured branches — for
only that change. A project that cannot move its overall number in one
pull request can still require that everything it adds is covered.

`--minimum N` exits non-zero below a floor (line coverage, and branch
coverage too when present, must both clear it), so it gates a change
alongside the existing thresholds. `--base` selects the ref to diff
against (the target branch, or its merge-base, in CI), `--find-renames`
follows a moved file instead of counting it as all-new, and `--json`
emits the rows the other read-only commands do.

Only files the report already tracks are scored, and a touched line
`LinesClassifier` deems never relevant stays out of the denominator the
same way it stays out of a file's total, so a comment-only change reads
as nothing to cover rather than a gap. See #1262.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: close patch-coverage gate gaps and slim the CLI module

Council review (pass 1) fixes. Each finding let the `--minimum` gate
pass over untested/misattributed code, or blocked CI:

- Extract the `usage` help heredoc into `lib/simplecov/cli/usage.rb`
  (kept a call-time method, not a constant) so `module CLI` is back
  under Metrics/ModuleLength (112 -> 47) without a rubocop:disable.
- parse_diff: split the diff into per-file sections and read only a
  section's first `+++` header. An added line whose own text begins
  `++ ` renders as `+++ ...` inside a hunk and previously hijacked the
  path, dropping later changes from the gate.
- CoverageFile.lookup: match an exact absolute/literal path before any
  suffix match, so a nested "vendor/lib/foo.rb" can't shadow the real
  "lib/foo.rb"; exact matches now read straight off the hash (O(1))
  instead of a linear scan per changed file.
- git_diff: reject a `--base` that begins with "-" (blocks git option
  injection like `--output=FILE` / `--line-prefix=`); pin
  `core.quotePath=false` (non-ASCII paths match report keys),
  `--inter-hunk-context=0` (never merge hunks over unchanged lines),
  and `--no-renames` unless `--find-renames` (git detects renames by
  default, so the flag was a no-op and the "count as all-new" default
  the docs describe never happened).
- docs/CLI.md: add `patch` to the command summary table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: harden the patch gate against ambiguous paths and hostile git config

Council re-review (pass 2) fixes, all confirmed:

- CoverageFile.lookup: resolve a subpath suffix only when exactly one
  key matches. Run from a subdirectory, `git diff --relative` yields
  cwd-relative paths that fall to the suffix scan; two files sharing a
  tail ("models/foo.rb" under app/ and lib/) previously resolved to
  whichever sat first in the hash, scoring the wrong file and flipping
  the gate. Ambiguity now reads as "not found".
- gate: compare the exact covered/relevant ratio, not the rounded
  percentage. A 19_999/20_000 patch is 99.995%, which rounded to 100.00
  and slipped past `--minimum 100`; EPSILON compounded it. Dropped the
  now-unused EPSILON constant.
- git_diff: add `--no-textconv` (a configured textconv driver runs a
  command and renumbers lines), pin `--src-prefix=a/ --dst-prefix=b/`
  (so `diff.noprefix`/`diff.*Prefix` can't make files miss the report
  keys), and read stdout via capture3 (stderr captured separately and
  dropped, as the comment always intended — capture2e had merged it
  into the parsed stream).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: gate on cross-multiplied ratio to avoid float-division error

Pass 2's exact-ratio gate divided as float, so covered/relevant*100
renders 23/40 as 57.4999… and failed a patch that exactly meets
--minimum 57.5. Cross-multiply instead (covered * 100 < minimum *
relevant): the covered side is exact integer arithmetic, so neither
boundary (99.995% vs 100, 57.5% vs 57.5) is misjudged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor: fold single-use patch render helpers

Behavior-preserving cleanup, no output change: inline the single-use
pct_cell into criterion_cell; share criterion_cells between the per-file
row and the total (one cell-builder, one branch-inclusion rule); and
collapse two two-line expressions (the git_diff argv append and the gate
below-floor check). patch.rb 362 -> 355; rubocop and steep green, 100%
line+branch dogfood coverage held.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: apply maintainer review to the patch command

Address sferik's review on #1280:

- Diff `--merge-base <base>` instead of `<base>...HEAD` so uncommitted
  work counts: running `simplecov patch` before a commit now scores the
  lines just written, while CI (a clean HEAD checkout) is unchanged.
- Reject a stray positional argument. A forgotten `--base`
  (`simplecov patch feature`) used to be silently dropped and diff the
  default, passing a `--minimum` gate over the wrong change.
- Gate on an exact Rational minimum. `minimum * relevant` overshoots in
  binary float (`64.4 * 250` lands at 16_100.000…2), failing a patch at
  exactly the floor; `Rational(minimum.to_s) * relevant` is exact.
- Extract the git half into `Patch::ChangedLines` and the presentation
  and gate into `Patch::Output`, dropping `Patch` under RuboCop's
  ModuleLength limit without a disable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Harden the patch command against wrong and vacuous answers

Scrub git's diff output before parsing. Open3 tags it with the
default external encoding, so one non-UTF-8 source file in a change
(a latin-1 magic comment is enough) made the regexp split raise
ArgumentError and abort the command with a backtrace. Scrubbing can
only touch content lines the parser ignores, since hunk headers are
pure ASCII.

Resolve changed files against the report by exact path, through a
realpath-normalized index built once per run. Diff paths are exact
root-relative names, so the suffix fallback the interactive commands
use for user-typed paths could only ever bind a changed file the
report does not carry to some other file's entry, scoring for
example a fixture copy's hits against lib/foo.rb's line numbers. The
index also keeps a symlinked project root resolving, and it replaces
the full-report scan the fallback performed for every changed file.

Anchor the diff at the repository toplevel instead of the working
directory. --relative from a subdirectory did not just reword paths,
it excluded every change outside the subdirectory, so a subdir run
passed a --minimum gate over files it never saw.

Score untracked files. A brand-new file that was never git added
appears in no diff, so entirely uncovered new code slipped through a
--minimum gate before its first commit. Every line the report knows
for an untracked file now counts as new, keeping the documented
promise that a pre-commit run scores the lines just written.

Warn when a changed line lies beyond the report's entry for its
file. Such lines read as never relevant and silently left the
denominator, so a stale cached coverage.json let new code gate as
nothing to cover.

Relay git's own first stderr line when the diff fails. The fixed
"is this a git working tree, and does the ref exist?" guess pointed
away from the real cause when git was actually saying unknown
revision, unknown option merge-base (git older than 2.30), or
dubious ownership. The guess remains only for the case where git
says nothing.

Unquote paths git C-quotes. A filename carrying a quote, backslash,
or control character is emitted as "b/lib/we\"ird.rb" even under
core.quotePath=false, and left quoted it matched no report key and
silently dropped out of the gate.

Name the candidates when a path suffix-matches more than one report
entry, in the coverage and tests subcommands too. The bare "no
entry" answer read like a typo hunt when the path existed twice and
a longer path would have picked one.

See https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/pull/1280.

Select the tests that touch changed code

`simplecov affected` turns the track_tests recording into test
selection. It diffs the working tree against the merge base of a git
ref (--base, default main) and HEAD, so uncommitted work counts as
part of the change while commits that landed on the base after the
branch point do not, includes untracked files, and prints the test
files whose recorded tests touch the changed files, one per line on
stdout, so the local inner loop can run
`simplecov affected --run bundle exec rspec` instead of the whole
suite. Everything after --run is the runner command, the selection is
appended to it, and the exit status is the command's own. A stray
positional argument is an error rather than silently ignored, because
it looks exactly like a forgotten --base ref and dropping it would
select tests for the wrong change.

The set intersection is the easy half. The hard half is knowing when
to distrust the map, because a test map is stale the moment something
changes that no test mentions by name. Any changed file outside the
tracked set fails open to the full suite, out loud: a changed
Gemfile.lock, .simplecov, spec helper, runner configuration, or any
file the report has no data for is named on stderr as the trigger,
while stdout prints nothing, which a bare runner reads as run
everything. Changed or brand-new test files always select themselves,
recorded or not. A test file deleted by the change drops out of the
answer, and a recorded test whose file no longer exists anywhere else
reads as staleness rather than being silently skipped. A locationless
test id (a Minitest method with no source location) touching changed
code also fails open, since there is no file to hand a runner. --json
emits the selection with its full_suite verdict and triggers for
tooling.

Like the patch command, the diff is anchored at the repository
toplevel, so a run from a subdirectory selects over the whole change
and --run starts the runner at that root, and changed files resolve
against the report through CoverageFile.exact_index, so a lookalike
entry elsewhere in the report can never stand in for a changed file
the report does not carry. Base refs beginning with "-" are refused
before git can read them as options, and a git failure relays git's
own first stderr line instead of a guess.

The recorded_contexts reader moved from the tests subcommand into
CommandHelpers so both context-consuming commands validate the
recording the same way.

Built for the local inner loop first, because a wrong answer in CI is
a green build on a broken change.

The spec fixture repos (the patch command's included) set
maintenance.auto=false and gc.auto=0 and remove themselves with
rm_rf rather than remove_entry. Since git 2.46 a commit can fork a
detached background maintenance process, and its transient
.git/objects/maintenance.lock raced the after-hook's directory
removal into Errno::ENOENT, nondeterministically failing CI jobs
across platforms.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1264.

Summarize a merged report's runs instead of enumerating them

A report merged from many runs printed every contributing run's name
in its footer. The merged command name joined each resultset's name
verbatim, without deduplication, so a CI matrix collating one
resultset per worker rendered "RSpec" a hundred times over, and
uniquified run names produced an unbounded blob that filled the
viewport before the report content began.

Dedupe the names at the merge: repeated names collapse to one entry
in the joined command_name. The distinct names also travel on the
merged result (Result#command_names, defaulting to the one name for
a single run) and into coverage.json's meta as an optional
command_names array, because a consumer that needs the components
cannot safely split the joined string, since a run name can itself
contain a comma. The joined command_name is unchanged for existing
consumers, and the viewer validator accepts documents without the
new key.

The report footer reads the array: up to three distinct runs render
inline as before, and more than three summarize as "A and N other
runs" with the full list behind a details disclosure that scrolls in
place. Documents from before the array fall back to the joined
string. As a backstop, the footer areas cap their height and scroll,
so no metadata value can displace the report content again, however
it was produced.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1284.

Survive a coverage.json another tool rewrote in its own shape

The concurrent-overwrite check introduced in 1.1.0 reads the previous
run's coverage.json and parsed its meta.timestamp with Time.iso8601,
rescuing only ArgumentError. But coverage.json is whatever wrote it
last: third-party formatters running after ours in the chain
(undercover's among them) rewrite the file in their own shape with an
epoch integer in meta.timestamp, and Time.iso8601 raises TypeError on
an Integer. The first run worked, wrote our file, and had it
overwritten. Every run after that failed the HTML report while
reading the foreign file back.

Epoch numbers now feed the concurrency check exactly like ISO 8601
strings, so the sibling-writer warning keeps working alongside such
tools, and a timestamp of any other shape disables the check for that
file instead of failing the write. A best-effort warning must never
be what takes report generation down.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1285.

Add undercover to the alternate formatters catalog

Its SimpleCov::Formatter::Undercover writes to the same default
coverage/coverage.json path the bundled formatters own, which is
worth a documented caveat now that
https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1285 showed the
two sharing a project, and the entry cross-references the bundled
patch command for the related per-line question.

Point Formatters.md at simplecov-cobertura's current home

The multiple-formatters example linked the gem's old dashingrocket
org while Alternate_Formatters.md links jessebs, where the repository
lives now. Same gem, same author, one canonical link.

Keep fully covered files off the lowest-coverage hint list

The list under a failed minimum-coverage check exists to say where
adding tests would help, but it took the five lowest files regardless
of their coverage, so a project with fewer than five incomplete files
saw the list padded with entries at 100.00%, suggesting tests be
added to files with nothing left to cover. Only files below 100%
qualify now, and the list simply ends early when there are fewer of
them.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1286.

Re-run tests on save and live-reload the served report

`simplecov watch <command...>` is the coverage inner loop the serve
and run commands were always two thirds of. It serves the report the
way serve does, polls the tracked files for saves, re-runs the given
command when something changes, and pushes a reload to every open
report tab over server-sent events the moment the report
regenerates, with the result line naming the change and the coverage
delta: "lib/result.rb changed, running 3 files... 100.00% (+0.40%)".

With a track_tests recording in the report, a save re-runs only the
tests that touch the changed files, decided by the same selection
walk `simplecov affected` uses and under the same fail-open rule.
The watch loop knows exactly which files changed, so the map answers
without a git diff. A report with no recording runs the full command
on every save, and a change no recorded test touches runs nothing
and says so.

The watched set is the report's own tracked files plus the recorded
tests' files, polled by mtime rather than through a filesystem-event
dependency, which keeps report writes from triggering the next run
and survives editors that save through a temporary file plus rename.
Saves are debounced: after the first detection the loop keeps
polling until a full interval passes quietly.

The server side reuses the serve stack in process. StaticFileHandler
gains a routes seam mapping exact paths to callables, on which watch
mounts an /events endpoint (one thread per open tab, forwarding each
broadcast as one SSE message) and an index route that appends the
reload listener on the way out, so the report on disk stays
byte-identical to a plain run's.

Child runs get a day-long merge window through the new
SIMPLECOV_MERGE_TIMEOUT environment variable, which merge_timeout
now honors generally, so subset re-runs keep merging into a whole
report across a session longer than the default ten minutes. The
command is the project's own test invocation and must produce the
report; a project with no SimpleCov.start hook composes
`simplecov watch simplecov run ...`.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1269.

Keep merge_timeout's memoization out of steep's logic operands

`env_merge_timeout || (@merge_timeout ||= 600)` crashed steep 2.0's
logic-type interpreter (UnknownNodeError on the or-assignment nested
in a logical operand), which spewed a FATAL backtrace into every
check, abandoned the file's type check mid-way, and still exited
zero, so the noise was the only symptom. With the file actually
checked, a second issue surfaced from under the crash: the ivar's
nilability leaked into the declared Integer return, since steep does
not carry instance-variable narrowing across statements. Memoizing
through a local fixes both, with identical behavior.

Print annotated source in the terminal

`simplecov show <path>` answers "what is missing in this file" the
way `go tool cover` and `llvm-cov show` do, without leaving the
shell or forwarding a port off a CI box. Hit counts sit in a
right-aligned gutter, blank for never-relevant and nocov lines, and
a caret line names each miss under the line it happened on, with
branch and method misses annotated the same way when the report
measured them. A line missing more than one way joins its labels on
one caret line. Counts and markers colorize under the same NO_COLOR,
FORCE_COLOR, and --no-color rules as every other subcommand.

`--uncovered-only` collapses the answer to `path:40,52-58,71`, a
form that greps, fits in a commit message, and hands a coding agent
exactly the lines whose tests are missing. It reuses the patch
subcommand's range collapser, which now takes a separator. A file
with nothing uncovered keeps stdout empty and says so on stderr,
like the other empty answers.

The source comes from the report itself when it embeds one, and
otherwise from the file on disk, accepted only while its line count
still matches the report's, since annotating drifted source would
put hit counts on the wrong lines. Paths resolve the way the
coverage subcommand resolves them, ambiguity message included, and a
report without line data says so rather than printing an empty
gutter.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1270.

Open the served report from the watch command

`simplecov watch --open` pops the report in the default browser once
the server is bound, through the same platform opener `simplecov
open` uses, detached so the session never waits on the browser. A
platform with no recognized opener prints the URL to open by hand
instead of failing the watch.

Emit the show annotation as JSON

`simplecov show --json <path>` emits the whole annotation as data for
editor integrations: the path, the missed line numbers, per-line hit
counts for the relevant lines, and the marker labels keyed by line.
It reads only the coverage data, never the source text, so it
answers even for a report without embedded source and no file on
disk, where the annotated text form has nothing to print.

Answer --help on every command with its own usage

`simplecov <command> --help` (and -h) prints just that command's
slice of the usage text: its row from the command table, its own
options section, and the shared options it accepts, assembled from
the one usage document so nothing is written twice.

The explicit handler also replaces what optparse's built-in --help
did before, which was to print a bare option summary under the host
program's banner and exit the process from inside the parser.

Share the CLI's git plumbing and resolve the default base ref

CLI::Git consolidates what the affected and patch commands each
reinvented: safe capture with a first-stderr-line detail and a
distinguishable never-ran state, repository toplevel resolution, and
the option-like ref guard, with each command keeping its own error
message shapes on top.

The shared module also gives both commands a smarter default for an
omitted --base: the branch origin's HEAD points at, so master and
trunk repositories work bare instead of failing on a hardcoded main,
which stays as the fallback where no origin HEAD is recorded.

Sweep the whole project with a bare show --uncovered-only

`simplecov show --uncovered-only` with no path prints one
`path:ranges` line per file with misses, sorted, with paths under
SimpleCov.root shown project-relative — a single command whose
output is the complete list of everything untested, ready for a grep
or a coding agent. A bare `--json` emits the same sweep as an array
of {path, missed} objects, and a fully covered project says so on
stderr. The annotated text form still wants one file, and the
missing-path error now points at the sweep.

Append the missed line ranges to the uncovered listing

`simplecov uncovered --missing` extends each row with the missed
line ranges (`50.00%  5/10  lib/foo.rb  missing 4-7,9`), following
the chosen criterion: zero-hit lines for line coverage, and the
lines missed branches and methods report on for the other two. The
--json rows gain a matching `missing` array. It reuses the show
subcommand's miss extraction and the patch subcommand's range
collapse, so the list says not just where to add tests but which
lines they're for.

Annotate GitHub workflows from the uncovered listing

`simplecov uncovered --annotate github` emits ::warning workflow
commands instead of rows, one per contiguous missed range with
project-relative paths, so a plain GitHub Actions workflow gets
inline diff annotations on uncovered lines with no upload step and
no code-scanning permissions. It implies --missing, follows the
chosen criterion, threshold, and top filters, stays silent when
nothing is below the threshold (a clean CI step is the answer), and
refuses to combine with --json. The missed-line extraction and the
annotation writer live in Uncovered::Misses.

Answer whether the report is fresh with a status command

`simplecov status` reads aloud the freshness metadata the artifacts
have carried all along: the report's age, the simplecov version and
run that produced it, the recorded commit and how many commits HEAD
has moved since (via the shared git plumbing), the measured totals,
whether a track_tests map is present and what to enable when it
isn't, and the resultset's entries with their ages. --json emits the
same facts as data, degenerate artifacts degrade to "not recorded" /
"age unknown" instead of errors, and a missing report errors like
every other reader. Every staleness question the change-aware
commands raise now has a one-command answer.

Generate shell completions from the usage document

simplecov completions fish|bash|zsh prints a tab-completion script
for the named shell: every subcommand with its description, and each
command's own options once a subcommand is typed. Rather than keeping
a parallel table that would drift, the command parses the usage text
itself. The Commands list provides the subcommand names and
descriptions, and the per-command options sections provide the
switches, their short aliases, and whether each takes an argument, so
a new command or option appears in completions the moment it is
documented. The one thing the usage tables do not carry, the shell
names the completions command itself takes, is wired in by hand in
each renderer.

fish gets one complete registration per command and per option, with
descriptions and required-argument markers. bash gets a _simplecov
function dispatching on the subcommand, completing option words when
the current word starts with a dash and falling back to file
completion otherwise. zsh gets a #compdef file built on _describe and
_arguments. All three outputs pass their shell's own syntax check,
which the specs run where the shell is installed, and the run command
offers no options at all since everything after it belongs to the
command being run.

Render the coverage percent as an SVG badge

simplecov badge writes a flat SVG coverage badge, shields.io style,
to stdout or to a file with --output, so a README or a CI artifact
can carry the number straight from the local report with no badge
service in the loop. The percent comes from the totals coverage.json
already carries, so the badge always matches what the other read-only
commands report, and a report that never measured the chosen
criterion draws a one-line error instead of a 0% badge. The color
follows the ladder badge services apply to coverage, bright green at
90 and above stepping down to red below 50. --criterion picks the
line, branch, or method percentage, and the label names the chosen
criterion (line coverage, branch coverage, method coverage) so the
badge says what its number measures, unless --label replaces it, with
markup in the replacement escaped.

The geometry follows the flat badge convention: text drawn twice for
the drop shadow at 10x scale, with textLength pinning the layout so
the estimated glyph widths never spill. The output passes xmllint,
which the specs run where it is installed. The badge options slot
into the usage document, which is also what makes the new command
appear in the generated shell completions with no completions change
at all. Fitting the new options section into the usage text
compressed the wrapped option descriptions onto single lines, which
also took away the only live input exercising the completions
parser's description folding, so the folding spec now feeds it a
wrapped description of its own.

Ship a man page generated from the usage document

man/simplecov.1 documents every CLI command and option, with the
environment variables and files the commands honor, a synopsis, and
pointers to the full documentation. Like the shell completions, it is
generated from the usage document rather than written by hand, so the
page cannot drift from what the commands accept: tasks/man_page.rb
parses the Commands table and each command's options sections through
the same helpers the completions command uses, escapes the text for
roff, and wraps it for readable source. The rendered page passes
mandoc's lint cleanly.

The committed page is a build artifact like the compiled HTML report
template. rake man regenerates it, and a freshness spec rebuilds the
page and compares it byte for byte against the committed copy, so any
usage or version change that lands without a regeneration fails the
suite everywhere the suite runs, CI included. The generator renders
against fixed stand-in default paths, so the page reads
coverage/coverage.json wherever it is generated from instead of the
generating checkout's own coverage directory. The artifact ships in
the gem through the gemspec's file list. RubyGems has no hook for
installing man pages onto MANPATH, so the page rides along for gem
contents, man -l, and system package managers to pick up.

Cover Rails views with cover_views

Rendering a template already produced usable data. ActionView compiles
each one with `module_eval(source, identifier, offset)`, where the
identifier is the template's own path and the offset cancels the `def`
line its wrapper adds, so eval coverage attributes the generated code
back to the `.erb` file at the template's own line numbers. The
`ERB#filename=` advice in the eval coverage docs is for hand-rolled ERB.
Nobody calls it in a Rails app, and nothing there needs remapping.

The gap was the other half. A template no test renders is never
compiled, so `Coverage` never hears about it and the report leaves it
out, which means the views with no coverage are exactly the ones that go
missing. `ViewCoverage` compiles every configured template the run did
not reach, immediately before the result is collected. Compiling defines
the method without calling it, which is enough: evaluating a `def`
records its body as executable and unexecuted, so the template arrives
at 0% with a full set of branch tuples. That is the shape
`SimulateCoverage` produces for a tracked `.rb` file nobody required,
except that the classification comes from the runtime compiling the
handler's real output instead of from static analysis approximating it.
No static pass could match it anyway, since erubi coalesces runs of
markup into a single buffer append and which lines carry code is a
property of that codegen.

Templates the run did render are filtered out rather than recompiled.
Evaluating the same identifier a second time replaces that file's entry
in `Coverage` instead of adding to it, so a blanket recompile would zero
the hits the suite earned and leave a duplicate set of branch tuples
behind.

The work has to happen per process, before `Coverage.result`, rather
than at the merge point where unloaded `.rb` files are injected.
Compiling needs ActionView and the merging process need not have it, as
a standalone `simplecov merge` never does. So each worker in a parallel
run compiles the templates it personally missed, and the merge takes the
maximum, which leaves a template one worker rendered with its hits.

`cover_views` defaults to `app/views/**/*.erb` and turns on eval
coverage, without which templates would come back empty rather than at
0%. It belongs to the `cover` family because that is what it does, which
is say which files are in the report. The `rails` profile gains a
matching `Views` group, empty until a project opts in, the way Channels
and Mailers sit empty in an app that has neither.

A template that does not compile is reported and skipped. It cannot
render either, so the suite has bigger problems than its coverage, but
the report is not where they should surface and one bad view must not
take the whole run down.

See https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1265.

Highlight each source file by its own language

The source view marked every line `class="ruby"` and fed the lot to the
Ruby grammar. That is right for all but the template files, and for a
`.erb` view it means the grammar declines to match nearly everything and
the file renders as one flat block of unhighlighted text, which is the
opposite of what a template needs. Markup and code look alike until one
of them is coloured.

Each file now carries the language its extension implies, which is Ruby
for everything except `.erb`.

The ERB grammar is ours rather than the one highlight.js ships. Theirs
delegates the markup to the full XML grammar, and that grammar carries
the literal script end tag in its rules for embedded scripts. The report
is a single `index.html` with the bundle inlined into a `<script>`
element, so that sequence would close the element early and truncate the
report. The asset build already refuses to inline a bundle containing
it, which is how this surfaced rather than shipping broken. XML would
also have added about 5KB to every report written, against 627 bytes for
what is here.

What is here highlights the Ruby between the tags, marks up tag names,
attributes, and attribute values around it, and leaves a bare `<` in
template text alone rather than opening a tag that runs to the end of
the line. It emits the same class names highlight.js does, so the
existing stylesheet colours it in both themes with nothing added.

See https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1265.

Cover Haml and Slim templates too

Nothing was needed to measure them. Both compile through an ActionView
handler like ERB does, and both generate Ruby that keeps the template's
line structure, so eval coverage already lands on the lines their authors
wrote. A rendered page reports its hits per line, a loop body reports the
count of iterations, and a conditional the run does not enter reports
zero, all against the `.haml` or `.slim` source. The same holds for any
other language a project registers a handler for, which now needs only
its extension named in a `cover_views` glob.

What was needed is the handler lookup. `handler_for_extension` answers an
unregistered extension with the raw handler rather than nothing, so a
default glob naming `.haml` in a project that has no Haml would compile
every such file as a lump of static text and report an untested view that
is not one. Asking `registered_template_handler` instead leaves those
files out of the report, which is what makes the widened default glob
safe: it now reads `app/views/**/*.{erb,haml,slim}` in every project,
including the ones with neither gem.

The source view highlights both as themselves. Haml has a grammar in
highlight.js. Slim has none anywhere, so this adds a small one, which
reads a line by what it starts with: a control or output marker is Ruby,
a slash is a comment, a pipe is text, and anything else is a tag with its
shorthand classes and id. It stops at the first space after the tag
rather than guess at what follows, because `h1 = @foo.bar` and
`a href="/x"` put different things on either side of the same character
and a wrong guess colours a template as something it is not. That is also
where highlight.js's own Haml grammar stops.

The rails fixture keeps both gems in an optional Gemfile group, the way
the faked_project keeps Cucumber and Minitest, so only the spec that
drives them installs them. `Rails.groups` does not name an optional
group, so its `config/application.rb` requires them itself when they are
there, which also leaves the project honest about the case where they are
not: one of the new examples asserts that a project without them reports
no templates at all rather than a wall of static text.

See https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1265.

Show cover_views in action with a checked-in demo project

test_projects/rails/view_demo is a small Rails storefront whose report
exists to be looked at, the way test_projects/screenshot's does for the
Ruby side of a Rails app. Its eight templates split evenly: four are
rendered by RSpec view specs and four by nothing, so the report shows
both halves of what view coverage does. ERB, Haml, and Slim each appear
on both sides of that divide, and every template runs ten to twenty
lines so the source view reads like a real view rather than a fixture.

Each rendered template deliberately leaves something unreached (a promo
banner, a coupon note, a past-due warning), so each one points at a
concrete untested conditional with a missed branch marker on the
template's own line. A partial renders once per product, putting per
render hit counts in the gutter. The orphaned templates, the layout
among them because view specs render without one, arrive compiled at 0%
with real branch tuples instead of being absent.

Like the screenshot project, `bundle exec rake` runs the specs and then
verifies the report's shape from coverage.json (rendered templates mix
covered and missed lines and branches, orphans sit at exactly 0%, every
language appears on both sides) so the demo fails loudly if a future
change stops telling this story.

See https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1265.

Ratchet per-file coverage floors from a checked-in baseline

`minimum_coverage` is one number for a whole project, so on a legacy
codebase it gets set to whatever the codebase currently scores and then
does nothing. A single per-file minimum is worse, because the worst file
sets the ceiling for the entire policy. What works on codebases like
that is a checked-in baseline with one floor per file, generated from
the current state: `.rubocop_todo.yml` applied to coverage.

`simplecov ratchet` writes `.simplecov_baseline.yml` from the current
report, one floor per file per measured criterion, and the exit check
fails any listed file that drops below its own floor. Rewriting only
ever tightens. Files that improved get their floors raised, files that
regressed keep the floors they are now below and are named in the
summary, entries for deleted files are pruned, and new files never get
an entry, so they answer to the real `minimum_per_file` standard rather
than to a floor cut at whatever they launched with. Files with an entry
are exempt from `minimum_per_file` for the criteria the entry covers,
which is the fall-through the whole workflow rests on. The diff on the
baseline file becomes the honest record of which direction the codebase
moved, reviewable in the same PR as the change that moved it.

The issue left open whether a floor should be a percentage or a count
of uncovered lines, since a percentage moves when a file is edited
without any coverage change at all and that churn means nothing. Each
floor stores both, because each number covers for the other's blind
spot: the percent is the policy, and the missed count is the dampener,
so a violation requires a lower percent and more misses together, and
an edit that only reshuffles covered lines fails nothing. The ratchet
tightens each axis independently (best percent, fewest misses), so the
pair is the envelope of the best state each axis has seen, and the
regressed list in the summary mirrors the violation rule exactly, so
"below its floor" always means the suite will fail. A hand-written
bare-percent entry (the issue's own example shape) is accepted and
decided by percent alone until the next ratchet records its missed
count, while a malformed baseline fails loudly rather than silently
un-enforcing every floor it carried.

`--init` deliberately regenerates the file from scratch, new files and
loosened floors included. `--dry-run` prints without writing, `--json`
emits the summary as data, and `--baseline` names the file, defaulting
to the project's `baseline_file` setting, which the command reads from
`.simplecov` the way the read-only commands read `coverage_dir`.
Baseline violations also land in coverage.json's `errors` section,
under schema 1.2 (additive, with 1.1 staying frozen for pinned
integrations).

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1268.

Auto-ratchet the baseline with a formatter

`SimpleCov::Formatter::BaselineFormatter` rewrites the per-file
coverage baseline at the end of every run, for teams that want floors
to tighten continuously instead of by deliberate `simplecov ratchet`
invocations. Add it to the formatter chain and the first run generates
`.simplecov_baseline.yml` with a floor for every reported file.

The semantics are exactly the CLI's, through the same Baseline core:
floors only tighten, files that regressed keep the floors they are now
below and are named in the status line, entries for deleted files are
pruned, and new files never get an entry, so new code stays answerable
to the global thresholds rather than being grandfathered at whatever it
launched with. The file is rewritten only when a floor actually moved,
so a run that changes nothing leaves the working tree clean.

Ordering with the exit checks needs no care: formatters run first, but
the checks read the baseline once per path and so judge the run against
the floors as they were when it started, and ratcheting never loosens a
floor, so tightening before the checks cannot flip a failing file to
passing either way. The file lands where the exit check reads it
(`SimpleCov.baseline_file` under the root), not under the coverage
directory, because it is checked-in policy rather than a report
artifact. That is also the trade-off of the auto mode: floors tighten
without a human in the loop, and the diff lands in the working tree for
the next commit to carry.

See https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1268.

Cap misses with maximum_missed and maximum_missed_per_file

The percent thresholds all ask for a ratio, and two policies cannot be
said in ratios. A team driving to 100% counts down in misses ("12
uncovered lines left"), a number that stays put as the codebase grows
and shrinks while the equivalent percentage moves with every edit. And
a per-file percent minimum systematically flatters big files: a
2,000-line file at 99% hides 20 misses while a 10-line file at 80%
fails over 2. `maximum_missed` caps the suite's total misses and
`maximum_missed_per_file` holds every file to the same absolute budget.

Both are per criterion in the criterion's own units, so `coverage
:branch { maximum_missed 3 }` caps missed branch arms and `coverage
:method { maximum_missed 2 }` caps missed methods, read from the same
per-criterion statistics the percent thresholds read. They are verbs in
the `coverage` block, with the same `only:` per-path overrides as
`minimum_per_file`, and flat helpers taking a bare count (primary
criterion) or a criterion-keyed Hash. A fractional or negative cap is a
configuration error rather than a silent truncation, and a criterion
the runtime did not measure is skipped the way the percent checks skip
it. Files with a baseline entry are exempt from the per-file cap for
the criteria the entry covers, the same fall-through `minimum_per_file`
honors, so `simplecov ratchet` and the caps compose: the baseline
grandfathers the legacy files, the caps hold the rest.

Violations land in coverage.json's `errors` section as `maximum_missed`
and `maximum_missed_per_file`, folded into the still-unreleased schema
1.2 rather than bumping again, reusing its maximum/actual shape with
counts in place of percents. The CoverageLimits snapshot now builds
itself from its member names, since every member is named after the
configuration reader that supplies it, and the miss-cap configuration
lives in its own configuration/missed_caps.rb, split from the percent
thresholds because the two families validate differently.

Scope thresholds with a per: argument instead of suffixed verbs

The coverage block encoded a threshold's scope three different ways:
suite scope in the bare verb, file scope in a `_per_file` suffix, path
scope in an `only:` keyword, and group scope in a suffix plus keyword.
That is one axis spelled three ways, and it is why the threshold matrix
was sparse: every new bound-times-scope cell needed a new method name.

Scope is now a uniform `per:` argument. `minimum 80, per: :file` sets
the per-file default, `minimum 100, per: "app/x.rb"` (or a Regexp)
overrides it for matching files, `minimum 95, per: group("Models")`
sets a group minimum, and `maximum_missed` takes the same targets for
its per-file cap. The `group(...)` wrapper exists because a group name
and a path are both Strings, and the target must say which it is. A
threshold is now a point in (criterion x metric x bound x scope) with
each axis spelled exactly once: criterion by the enclosing block, bound
and metric by the verb, scope by `per:`. A scope the enforcement cannot
check is refused at configuration time rather than silently stored,
which today means `maximum_missed` rejects `per: group(...)` until
group caps exist.

The suffixed forms are deprecated, not removed: `minimum_per_file`,
`minimum_per_group`, `maximum_missed_per_file`, and the flat
`SimpleCov.maximum_missed_per_file` setter warn with the exact `per:`
replacement built from their own arguments and delegate to the same
stores, so enforcement is unchanged. The `minimum_coverage_by_file` and
`minimum_coverage_by_group` deprecation messages now suggest the `per:`
grammar directly, instead of pointing migrating users at a spelling
that would immediately warn again.

This is phase one of a larger cleanup of the configuration DSL, written
down in docs/Configuration_Roadmap.md: the remaining matrix cells
(group-scoped miss caps, scoped drops, a count analog of
refuse_coverage_drop), the `:eval` pseudo-criterion, unifying the
baseline's two configuration homes, one boolean grammar, and the
eventual single-surface 2.0 configuration, each step warn-and-delegate
with nothing removed before a major version.

Turn deprecations into errors with deprecations :raise

The configuration DSL migrates by warn-and-delegate (see
docs/Configuration_Roadmap.md), which means every deprecated spelling
keeps working indefinitely, and a project can run on old API forever
without noticing. `deprecations :raise` makes any deprecated API a
ConfigurationError naming its replacement, so a migrated project can
guard in CI against old spellings creeping back, and early adopters can
hold themselves to the current surface as the DSL evolves. This is
groundwork for the roadmap's remaining phases: each future deprecation
becomes instantly enforceable per project the day it ships.

The error bypasses the warning path's per-location dedup, since an
error is not a notice to collapse and a CI guard must fail on the
second offender file as surely as on the first. The default stays
`deprecations :warn`, and there is deliberately no silencing mode,
because a deprecation you cannot see is a migration you never make.

Scope entry filters with a coverage-block ignore verb

`ignore_branches` and `ignore_methods` had the criterion baked into
their names, the same disease the suffixed threshold verbs had before
the `per:` axis. The coverage block is the criterion-scoped home, so
the filters become one verb whose criterion comes from context:

  coverage :branch do
    ignore :implicit_else, :eval_generated
  end
  coverage :method, ignore: :eval_generated

`ignore` dispatches to the same stores the flat setters fed, raises for
criteria with no ignorable entry types (line has none), and rides the
one-liner keyword form with a single token or an Array. The flat
setters are deprecated with warn-and-delegate, the replacement named
from their own arguments.

One behavior rides out the deprecation period on the legacy setters:
naming a criterion in the coverage block enables it, while the flat
setters record the filter without enabling, which some configurations
use to declare the filter before deciding on the criterion. The
deprecated spelling remains the way to say that until a need for an
enable-free spelling proves itself.

Select bundled formatters by name with formats

`SimpleCov::Formatter::HTMLFormatter` and its siblings are the
most-typed constants in every README snippet, and choosing formatters
spanned three shapes (`formatter`, `formatters`, and
`MultiFormatter.new([...])`). `formats` collapses the common case to
names:

  SimpleCov.start do
    formats :html, :json
  end

`:html`, `:json`, `:simple`, and `:baseline` map to the bundled
formatter classes, resolved lazily so `:html` works even under
SIMPLECOV_NO_DEFAULTS, where nothing else has loaded the HTML
formatter. Formatter classes and ready-built instances (the way
constructor options are passed) mix freely beside the names, so
third-party formatters need no second spelling, an unknown name raises
naming the built-ins rather than failing later as a "formatter" without
a format method, and the bare call reads back the configured chain the
way `formatters` does. The constant-spelled forms are unchanged and
equivalent, and nothing is deprecated by this: `formatter` remains the
way to pass a single configured instance.

Chart the remaining configuration grammar unifications

Three more incoherences join the roadmap, each surveyed and deliberately
deferred rather than fixed piecemeal. The matcher grammars: `cover`
takes a glob while `skip` takes a path-segment substring, invisible at
the call site, and unifiable only at 2.0 because changing `skip`'s
String semantics silently alters which files existing configurations
exclude (a `skip glob(...)` wrapper can bridge earlier). The exclusion
comments: `# :nocov:` toggles and `# simplecov:disable` directives
overlap, the `nocov_token` hook is already deprecated, and retiring the
comments themselves waits for 2.0 because they live in thousands of
shipped codebases. The three spellings of "primary": the `coverage`
forms become canonical and `primary_coverage` a legacy alias. The merge
family's six flat names get a footnote rather than a phase, since a
`merge` sub-block would add structure without removing anything.

The roadmap also records the groundwork that shipped as Phase 1.5 (the
criterion-scoped `ignore` verb, `formats` by name, and `deprecations
:raise`) and names `deprecations :raise` in the principles as the lever
that makes every warn-and-delegate migration enforceable per project.

Measure coverage in production to find dead code

Oneshot lines coverage is cheap enough to leave running in production,
which makes a supported production mode a modest addition rather than a
separate project. `require "simplecov/production"` loads a standalone
runtime, none of the reporting machinery, that is a no-op until
`SimpleCov::Production.start` is called explicitly: it measures
`:oneshot_lines`, whose report-first-hit-only semantics are what make
the overhead viable on live traffic, and a background thread drains the
runtime's table every flush interval into a pluggable sink instead of
assuming one report per process at exit.

The store is the part a repository's coverage directory cannot be, so
the sink is one method: `store(coverage)` receives root-relative paths
mapped to sorted line numbers, must union-merge (each process holds
only a slice), must tolerate duplicates, and raises on failure, which
makes the runtime keep the delta and retry, bounded by a configurable
buffer ceiling whose drops self-heal for still-running code because a
drained line re-reports on its next execution. A locking single-file
FileSink ships in the box; Redis or S3 implement the same method
outside the gem. `sample_rate` duty-cycles measurement through
Coverage.suspend/resume, a test suite's running Coverage always wins
over `start`, forked workers re-`start` from the worker-boot hook and
pick the inherited measurement back up, and configuration mistakes
raise while environmental declines warn and no-op.

`simplecov dead-code --production PATH` then crosses the accumulated
store with the test report. Per line: run by both is normal, run in
production but untested (`--untested-in-production`) is the
highest-value place to add a test, tested but never run in production
is possibly dead with only its own spec as a defender, and run by
neither is dead. The default view prints the two deletion-candidate
rows in the greppable path:ranges form, marks a file whose every
relevant line skipped production as "(entire file)", and names the
window the data spans in the header, because the window is the
evidence: a day of traffic misses monthly jobs. `--json` emits every
category as data. The union of a test suite and real traffic answers a
question neither answers alone, and coverage over a long enough window
is far better evidence for deleting Ruby than any static analysis of
it.

The first hyphenated command name also surfaced a latent assumption in
the man page spec, which looked commands up unescaped; it now goes
through the generator's own roff escaping.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1271.

Give diff and ratchet the Output split their siblings have

The patch and dead-code commands keep their rendering in an Output
submodule beside the computation; diff and ratchet were the two
remaining commands mixing the halves at a size where the seam is worth
cutting. diff's row formatting (the sign-colored delta columns and
status suffixes) moves to Diff::Output, leaving the module that
computes rows, deltas, and the fail-on-drop gate; ratchet's write
summary, below-floor note, and JSON form move to Ratchet::Output,
leaving the floor computation. Pure moves, no behavior change, and the
remaining commands are either already split or small enough that a
file boundary would add structure without buying clarity.

Keep a coverage history, not just the last run

.last_run.json holds one number per criterion for the sole benefit of
the drop check, which is a lot of policy resting on a single data
point: a run that dipped for an unrelated reason quietly becomes the
baseline the next run is judged against. Every successful run now also
appends to coverage/.history.json: the per-criterion totals, the
per-group and per-file percentages, a timestamp, and the branch and
commit when the project is a git checkout. The file is bounded
(history_limit, 100 entries by default, 0 disables), written atomically
with the corrupt-file tolerance .last_run.json has, and plain
committable JSON so the trend can survive a clean CI checkout.
.last_run.json itself keeps working exactly as it did.

The history buys three things. The HTML report grows a Trend column:
one sparkline per file and per group, drawn only when the report
embeds two or more recorded runs, so existing reports render exactly
as before. Direction of travel is a quiet line in the report's
secondary ink and the newest run is a dot in the row's own
coverage-band color, which keeps the trend speaking the palette the
report already uses, dark mode and the colorblind toggle included.
Gaps in the record break the line rather than being interpolated
over, series are min-max scaled because direction is the message, and
the tooltip carries the absolute numbers. `simplecov history` prints
the same trend in the terminal as Unicode sparklines with the run
rows beneath, and --file follows one file's trajectory. And
`drop_baseline :median` / `:branch` let maximum_coverage_drop compare
against the median of the recorded history, or the newest recorded
run on the current git branch, instead of whatever ran most recently.

The report's data path is an optional top-level `history` array in
coverage.json, folded into the still-unreleased schema 1.2, carrying
the recorded entries with the reported run appended, since recording
happens after the exit checks pass and the sparklines should include
the run being looked at. Recording rides the same successful-run
condition .last_run.json uses, so a failing run becomes neither the
drop baseline nor a data point in the trend.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1267.

Spell SimpleCov in CamelCase throughout the documentation

The docs and changelogs referred to the project as simplecov or
Simplecov in prose. Fix the casing wherever the name means the project
itself, including the CLI usage text that feeds the man page, and leave
the gem name, executable, require paths, and file paths lowercase.

Table sorting binds click-to-sort and the sort indicator to every
header cell by position, so the new Trend column advertised a sort it
could not deliver: clicking it reordered rows by serialized SVG markup.

indicator, no pointer cursor, and no click handler, and marking another
column's sort no longer decorates it.

The trend sparklines drew only the primary criterion because that was
all the history recorded per file. Entries now record every measured
criterion for every file, the same {criterion => percent} shape the
totals and groups already use, so the history carries branch and
method trajectories too. simplecov history --file renders one
sparkline per criterion like the totals view, its JSON rows carry a
percents object instead of a single number, and the schema's
history_entry matches (still unreleased, changed in place).

The HTML report stops rendering the Trend column for now: the history
still rides into the embedded data and coverage.json, but the viewer
keeps it as data only until the sparklines can do the richer record
justice. The trend-header sorting exclusion goes with the column.

See https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1267.

though methods share the branch report shape. A touched method now
gets its own column, missing note, JSON stats, and --minimum gate,
through the same scorer branches use, appearing only when the change
actually touched one.

regardless of configuration. The result line now follows the report's
own meta.primary_coverage, falling back to line coverage for documents
from before meta carried one.

data must not fail the suite that measured the tests.

Two additions back the report. The bundled FileSink stamps each file
with the last drain that carried it (last_seen, optional on read, so v1
stores and remote sinks that only fill the documented shape keep
working). Oneshot clears on drain, so still-running code re-reports
every interval and the stamp tracks real recency, which is far stronger
deletion evidence than a binary bit over the whole window. And the
runtime adds a fresh random share of flush_jitter (default a tenth of
flush_interval) to every wait, so a fleet of workers booted together
drifts apart instead of contending on the shared sink at the same
instant every interval, forever.

Date each dead-code row with the store's last sighting

The FileSink's last_seen stamps reached the HTML report but not the
command that owns the deletion question. Each dead-code row now carries
the date the store last saw its file run, in the same parenthesized
position the entire-file marker uses, and the two combine when both
hold. On a dead or possibly dead row the stamp means other lines of the
file (or lines the report deems irrelevant) ran then, so a recent date
says the file is alive around its dead lines, while no date says the
window never saw the file at all, which is the strongest form of the
evidence. The untested-in-production view dates its rows the same way,
--json entries carry the full stamp as last_seen where the text prints
its date, and rows from a stamp-less store (a v1 file, or a remote sink
that only fills the documented shape) print bare, exactly as before.

Link the production coverage document from the README

docs/Production.md declares itself part of the SimpleCov documentation,
but the README never pointed back at it, so the only paths to the
production mode ran through the configuration and CLI documents. The
README now names the mode and links the document beside its pointer to
docs/Configuration.md.

Default dead-code's --production from the configured store

A project that sets `production_coverage` in `.simplecov` had already
told SimpleCov where its production store lives, and `simplecov
dead-code` made it repeat the answer on every run. The command now
fills in --production from the configured setting, read through the
CLI's neutered dotfile loader exactly the way ratchet reads
`baseline_file`, so the DSL is the single source of truth for where the
store lives and the flag becomes an override. An explicit --production
still wins, a project with no configured store gets the same missing
flag error as before (now also naming the setting that would default
it), and a dotfile that cannot be read warns and falls back to nothing
rather than guessing, because unlike coverage_dir there is no sensible
fallback path and the command's own missing-store error is the right
answer.

Record production coverage's place in the configuration roadmap

The roadmap exists so each change lands as part of one plan rather than
as another accretion, and `production_coverage` shipped without a line
in it. The new section records three decisions so future cleanups
preserve them. It belongs to the report family, and its `*_coverage`
name does not make it a criterion, any more than the Phase 3 target
name `eval_coverage` is one, since the `:eval` lesson is about riding
the criteria switch, which it never does. The two configuration
surfaces are split on purpose: `SimpleCov::Production.start` stays
outside the DSL because `.simplecov` is loaded by every test run and by
the CLI's dotfile reader, and loading a config file must never be able
to boot a production measurement tap, while the report-side pointer
lives in the DSL and the CLI defaults from it. And growth follows the
page's existing patterns: a second report-side knob converges on the
Phase 4 keyword-construct template rather than a second `production_*`
flat name, and any future enforcement cell belongs in the `coverage`
block grammar, shipped only when its enforcement ships.

List coverage-redundant tests with tests --redundant

A test whose covered lines are all covered by other tests contributes
no coverage of its own. `simplecov tests --redundant` lists those
tests from the track_tests recording the report already carries. Per
file, two bitmaps find the lines seen exactly once, a second pass
credits each uniquely covered line to its owner, and every context
left without one is redundant, contexts that covered nothing included.
The flag composes with the existing narrowing, so a path or path:line
argument intersects the redundant set with the tests touching it.

The sweep reads tables no query named, so a malformed one anywhere
poisons the whole answer, matching the targeted queries'
all-or-nothing tolerance. An empty answer over a real recording is
good news and the stderr note says so, while an empty recording keeps
the plainer no-tests-recorded message. The docs frame the list the
way dead-code frames its buckets: candidates for review, not a delete
list, because assertions and mutation-killing power are invisible to
coverage and two mutually subsuming tests are both listed even though
deleting both would lose the lines.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1288.

Adopt mutation testing with mutant

Line coverage says a line ran. It does not say an example would have
noticed the line being wrong. Mutant answers the second question: it
rewrites the code a piece at a time and reports each rewrite the suite
still accepts.

Configured with the full operator set, because a reduced one leaves
whole families of rewrite unasked. A mutation that takes the test
process down, by timeout or by abort, counts as caught: the suite
noticed, which is the only thing being asked.

The support the runs need comes with it. Fixture repositories are built
once and copied per example rather than rebuilt per mutation, the
browser is kept out of the suite, colour and parallel environment
variables are scrubbed so an inherited one cannot decide an assertion,
and the dogfood report records which example covered each line.

Let the checks answer their reports as values

The roadmap's fourth item, in its non-breaking form. Every threshold
check already computed structured violations through
CoverageViolations; what stayed buried was the rendering, which each
check printed line by line from inside report_violation. Testing a
message meant capturing stderr, and a message nothing captured could
say anything.

Checks now answer `violations` and `report_lines` as public values,
each check renders its violations into lines, and printing happens in
exactly one place, the base class's `report`. The lines are gathered
by concatenation rather than flat_map, so a check answering a bare
string instead of its list is an error a test sees, not a spelling the
flattening would forgive: flat_map wraps strays, and fourteen
mutations dropping the array literal survived through it before the
spelling changed.

Every stderr-capturing example in the check specs becomes an assertion
on values, and the base class gains examples of its own for both sides
of `failing?`, the stashed readers, the memoized violations, and the
one printing seam. `ExitCodeHandling.call` keeps its signature and its
behavior.

Answer the exit path instead of performing it

The roadmap's fifth item, in its non-breaking form. `run_exit_tasks`
now does everything the end of a measured run does — the configured
at_exit hook, the previous-error notice, the result processing with
its report — and answers the exit status the process should end with,
without ending it. `run_exit_tasks!` stays as the exiting adapter the
at_exit block and `collate` call: one `Kernel.exit`, guarded by the
same `successful?` the rest of the exit handling asks.

The two methods that printed and exited in one breath are gone.
`report_previous_error` says its piece and returns, and
`report_processing_failure` answers the status it was handed after
explaining a positive one. Every branch of the path is now pinned by
examples that hold the status as a value and assert the process was
never ended, which is what makes the behaviour that decides a build's
status answerable in process.

Give the run its own object

The roadmap's first and third items, in their non-breaking form. The
state one measured run accumulates — pid, start time, result, the
collate and forked-subprocess flags, the serial the parent counts for
its forks — moves off the singleton's instance variables onto one
`SimpleCov::CurrentRun` object, and `start_tracking` begins a new run
as a new object. The singleton keeps every method it had: the
delegators are generated by Forwardable, which keeps the state's
behaviour a CurrentRun question rather than fifty of the singleton's.

Not everything a run holds dies with it. The fork genealogy carries
into the successor, because a forked child that restarts tracking must
not forget it was forked, or it produces the final report itself, and
a parent must not recount its serials from zero, or its next
children's names collide with its first ones. The Rails parallel
sandbox suite is what caught the version of this change that forgot
that.

Examples stop unsetting singleton state by hand: the specs that
shepherded five instance variables through arounds now swap one run
object in and out, and one cross-example leak (a forked mark that
outlived its example and failed an unrelated at_exit hook test in some
orders) died of the same change, which is the class of failure this
item exists to remove.

The merge path is respelled on the way through: `result` binds the
merge decision once, and `merge_own_slice` stores this process's slice
reading it back through `result` itself, whose memoized answer it is,
so no spelling of that read survives unobserved.

Give every setting a writer of its own

The roadmap's second item, in its non-breaking form. Seventeen
dual-purpose configuration methods distinguished reading from writing
by a sentinel or a nil check, which left each one carrying two
behaviours. Each now has an explicit writer — `SimpleCov.color =
:never`, `SimpleCov.merge_timeout = 300`, and the rest — holding the
write arm's whole behaviour: root expands and invalidates the derived
coverage path, an assigned coverage path is created on the spot,
primary_coverage refuses a criterion that is not enabled,
history_limit refuses a negative count, the timeouts ignore anything
but an Integer, and production_coverage expands against the root.

The dual methods keep their spelling and their answers, and their
write arms delegate to the writers, so the write behaviour lives once.
The breaking half of the item — retiring the dual spelling and giving
the DSL a builder — stays on the roadmap.

Kill the mutation run's five survivors

A full run under Ruby 4.0.6 left five mutations alive.

Two erased the ready_to_process_results? guard in run_exit_tasks: the
example for the not-ready path asserted the SUCCESS answer but not
that processing was skipped, and processing a mutant environment's
empty result lands on SUCCESS too. The example now asserts
process_result was never called.

The other three replaced File.open with self.open in FileSink#locked,
ResultsetStore#holding_writelock, and SourceLoader#call. Those were
killable while Kernel#open ran a leading-pipe path as a command, which
is what the pipe-path examples proved. Ruby 4.0 removed that mode, so
under the Ruby the mutation run uses the two spellings are
indistinguishable, and the open moves into a one-line wrapper with a
scoped mutant:disable. The flag, permission, and flock mutations stay
in the callers, where their tests still kill them.

All four subjects re-measure at 100% under Ruby 4.0.6.
