Remove four of the six steep:ignore sites

Each removal says something true instead of silencing the checker.

Marshal.load reads from an IO at runtime, but core RBS's
Marshal::_Source refuses IO nominally over its nil-able getbyte and
read returns. A shim overload records what the runtime accepts.

The delegators were generated through Forwardable extended onto the
singleton class, whose ancestors RBS has no way to speak about.
SingleForwardable at module level means the same thing where Steep
can see it.

CommandHelpers is only ever extended into named modules, so its sig
now declares Module#name as the String it always is there.

The ensure cleanup in spawn_worker carries @type var annotations for
the body locals Steep cannot type in an ensure. Annotations are
comments, so unlike a cast they add nothing a mutation could remove.

The two ignores left are the truthful minimum: org exists only on
JRuby so no declaration for it can be honest, and Steep resolves a
define_method block's super lexically rather than through the prepend
chain it dispatches to at runtime.

Sweep two thirds of the rubocop directives out of the code

63 rubocop:disable and enable markers become 22, all three ways.

Whole-file judgments move into .rubocop.yml, justification and all:
the Metrics exemptions for the one-concern homes (Production,
CoverageViolations, the usage document, the location conventions, the
viewer-data validator, the sandbox harness, the dogfood report), the
Naming/PredicateMethod allowance for commands that report whether
they acted, the class-variable fakes that mirror Minitest's own flag,
and the behavior-describing specs no single class owns. Fixtures are
now excluded wholesale as the byte-stable inputs they are, which
retires their inline markers and the per-fixture exclusion list. The
two directive lines inside fixtures become plain comments rather than
disappearing, so the line numbers the specs assert against stay put.

Two sites are refactored instead: the RSpec stand-ins in the test
tracker spec become verified class and instance doubles, and the
shadowing inspect's unused parameter gains its underscore.

What remains inline is the deliberate minimum, each with its reason:
Marshal on our own pipes, stderr that must not be warn, the literal
/dev/null of a git diff, evals whose foreign location is the point,
and their kin.

Remove the coverage exclusions the suite has outgrown

A cross-reference of every simplecov:disable region against the raw
merged dogfood coverage found most of them hiding code the suite now
reaches: the stub-driven examples the mutation-testing sweep added
(platform stubs for the Windows rename retry and the fork hook, era
stubs for the extractor's version arms, respond_to? stubs for the
criterion fallback, invalid-byte feeds for the directive parser,
loaded shims for ActionView) cover what the directives were written
to excuse. 122 directive markers in lib/ become 56.

The one gap the removals exposed was real: on 3.2 and 3.3 the modern
arms of the location conventions never run natively and were only
green inside the blanket exclusion. A new "modern branch conventions"
describe mirrors the legacy one, stubbing the era constant the other
way and pinning the modern tuple shapes, with a parens-opacity
example alongside for the container fold. The exclusions that remain
are the ones the data says still earn their keep: the run-mode
dependent parallel coordination, load-time guards no stub can reach,
and arms genuinely fixed at class definition time.

Verified at 100% line, branch, and method dogfood coverage on 3.2.11,
3.3.12, and 3.4.10, with the counted denominators growing by 151
lines and 108 branch arms that were previously excluded.

Remove the fifteen examples the whole quality lattice calls redundant

The track_tests recording (SIMPLECOV_TRACK_TESTS=1, run serially so no
worker's context map is lost, with the tracker's own specs excluded)
fed simplecov tests --redundant, which flagged 3,402 of 3,511 recorded
examples as covering no line uniquely. That number mostly measures how
unit tests share lines, so it was treated as a candidate pool and
filtered through three gates: judgment (out-of-process and contract
specs excluded, then only exact coverage-bitmap duplicates kept),
the dogfood report (line-identical examples still cover distinct
branch arms, and the recording named which spared 295), and a full
mutation run, which rejected all but fifteen: 1,373 mutations went
alive without the wider deletion, naming the examples that assert
distinct values on shared lines.

The fifteen that remain, eight in the results combiner's spec, five in
the lines classifier's, and two in last_run's, are duplicate in the
only sense that survives every gate: no unique line, arm, or method,
and no unique mutation kill. Verified by a second full run: 52,917
mutations, everything killed (three flaky survivors in
SimpleCov.successful? die in a targeted run, the known worker-exit
misreport).

docs/Redundant_Tests.md turns the method into a guide for anyone
pruning their own suite with track_tests, from recording through the
gates, with this sweep as its calibration.

Accept the shell's exit status for a missing command on JRuby

JRuby's spawn hands the --run command to the platform shell, which
reports a nonexistent file as 127 (not found) on Linux but as 126
(cannot execute) on macOS, so the two affected-subcommand examples
failed under JRuby on macOS. The assertion stays exact at 127 on
CRuby, where the CLI itself maps Errno::ENOENT to 127, and accepts
either shell code on JRuby only.

Run the spec suite in parallel on JRuby too

parallel_tests sat in the CRuby-only Gemfile group, so rake spec fell
back to the serial task on JRuby. Nothing about the fan-out is
CRuby-specific. The workers are plain spawned subprocesses rather than
forks, the per-worker environment scrubbing in spec/helper.rb is
engine-agnostic, and the dogfood report already stores and merges
worker partials on any engine. Moving the gem out of the exclusion
takes the JRuby suite from 2:28 to 1:45 on a 10-core machine (the
remaining critical path is the worker that draws spec/cli_spec.rb) and
lets CI's JRuby jobs fan out across their runners' cores as well.

The watch subcommand examples get a higher wait ceiling on the JVM
engines to match. Their fake suite boots a fresh interpreter per
change, and on a loaded CI runner whose cores the parallel workers
already saturate, a JVM boot can outlast the flat ten second timeout.

Cache successful bundle checks across sandbox examples

Every sandbox example paid a subprocess Bundler boot in its before hook
to re-ask bundle check a question whose answer cannot change mid-suite.
No sandbox example rewrites its copied Gemfile, so one success per pair
of fixture Gemfile and opted-in groups now covers every later example
that sets up the same pair.

Merge sandbox examples that repeated the same child run

The template language examples ran the full rails child suite once per
assertion, which made them the slowest examples in the suite, and the
cover_views examples in the rspec-rails spec did the same. Each pair
asserted on the same report from an identical run, so one example per
setup now makes the run once and checks both facets.

Split rake spec workers by recorded runtime

parallel_tests splits by file size unless it has a runtime log, and
sandbox spec files are tiny on disk while each spends seconds driving
fixture subprocesses, so the default split could park them on a couple
of workers and leave others nearly idle (two workers finished in under
a second while the busiest took 24).

A RuntimeLogFormatter subclass in .rspec_parallel records per-file
runtimes during every parallel run. The stock RuntimeLogger records
nothing here because spec/helper.rb scrubs TEST_ENV_NUMBER from the
worker process, so the subclass restores the saved worker identity
around the one call that writes the log, the same dance DogfoodReport
does around ParallelTests.wait_for_other_processes_to_finish.

The rake task opts into the grouping only once the log exists, because
grouping by a missing log is an error, and passes allowed-missing 100
so a log that predates new or renamed spec files cannot fail the run.
With the log in place the worker spread tightens from 0.3-24s to
14-22.6s.

Move TruffleRuby to the unstable CI tier

TruffleRuby leaves the stable workflow's matrix and joins
truffleruby-head in the nightly unstable workflow, which is
informational and allowed to fail. With that demotion the engine no
longer earns special cases in the suite: the oneshot_lines skip, the
return-codes skip pinned to a fixed TruffleRuby bug, and the dogfood
coverage threshold all go, so a TruffleRuby run now gets an
informational coverage report like any other unlisted engine. Comments
and docs that enumerated TruffleRuby among the supported runtimes now
name only CRuby and JRuby. The released changelog entries keep their
mentions, since they describe what those versions shipped.

Pitch the headline features in the README and production doc

The README gains a section for each of the release's headline features,
each with a short example: test attribution, production dead-code
hunting, patch coverage, view coverage, the redesigned configuration
grammar, per-file ratchets with run history, and the expanded CLI. The
production coverage paragraph that already closed the configuration
section moves into its own section unchanged.

docs/Production.md now opens the same way: a "Why measure coverage in
production" section makes the case (only real traffic settles whether
code is dead, and oneshot coverage collects that evidence at near-zero
cost) before "How to set it up and use it" explains the mechanics.

Strip redundant comments across the codebase

Code should read as its own explanation. A comment that restates the
method name below it earns nothing, drifts out of sync with the code it
describes until it is actively wrong, and pads every download and install
of the gem. This removes about 9,700 net lines of comment, keeping only
the ones carrying knowledge the code cannot: per-Ruby-version Coverage
conventions, merge invariants such as nil table versus empty table,
rationale for deliberately unusual code written for speed, security notes
on path traversal and script-terminator escaping, and the pragmas
themselves.

Where a comment was propping up an unclear name, the name changed
instead. Combine::CoverageAccumulator#judgeable? is now lines_measured?,
and the empty adapter subclass in the parallel adapters spec is a plain
Class.new rather than a block with a comment for a body.

Style/Documentation is disabled, since it mandates a banner comment on
every class and module. Two empty rescue bodies keep a one-line reason,
because Lint/SuppressedException reads a comment as the deliberate
marker.

Issue references now live once, beside the behavior in lib, rather than
being repeated in the specs that cover it.

Fixtures under spec/fixtures and test_projects are untouched: their line
numbers, layout, and directive markers are what the specs assert against.
Prose documents and CI configuration are also left alone.

The gem shrinks from 279,552 to 213,504 bytes, and its uncompressed
payload from 912,055 to 712,636. Compiled frontend assets are unaffected,
since the minifier already dropped those comments.

Give SimpleCov::Deprecation a life of its own

The module reached up into the singleton it is part of. `warn` read
`SimpleCov.deprecations` for the mode and raised `ConfigurationError`,
so the lowest-level piece of the deprecation machinery depended on the
whole configuration surface being loaded.

Both dependencies now point the other way. `ConfigurationError` moves to
its own file, which the module requires directly, and the mode lives on
`Deprecation` itself, with `SimpleCov.deprecations` as the front door
that writes it. `Configuration::DEPRECATION_MODES` becomes an alias of
`Deprecation::MODES`, so the public constant is unchanged.

Moving the mode also connects two things that were only nominally
related. `SimpleCov.deprecations` wrote an instance variable on whatever
received it, while `warn` always consulted the `SimpleCov` singleton.
That is the same object in every real use, but it left the configuration
spec, which exercises a throwaway config object, asserting an accessor
wired to nothing. Now every writer reaches the one emitter, and `reset!`
clears the mode alongside the emitted set so nothing leaks between
examples.

Rename methods whose comments described their return value

A comment whose first sentence says what a method answers is the name
failing, not the code being subtle. Ten such names now carry what their
comment did, and the comments keep only the part a name cannot: the
reasoning behind the behavior.

  TestTracker#enter                    -> begin_track
  CoverageViolations.percent_for       -> floored_percent_for
  Production.next_wait                 -> interval_with_jitter
  FileSink#locked                      -> with_exclusive_lock
  SourceFile::SkipChunks#for           -> chunks_for
  ParallelResultMerger.collect         -> collect_payloads
  CLI::Show.locate                     -> locate_or_report
  CLI::Status::Facts.resultset         -> readable_resultset
  CLI::Affected::ChangedFiles.toplevel -> repository_toplevel
  Baseline.read                        -> read_if_exists

TestTracker's local `entry` becomes `nested_opening`, which is what makes
the deleted sentence about the return value unnecessary at the call site.

Only the last of these needs an alias. The gemspec draws the line: it
packages sig/simplecov.rbs, "the public API signature file", and leaves
sig/internal out as "skeleton signatures for internal classes so Steep
can type-check the whole codebase". `Baseline.read` is the only one
declared in the file that ships, so it keeps its old spelling delegating
with a deprecation warning. The rest are declared only in sig/internal
and were renamed outright. `UselessResultsRemover.root_regx`, a typo
long preserved as an alias of `root_regex`, now warns as well.

Pin the deprecation mode against mutation

Mutation testing the renames turned up nineteen survivors, every one of
them in the mode accessors the previous commit moved onto
SimpleCov::Deprecation. The mode's validation was only ever exercised
through SimpleCov.deprecations, whose spec block is scoped to
SimpleCov::Configuration, so mutant never selected it for the
Deprecation subject and nothing held the new code to account.

The guard could be deleted outright, inverted to `unless mode`, or have
its raise reduced to a bare `raise`, and every one of those passed. So
could dropping the mode from reset!.

Seven examples close it: the default, both valid assignments, a truthy
invalid mode and a nil one, that a refused assignment leaves the mode
alone, and that reset! puts it back. Two of them borrow the trick the
`emitted` specs already use, removing the instance variable before
asserting the default and reading it back directly after reset!, because
the before hook meant `||=` never reached its fallback and reset!'s own
mutation hid behind it.

Mutant now reports 100% over the 33 subjects this branch changed.

Shard the mutation analysis across a matrix

The mutation job timed out on the comment-stripping push. Mutant selects
a subject whose line range the diff touches, and removing a comment above
a method moves every method below it, so a formatting pass over the tree
selects most of the library: that push touched 186 of 190 files in lib
and selected 790 of 1320 subjects. Measured locally the run needed about
five hours against a thirty minute timeout, and it was still reporting no
survivors when it was stopped.

A plan job now lists the subjects the change touches and fans them out
over a matrix, fifty to a runner. Fifty is the size where even a shard of
the slow subjects, the ones whose examples shell out, stays inside the
timeout at the twenty-odd seconds each they cost, while an ordinary pull
request still fits on a single runner and pays nothing for the fan-out.
Ten would have spread that same push over seventy-nine runners, most of
their time spent cloning and installing; a hundred would have put a
worst-case shard at roughly forty minutes, back over the timeout. The
same push now plans sixteen shards.

Subjects go round robin rather than in contiguous slices. Mutant lists
them sorted, so a namespace lands together and the expensive ones
cluster: every `SimpleCov::CLI::Diff` subject shells out, and contiguous
slicing would put them all on one runner, which is the runner that times
out.

A ceiling of twenty-four shards keeps a runaway selection growing the
shards rather than the runners, and a change that selects nothing skips
the matrix entirely, so a docs or spec only change stops at the plan job.

The partition is a Rakefile function with its own spec, because a shard
that silently drops a subject leaves it unmutated and says nothing.

Load the shard partition instead of shelling out for it

The sharding spec drove the Rakefile through a subprocess, which broke
two CI jobs.

On Windows the multi-line `-e` script reached `bundle.bat` through
cmd.exe and lost everything after its first line, so the subprocess
loaded the Rakefile, printed nothing and exited zero. The helper read
that as three missing values, and the example asserting every subject
lands in exactly one shard compared nil to nil and passed: a spec that
could only fail by accident.

On Ruby 3.3 the same subprocess ran `bundle exec` while four parallel
workers were shelling out to fixture frameworks, and RubyGems wrote
"isn't a Gem::Specification (NilClass instead)" to stderr as the
specification cache was rewritten underneath them, which the return
codes spec reads as noise it must not see.

The partition moves to tasks/mutant_shard.rb, which the Rakefile and the
spec both load directly, the way tasks/man_page.rb and its spec already
do. No subprocess, so neither failure has anywhere to happen, and the
spec now names the module it covers rather than needing an exemption
from the path cop.

`subjects_since` is specified too, since loading the file into the suite
brings it into the dogfood report: the rule that tells a subject name
apart from the "Subjects in environment: N" line mutant ends its listing
with is worth pinning anyway.

Stop running the checks twice on every pull request

A branch in this repository fires both `push` and `pull_request`, so an
unfiltered push trigger ran the whole of stable, lint and typecheck twice
for each pull request: nine duplicated jobs, the seven-way test matrix
across Windows, macOS, Linux and JRuby among them. The probe branch that
exercised the mutation matrix showed twenty-one checks where twelve would
have said the same thing.

Scoping push to main leaves the pull_request run, which is the better of
the two. It builds the branch merged into its base rather than the branch
alone, so it sees a conflict with a base that moved since the branch was
cut, and it is the only one a fork's pull request fires at all. The
mutation workflow has been scoped this way since it was sharded, which is
why it was the one workflow not running twice.

Two consequences worth knowing. Pushing a topic branch with no pull
request open now runs nothing until the pull request exists, draft or
otherwise. And a version tag no longer re-runs the checks, since it is
pushed from a commit on main that has already run them; push_gem, which
triggers on the tag, is untouched.

Run the checks again on a release tag

Scoping push to main took tag pushes with it, so a release ran push_gem
alone. The tag is cut from a commit on main that has already run
everything, so nothing was going unchecked, but a release is the one
moment worth confirming against the exact tree being published rather
than against the commit it was cut from.

Tags sit alongside the branch filter, so a pull request still runs each
of these once: a ref is a branch or a tag, never both, and pull_request
is untouched.

The mutation workflow keeps branches only. It analyses what a change
touches, and a tag changes nothing relative to the main commit it points
at, so it would select no subjects and add a job that always skips.

Stop mutant from running specs RSpec would filter out

Mutant's RSpec integration collects examples straight from RSpec.world
and pushes the selected ones into filtered_examples, bypassing the
conditional-filter pruning, so every example runs under mutant whatever
its :if metadata says.

That made the value-position spec, guarded by
if: !LEGACY_COVERAGE_LOCATIONS, run on 3.3 and fail, aborting 12 Visitor
subjects as neutral failures. Stub the constant instead, the way the
modern and legacy convention describes already do, so the example runs
on every Ruby.

The env-gated fuzz spec was running in every killfork for the same
reason. Marking it mutant: false takes the Visitor namespace from 86.7s
to 9.3s, and nothing in the lib relied on it as a killing test.

Kill the survivors the neutral failures had been hiding, along with the
LEGACY guards that go unexercised on a legacy Ruby, by descending into
unless and loop bodies, keeping a folded falsy unless body, and adding
four modern convention cases. The whole lib now runs clean under mutant
on 3.3.12.

Run the extractor fuzzer on purpose rather than by accident

The differential fuzzer had no rake task and no CI job, so the only thing
running it was mutant, which ignores the :if metadata gating it behind
SIMPLECOV_FUZZ. Marking the spec mutant: false in beee3e37 closed that
path and left it running nowhere at all.

Add a rake fuzz task taking optional seed counts, and a nightly ruby-head
job that calls it. The task suppresses the own-coverage dogfooding, which
enforces 100% line coverage at exit and would fail any run of a single
spec file.

The job asks for 500 seeds, which generates 30000 programs in 21 seconds
against a 20 minute timeout, where the default 20 seeds generate 1200.
Only CRuby gets a job, since the extractor needs Prism and the spec skips
itself where branch coverage is unsupported.

Feed the result benchmark the shape a Result expects

Plain Coverage.start yields the pre-0.18 shape, a filename pointing
straight at a line array, while Result has required the lines, branches
and methods hash since. The script raised NoMethodError on
transform_keys inside SourceFileBuilder for anyone who ran it.

Adapt through ResultAdapter, which is what result_processing does before
building a Result, so the benchmark measures the input shape production
actually hands over.

Add rake tasks for the benchmarks

The four scripts under benchmarks/ were reachable only by remembering
their paths and their arguments. Wrap each one in a task under a
benchmark namespace, appending the optional arguments only when given so
each script keeps its own defaults rather than the Rakefile repeating
them. The env knobs COUNT, SCALE, PROCESSES, SKIP, REBUILD and BREAKDOWN
pass through as before.

Type-check the frontend from rake, not only from CI

bun run typecheck was the one check CI ran that rake did not, so a
TypeScript type error passed a clean local rake and failed the typecheck
workflow. Add frontend:typecheck and put it in default, alongside the rbs
and steep tasks that cover the Ruby side.

Add frontend:install as well, and hang typecheck and test off it, so a
fresh clone installs what it needs instead of failing on a missing
node_modules. Installing costs a third of a second once bun has cached
the packages, and --frozen-lockfile means a lockfile that has drifted
from package.json fails here the way it already fails in CI.

The bun presence guard now lives in one helper rather than being spelled
out in each task.

Let the nightly workflow be triggered by hand

unstable.yml was schedule-only, so neither the ruby-head matrix nor the
new fuzz job could be exercised against a change without waiting for
midnight.

Collect the type checks behind one task

rbs, steep and frontend:typecheck all answer the same question on
different sides of the project, so give them an aggregate the way spec
and frontend:test already have one in test. The default task is now
rubocop, typecheck and test rather than a flat list of five, and the two
type checks run before the suites instead of straddling them.

The individual tasks stay invokable on their own.

Adopt Standard as the Ruby style, on top of RuboCop

Add standard, standard-performance and standard-rspec. .rubocop.yml
inherits the first two, and .standard.yml gives Standard its own entry
point. Where the two tools disagreed, Standard wins: the outdent override
for access modifiers is gone and 87 modifiers are reindented,
keyword_init: true comes off five Structs, and validate_contexts! no
longer mixes || and && inside an unless. The remaining offenses on both
sides were mechanical and went through rubocop -a.

standard has to be pinned above 1.35.1. Unpinned, Bundler resolves the
1.35.0.1 placeholder gem that exists only to print a warning about itself.
Adopting Standard also caps RuboCop at 1.88.2.

Three changes here are not mechanical and are worth reading closely:

  * Two evals in configuration_spec deliberately misreport their source
    location to test exception anchoring, and Style/EvalWithLocation
    rewrote them to __FILE__ and __LINE__, which broke both specs. They
    are restored, behind a directive that actually works.

  * Five `# rubocop:disable-next` comments were ESLint syntax that RuboCop
    has never understood, so the cops they named were never suppressed.
    Lint/CopDirectiveSyntax found them. They are disable and enable pairs
    now.

  * standard-rspec reaches RuboCop through .standard.yml rather than
    inherit_gem. Inheriting its config requires loading the Capybara,
    FactoryBot and RSpecRails plugins, none of which this project uses,
    and it sets a Language parameter on RSpecRails that
    rubocop-rspec_rails rejects, warning on every run. While those plugins
    were loaded, FactoryBot/FactoryNameStyle also read generate("fish") as
    a factory reference and rewrote the argument to a symbol, breaking
    four completions specs. `rake standard` still enforces standard-rspec.

Standard takes no configuration beyond ignores, so the RSpec thresholds
.rubocop.yml sets deliberately, each with a TODO to tighten, and the spec
layout this project owns are listed as ignores in .standard.yml rather than
refactored away. RuboCop stays the enforcer for those.

Lint the frontend with oxlint, wired up as frontend:lint, and collect the
three linters behind a lint task that replaces rubocop in default.

Kill four subjects' mutations regardless of example order

CI's mutation shards reported 16 survivors across GroupNames#normalize,
StringFilter#compute_segment_pattern and two Completions::Scripts methods.
The same survivors reproduce on the commit before the Standard adoption, so
they predate it. .rspec sets --order random, so each mutant invocation
draws a fresh ordering, and repeated runs of one unchanged subject returned
6, 1, 5 and 0 alive. Something order-dependent was failing under some
orderings and counting as a kill for every mutation in the run, which is
why these subjects have read as covered.

The mutations these four subjects actually leave uncovered:

  * normalize's rejection message interpolates the value and its class, and
    the only spec matched /Group names must be Strings/, asserting neither.
    Assert the whole message, and add a nil case, whose inspect and to_s
    differ where 42's do not.

  * compute_segment_pattern was unguarded for regexp escaping, for the
    segment boundary on a directory-only filter, and for the condition
    choosing the bare-filename relaxation. Three specs cover those.

  * The zsh renderers quote command and option descriptions, and the script
    fixtures contain no quote to escape. Add descriptions that do, mirroring
    the fish escaping spec.

The boundary in the bare-filename branch is genuinely redundant, since the
preceding [^/]* already reaches back to the segment start. Checked over
every combination of 84 filter arguments and 5460 paths drawn from a, b,
dot and slash, the two forms agree everywhere, so the mutation is accepted
rather than exempted.

Refactor the specs to the standard-rspec shape

standard-rspec caps an example at one expectation and five lines, and
wants a spec file's path to spell its constant. The suite met none of
the three: 1433 examples carried more than one expectation, 767 ran past
five lines, and 73 files sat beside the constant's namespace rather than
inside it. .rubocop.yml raised the two caps to 6 and 20 and exempted the
path cop outright, which is what kept the suite green.

Move the 73 files under spec/simple_cov, drop the three exemptions, and
rewrite every offending example. Splitting is honest rather than
mechanical: an expectation that describes a second thing becomes its own
example, several attributes of one object fold into have_attributes or
match, and an expensive arrangement is hoisted into a let or a before
hook shared by the examples that came out of it, so no subprocess, server
or real report is formatted twice. Where a run's exit status was only ever
a sanity check, it moves into a helper that raises, which is setup and not
an expectation.

Length came down the same way: heredocs, coverage hashes and expected
documents moved into lets or helper methods, and ensure cleanup moved into
after hooks, since ExampleLength counts both.

Two things the refactoring had to preserve. Mutant selects a subject's
tests from the most specific expression matching it, so no example group
gained a method-named describe it did not already have. And the static
fixtures that pushed eight groups past RSpec/MultipleMemoizedHelpers are
plain methods rather than lets, which do not count against that cap.

The suite goes from 3053 to 5902 examples.

Also stub Pathname.new with a default before the specific one in the
formatter base spec. Stubbing only the specific argument left the lazy
Pathname.pwd in the same before hook calling the stub with an argument it
did not expect, so the example failed under some orderings. Mutant counts
that failure as a kill for every mutation in the run, which masked real
survivors across 27 subjects.

Four subjects lost a mutation the splitting had been killing, and get it
back. The overlapping-tracks example warned once because it tracked once,
which stopped saying anything about the guard that warns only the first
time, so it overlaps twice again. coverage_dir's second reader argument
and coverage_dir='s path invalidation were only ever exercised from a
configuration that had answered neither yet, so two examples ask them
after an answer is already cached. And pct_for's zero-total guard had no
report whose percent outlived the branches it was computed from.

Create the directory the last-run reading specs write into

The examples that plant corrupt or non-object JSON reach past
LastRun.write, which is what would otherwise create the directory to write
into. They passed because some earlier example in the same worker had
already created it.

rake spec only passes --group-by runtime when tmp/parallel_runtime_rspec.log
exists, and a fresh checkout has none, so CI groups the files by size.
Rewriting the suite changed every file's size, which changed the grouping,
and the group that ended up holding these examples no longer had anything
creating tmp/coverage<n> ahead of them. That is also why this was invisible
here: a working copy that has run the suite before has both the log and the
directories.

Reproduces on the parent commit with the seed CI drew:

  rm -rf tmp/coverage99
  TEST_ENV_NUMBER=99 bundle exec rspec spec/simple_cov/last_run_spec.rb --seed 43825

Cut the JRuby job down, and start it first

JRuby is the long pole in CI. Measured on jruby-10.0.6.0 over four workers,
which is what the runner gives us, the suite takes 289s against 77s for CRuby
on the same machine, and that matches the 4m49s the JRuby entry takes in CI.
Three things account for it.

cli_spec.rb was a 269s floor on its own. parallel_tests splits by file, so no
worker count could get under one file, and the sandbox specs that make up most
of the suite skip themselves on JRuby, which leaves little else to overlap it
with. Two subcommands held most of the file: affected at 100s and watch at
44s. Both now have spec files of their own under spec/simple_cov/cli/, sharing
the stdout, stderr and run helpers through a context in spec/support. The rest
stays in cli_spec.rb. Extracting more would not lower anything, since four
workers over the remaining 357s cannot finish sooner than 89s in any case.
RSpec/SpecFilePathFormat is excluded under that directory, since one class's
specs now span several files.

Spawning a process costs about fifteen times more on JRuby than on CRuby, so
the specs that shell out dominate what is left. Where several examples only
read back the result of one identical invocation, they now share a single
capture: return_codes_spec drops from 123s to 29s, assets_spec from 121s to
18s, coverage_for_eval_spec from 45s to 9s and gemspec_spec from 19s to 5s.
The four standalone-process examples in cli_spec ran the same invocation twice
each and now run it once. production_integration_spec keeps spawning per
example, because it union merges successive runs and the repetition is the
point.

CI never grouped by runtime. rake spec only passes --group-by runtime when
tmp/parallel_runtime_rspec.log exists, and a fresh checkout has none, so
parallel_tests split by file size instead. Cache the log per matrix entry,
keyed by sha so each run writes a fresh one and restore-keys picks up the
last.

Together the JRuby suite goes from 289s to 105s with the log, or 146s without
it, and CRuby from 77s to 61s. JRuby also now leads both matrices, since the
scheduler dispatches entries in order and the long pole belongs off the
critical path.

JRUBY_OPTS="--debug" stays. It reads like the obvious thing to drop, but the
suite fails without it, exactly as docs/Troubleshooting.md says.

Stop caching the parallel runtime log

Grouping by runtime made CI slower rather than faster. Re-running the JRuby job
on 72109e82 with the cache warm took 817s, against 293s for the same tree with
the cache cold. Two workers finished about 270s and 325s into the step while
the other two ran the full 830s.

The log it feeds on is not trustworthy. Every worker opens
tmp/parallel_runtime_rspec.log with "w" before appending to it, RSpec's own
"Run options" banner lands in the same file, and a local four worker JRuby run
produced 85 lines carrying three workers' results, the fourth contributing a
single entry. --allowed-missing 100 then turns an incomplete log into a
lopsided split instead of an error. A ten core machine absorbs that imbalance,
which is why it measured well here. A four core runner is defined by it.

restore-keys made it worse still. The 3.4 entry restored a log written by
9c823820, a commit that was reverted and never merged, and grouped against
spec paths that no longer exist.

Splitting by file size is what CI did before, and it is at least honest about
knowing nothing. The subcommand split and the shared captures stand without
this, and took the JRuby job from 363s to 293s on their own.

Give each parallel worker its own runtime log

parallel_tests points every worker at one shared log and opens it with "w", so
the workers truncate one another, and RSpec delivers `message` notifications to
every formatter descended from BaseTextFormatter. LoggerBase silences the
siblings it inherits but not that one, so the "Run options" banner lands in the
log as well. A four worker JRuby run produced 85 lines: three workers' results,
three banner lines, and a single entry from the fourth.

--group-by runtime reads a log like that as a suite of thirty files and parks
everything it has never heard of on one worker. That is what took the JRuby job
to 817s against 293s for the same tree without grouping.

Each worker writes tmp/parallel_runtime/<n>.log now, and rake spec merges them
once the run has finished, so a suite that dies partway cannot replace a whole
log with its fragment. The same JRuby run logs 84 entries after the change, one
for every spec file JRuby actually runs, and no banners.

rake spec also looks at a log before trusting it. One whose paths have largely
stopped existing describes some other tree, which is how the 3.4 entry came to
group against a log written by 9c823820, a commit that was reverted and never
merged. Such a log is discarded rather than used, which is what makes
restore-keys safe enough to bring the cache back.

Locally the JRuby suite goes from 137s cold to 103s grouped. That is measured on
ten cores for four workers, where imbalance costs little, so it is not evidence
about a four core runner. CI is.

Keep in .rubocop.yml only the cops that run

Standard disables most of what this file configured, and a cop Standard
disables stays disabled however you configure it. The Metrics department,
Naming/FileName, Naming/PredicateMethod, Style/CollectionMethods,
Style/ClassVars, Style/FrozenStringLiteralComment, Style/ModuleFunction and
Layout/LineLength were all inert, and so were the excludes and the reasoning
written beside them. A file with seven parameters, no frozen_string_literal
comment and `map` where this project prefers `collect` draws no complaint from
either runner.

Layout/LeadingCommentSpace, Layout/SpaceInsideHashLiteralBraces,
Style/StringLiterals, Style/Documentation and Style/EnvHome were set to exactly
the value Standard already sets, so restating them only invited drift.

Style/ClassVars had drifted already. It excluded spec/simplecov_spec.rb, which
64c22369 renamed, and nothing noticed because the cop was not running either
way.

What survives is what bites: the RSpec department, which Standard does not run
from here, Lint/ConstantDefinitionInBlock, and the excludes that describe this
repository's layout rather than its style.

The rules worth keeping move to where they can be read.
lib/simplecov/load_global_config.rb already explains the JRuby Dir.home hazard
in full. docs/Contributing.md already covered `extend self`, though it claimed
RuboCop enforced it, which has not been true under Standard, and it now says
what actually holds the line. The predicate naming that Naming/PredicateMethod
described is written down there as well.

The uncommitted edits already in the tree are folded in, since they touch the
same lines.

Wait for every worker's coverage before merging it

rake spec failed on JRuby about one run in three, always as a coverage error
that had nothing to do with coverage. Line coverage came back at 91.38%, or
87.46%, or 79.83% against a 96.5% minimum, and the denominator moved with it,
which is the tell: whole workers were missing from the merge rather than lines
being uncovered.

The first worker merges the others' partial results and waited for them with
ParallelTests.wait_for_other_processes_to_finish, which counts the entries in
the pid file the parent keeps. ParallelTests::Pids#add appends to a shared
array outside its own mutex, and parallel_tests spawns with in_threads, so on
JRuby, where those threads run in parallel for real, appends are lost. The file
then names fewer workers than are running. Instrumenting caught it holding one
pid while two workers were still going, which reads as everyone else being
finished, so the first worker merged the two partials that happened to be on
disk and reported the coverage of half a suite. CRuby never showed it because
the GVL makes the append atomic there by accident.

Each worker now leaves a marker as its suite starts, and the merging worker
waits until it has a partial for every marker. That counts the workers that
actually ran, which neither of the things parallel_tests offers can do:
PARALLEL_TEST_GROUPS is the process count that was asked for, before the empty
groups are dropped, and the pid file cannot be trusted at all. There is no
longer any path that ends the wait early, only a timeout that raises rather
than reporting a number it knows is short.

Partials are written through SimpleCov::AtomicFile as well, since the merging
worker reads that directory while the others write into it and half a JSON
document is not a partial result.

Six consecutive JRuby runs, against a third of them failing before.

and Steep 2.1 both need Ruby 3.3, and the stable matrix resolves the

Omit groups that match no files from the report

A group no file matched used to appear in every formatter as 100%
covered with nothing in it, so the rails profile's Channels, Mailers,
and Views tabs padded the HTML report of any app without those
directories, and declaring a group per directory a project might have
meant checking each one for Ruby files first. SimpleCov.grouped now
drops empty groups the way it already dropped an empty Ungrouped
bucket, which also lets the Ungrouped guard go.

minimum_coverage_by_group looked groups up in the result, so an empty
configured group would have drawn the "no group named" notice. Result
now answers configured_group? from its group configuration, and the
lookup stays silent for a group that is configured but matched nothing,
which passes as it did when the empty group reported 100%.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1293.

Alphabetize the rails profile's groups by name

Inspired by https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1294.

Honor simplecov directives inside ERB templates

The directive scan tokenizes a whole file as Ruby to find its comments.
An ERB template is not Ruby: its first `%>` opens a percent literal
that runs to the next `>`, so every comment after the first tag was
swallowed and a template's directives were never found. That is why a
Devise app could not disable the confirmable link it never renders.

SkipChunks now hands the scan only the Ruby inside a `.erb` file's tags,
at the template's own lines and columns. Text outside the tags is
blanked, tag delimiters become spaces, and a `<%# %>` comment tag
becomes a Ruby comment, so `<%# simplecov:disable %>` works as the
template's own form of the directive alongside Ruby comments inside a
code tag.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1295.

Honor simplecov directives inside Haml and Slim templates

The ERB fix left Haml and Slim behind, and they fail differently. Their
comment syntaxes (`-#` and `/`) are not Ruby comments, so a directive
written in them was never found, and a Slim `- # simplecov:disable`
control line read as an inline directive that disabled only itself,
because the `-` marker counts as code before the comment.

Each language now has an extractor that keeps the Ruby of its script
lines, turns its own comments into Ruby comments at the same column, and
blanks the rest, so both the native comment forms and Ruby comments on a
code line work. The two share a driver for the one thing that is not
line-local: a comment or an embedded block runs over the deeper-indented
lines below it, and an embedded `ruby:` block's lines are Ruby as
written. A `Directive::Template` module picks the extractor by extension,
which moves the dispatch out of SkipChunks.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1295.

Exempt templates from the eval_generated filter

The filter keeps a Coverage entry only when Prism finds a matching
construct in the static source, which for a template measured with
cover_views meant parsing ERB, Haml, or Slim as Ruby. That usually fails
and the entry is kept, but a template whose text happens to parse (a
Haml or Slim `#id` tag reads as a Ruby comment, and so does an ERB text
line starting with `#`) yielded a confident wrong parse with an empty
branch set, and the template's own conditionals vanished from branch
coverage.

BuilderContext now answers nil positions for a template without parsing
it. Everything a template reports is eval-generated by construction, so
the filter has nothing to distinguish there and every entry is kept, as
it already was when the parse failed.

Honor the deprecated nocov toggle in template comments

The toggle matcher read raw source lines and needed the line to begin
with `#`, so `<%# :nocov: %>`, `-# :nocov:`, and `/ :nocov:` were
silently ignored, and without a detected toggle the deprecation warning
never fired either. The Ruby-comment form inside an ERB code tag
happened to work because its inner line does begin with `#`.

SkipChunks now runs the matcher on the same extracted Ruby the
directives read, which it already computed, so every form skips its
block and emits the warning that names the `simplecov:disable`
replacement.

Warn and leave out templates a cover glob matches

A template no test rendered that a `cover` glob swept in went through
the unloaded-file simulator, which is built for Ruby: its line
classifier counted a Haml comment as a missed line and an `#id` tag as
never relevant, and Prism synthesized no branches because a template
does not parse. The template appeared at 0% in a shape that was wrong
in every criterion.

Tracked-path discovery now leaves templates out and warns once, naming
them relative to the root and pointing at `cover_views`, which compiles
an unrendered template and measures the real thing. Rendered templates
are unaffected: they are loaded, so they were never candidates.

Report a file with no branches as fully covered everywhere

A file tracked but never loaded had its empty branch and method sets
forced to 0%, from a time when simulation recorded no tuples for such a
file and an empty set really did mean nobody knows. Simulation has
synthesized those tuples statically for a while now, so an empty set is
a fact about the file: it has no branches, or a directive skipped the
ones it has. The file list read that 0% straight from the report while
the source view recomputed 100% from 0/0, so the same file showed both
numbers, and a per-file branch or method minimum failed a file with
nothing to cover.

The override now applies only to a file that carries no table for the
criterion, or to any never-loaded file when the extractor those tables
come from is absent. Both are still genuinely unaccounted for. The
source view also takes each header percentage from the report instead of
recomputing it from the fraction, so the two views cannot drift again.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1296.

Drop support for Ruby 3.2

Ruby 3.2 reached end of life in March 2026. Raising the floor to 3.3
makes Prism a default gem on every supported Ruby, so the static
coverage extractor stops probing for it: `available?` and the empty-hash
fallbacks for its absence are gone, and so is the emulation of 3.2's
constant folding, where parentheses were transparent for every literal
and a folded dead arm's branches survived in the branch table.

That removes the last thing the not-loaded percentage rule was asking.
A never-loaded file is unaccounted for when it carries no table for the
criterion, full stop, which is the per-file signal the merge path
already relied on. The specs reach that case the way the code does, with
coverage data that carries no table, rather than by stubbing a method
that no longer exists.

Name the simulation context by its subject, not by Prism

The context said "when Prism is available", which stopped being a
condition once every supported Ruby bundles it. What the examples in it
actually share is that the source was never loaded.

The examples said "for unloaded files" only because the context said

Look up Action View handlers on the new registry

Rails main removed Template.registered_template_handler, so cover_views
skipped every unrendered template. Read Template::Handlers.template_handlers
instead, and keep the old method when it is still there. An extension
with no handler stays skipped rather than compiling as raw text.

Load Prism only when the static extractor runs

SimpleCov 1.3.0 required Prism as soon as it loaded, and dropped the
LoadError guard around that require when Ruby 3.2 support went away. On
JRuby on Windows, Prism's FFI backend cannot open libprism, so a bare
require "simplecov" raised before any test ran.

Prism now loads the first time the static extractor is asked for
branches or methods. A line-only run, which is every JRuby run, never
loads it. Where the load fails, the extractor answers nil like any other
failure and never-loaded files fall back to empty branch and method
tables, as they did before 1.3.0. The answer is memoized, because a
failed load leaves nothing in $LOADED_FEATURES and would otherwise be
retried for every file. It is recorded explicitly rather than read off
defined?(Prism), since the FFI backend raises after module Prism is
already open.

A fixture stubs prism.rb to fail the same way and runs SimpleCov in a
subprocess. Specs that assert on Prism's output are tagged and skipped
where it cannot load. CI gains JRuby on macOS and Windows, so JRuby now
runs on all three operating systems alongside CRuby.

Getting the suite itself through on JRuby on Windows took more work.
JRuby there ignores the options Kernel#system takes and warns that it
does, which fails the spec worker, so the git fixtures and the tool
probes run through Open3 instead. Its Open3 hands a command straight to
ProcessBuilder, which neither finds ruby.bat or bundle.bat nor raises
Errno::ENOENT for a missing program, so the specs start Ruby through
RbConfig.ruby and the tool probes rescue what it raises. It also builds
a child's environment from the one the JVM started with, so the parallel
runner's variables the spec helper deletes from ENV still reached every
child that ran SimpleCov, which then took itself for a parallel worker
and left the report to a sibling that never came. Those children now
get the variables explicitly unset. And a double quote inside an
argument reaches the child unescaped there, which broke every -e script
that quoted a string, so those scripts go in on stdin instead.

A same-process flock probe cannot observe a JVM-wide FileChannel lock,
File.mkfifo raises NotImplementedError, and a filename that starts with
a pipe raises ENOENT rather than EINVAL, so the specs allow for each.
The one ParallelResultMerger example that waits on a pid runs only where
fork does. The watch specs wait as long for a stopped watcher as for
anything else on JRuby, since a watcher still inside its Dir.chdir block
kept the next one from starting. And parallel_tests serializes worker
output under an exclusive flock on a read-only handle, which JRuby on
Windows refuses with NonWritableChannelException, so the spec task
leaves out --serialize-stdout there and lets the output interleave.

That interleaved output is buffered, so when one worker stalled until
the job's time limit, nothing said where. On JRuby on Windows an example
that runs past three minutes now fails, after printing every thread's
backtrace, so a stall costs minutes rather than the job and names itself.
The one socket read in the watch specs that could wait forever is bounded
too.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1299.

Resolve paths and wait on runners correctly on JRuby on Windows

The JRuby on Windows CI job found two CLI bugs there.

simplecov affected --run crashed with NoMethodError, because
Process.wait2 answers a nil status on JRuby on Windows. The runner now
starts through Kernel#system inside Dir.chdir on that platform, since
system ignores its chdir option there but does report the status. Every
other platform keeps spawn and Process.wait2. The runner there still
receives a double quote inside an argument unescaped, as everything
JRuby starts on Windows does, so the specs quote with single quotes.

JRuby on Windows also follows no symlinks in File.realpath, and its
File.realdirpath accepts a parent directory that does not exist.
simplecov serve relies on realpath to refuse a symlink inside the report
that points outside it, so it would have served that file, and clean and
the coverage.json lookup compare resolved paths too. On JRuby all three
now resolve paths through the JDK's Path#toRealPath, after expanding
them against Dir.pwd, which the JVM's own working directory does not
follow.

Stop leaking a flush thread in the forked-child production specs

inherit_measurement started a real flush thread for the simulated parent
and then cleared @running without waking or joining it. On slow runners
(JRuby on Windows) that thread reached flush_loop only after the second
start had swapped in a fresh mutex and condition variable, so both
threads waited on the same one. reset! signals once, which woke only one
of them, and joining the other ran into the 180s watchdog.

A forked child inherits no flush thread, so the simulated parent now
starts without one and only the child's start spawns a real thread.

Format a result collected before exit on Rails 8.1.4

Rails 8.1.4 changed ActiveSupport::Testing::Parallelization#shutdown to
run the parallelize_teardown hooks in the parent process too, after the
workers have exited. Suites that call SimpleCov.result from that hook,
a long-standing pattern for parallel Rails tests, now collect the result
in the parent before the suite ends. SimpleCov.result calls
Coverage.result, which stops Coverage, and at_exit_behavior bailed out
whenever Coverage was no longer running, so the collected result was
never formatted and no HTML report was written.

The exit handler now also proceeds when this process already holds a
SimpleCov result. A test that stopped Coverage by calling Coverage.result
directly leaves no SimpleCov result behind, so that case still skips the
exit tasks.

Resolves https://github.com/simplecov-ruby/simplecov/issues/1308.
